self: You, an Athenian, as your fellow citizens resolve to abandon the city and fight on the sea for Greece's freedom, propose they stay at home and open the gates to the Persian king, thinking it expedient.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero
source_quote: a man named Cyrsilus proposed that they should stay at home and open the gates of their city to Xerxes
source_reason: he was working for what he thought was expediency
source_lesson: And yet he was working for what he thought was expediency; but it was not — not at all, for it clashed with moral rectitude.
source_verdict: And yet he was working for what he thought was expediency; but it was not — not at all, for it clashed with moral rectitude.
stoic_judgement: propose they stay at home and open the gates to the Persian king, thinking it expedient
stoic_reason: Under R1 and R2, he acts from the judgement that externals are goods worth the city's freedom and its faith to Greece: safety, property, staying at home. In his role as a citizen (R6, Discourses 2.10) that judgement is wrong, though sincerely held (Handbook 42). He is the man of Discourses 1.4 who, shunning what is not up to him, 'must end by subordinating himself' to whoever can grant or withhold it, here Xerxes.

other: You see a Roman magistrate debar foreigners from enjoying the advantages of the city and exclude them from its borders.
self: You, a Roman magistrate, debar foreigners from enjoying the advantages of the city and exclude them from its borders.
contested_note: Cicero, writing as an Academic following Panaetius, calls the act wrong and 'contrary to the laws of humanity'. R9 says his verdict is not by itself a Stoic verdict. Epictetus's framing does not settle this case, because he judges the judgement behind the act and none is shown. Cicero also grants that non-citizens may rightly be denied the rights of citizenship, so a magistrate acting from duty to the law could be acting well in his role.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, giving historical examples in his treatise of moral advice (addressed to his son)
source_quote: would debar foreigners from enjoying the advantages of their city and would exclude them from its borders
source_lesson: Still, to debar foreigners from enjoying the advantages of the city is altogether contrary to the laws of humanity.
source_verdict: They, too, do wrong who would debar foreigners from enjoying the advantages of their city and would exclude them from its borders
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: The vignette shows only the outward act. Under Discourses 4.8 and Handbook 45 (R1), we cannot praise or blame it until we know the judgement it comes from. A magistrate may be enforcing the law in his role (R6), or he may hold that the city's advantage, an external, is a good to be kept from others. Neutral is ruled out because unknown judgement is not neutral (R7). Vice is a provisional label: barring people from the city's advantages is the kind of act reason forbids under justice's 'apportioning of what is due' and 'good fellowship', but the vignette does not show the assent that would settle it.

self: You depose your colleague from the consular office, a man who had helped you drive out the royal family, because the leading men had determined every reminder of the monarchy be obliterated, to serve the country's interests.
contested_note: Cicero, writing as an Academic, judges the deposition pre-eminently right, and his praise is not by itself a Stoic verdict (R9). Epictetus's framing settles that the motive (the country's good, in the consul's role) is sound. It does not settle whether removing a faithful associate, for his name alone, is fair dealing towards him. Cicero himself grants it 'might have been thought unjust'.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero
source_quote: deposed his colleague Collatinus from the consular office
source_reason: to serve the country's interests
source_lesson: And so expediency gained the day because of its moral rightness; for without moral rectitude there could have been no possible expediency.
source_verdict: the course that was expedient — namely, to serve the country's interests — was so pre-eminently right, that it was even Collatinus's own duty to acquiesce in its justice
stoic_judgement: because the leading men had determined every reminder of the monarchy be obliterated, to serve the country's interests
stoic_reason: The consul acts from the judgement that his role requires him to serve his country, not from a wish for power or office. Office is not up to us, so Collatinus loses an external, not a good, and the act proceeds from a correct judgement in role (R1, R6; DL 7.108 counts disregarding the country's interests as contrary to duty). Read this way it is acting well as a person making progress (R5), with justice most at stake (R8).

self: You, the king who founded the city, slay your brother, because you have decided that it is more expedient for you to reign alone than to share the throne with another.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, addressing his son Cicero (the addressee of the book)
source_quote: when he decided that it was more expedient for him to reign alone than to share the throne with another, he slew his brother. He threw to the winds his brotherly affection and his human feelings, to secure what seemed to him — but was not — expedient
source_reason: it was the specious appearance of expediency that actuated him; and when he decided that it was more expedient for him to reign alone than to share the throne with another
source_lesson: And yet we are not required to sacrifice our own interest and surrender to others what we need for ourselves, but each one should consider his own interests, as far as he may without injury to his neighbour’s.
source_verdict: He committed a crime, therefore, with due respect to him let me say so, be he Quirinus or Romulus.
stoic_judgement: he has decided that it is more expedient for him to reign alone than to share the throne with another
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a bad judgement (R1, Discourses 4.8): he treats sole rule, an office not under his control (Handbook 1), as a good worth more than his own moral purpose, and so craves the throne rather than being free (Handbook 19). He violates what the role of brother asks (R6, Discourses 2.10, Handbook 30) and kills to get it, which reason forbids (DL 7.108). Justice, the apportioning of what is due, with kindness and good fellowship, is the virtue most failed (R8).

other: You see a wise man who is starving to death take the bread of some perfectly useless member of society, merely for his own benefit.
self: You are a wise man starving to death, and you take the bread of some perfectly useless member of society, merely for your own benefit.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, answering a question he puts in the mouth of a hypothetical objector ('someone may say')
source_quote: suppose a wise man were starving to death, might he not take the bread of some perfectly useless member of society?
source_reason: merely for one's own benefit
source_lesson: We are not to say, therefore, that sickness or want or any evil of that sort is more repugnant to Nature than to covet and to appropriate what is one's neighbour's; but we do maintain that disregard of the common interests is repugnant to Nature; for it is unjust.
source_verdict: Not at all; for my life is not more precious to me than that temper of soul which would keep me from doing wrong to anybody for my own advantage. ... For, if merely for one's own benefit one were to take something away from a man, though he were a perfectly worthless fellow, it would be an act of meanness and contrary to Nature's law. But suppose one would be able, by remaining alive, to render signal service to the state and to human society — if from that motive one should take something from another, it would not be a matter for censure. ... And therefore Nature's law itself, which protects and conserves human interests, will surely determine that a man who is wise, good, and brave, should in emergency have the necessaries of life transferred to him from a person who is idle and worthless; for the good man's death would be a heavy loss to the common weal; only let him beware that self-esteem and self-love do not find in such a transfer of possessions a pretext for wrong-doing.
stoic_judgement: merely for his own benefit
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement behind the act (R1): he treats his own life, a preferred indifferent that is not up to him, as worth more than not wronging another for his own gain. That is a bad use of impressions and a loss of his own moral purpose (Discourses 1.29, 1.18), so taking the bread is acting badly against justice, the apportioning of what is due (Arius 5b2, R8), whatever the worth of the man he robs.

source_quote: at the instance of Aristides they rejected the whole proposition without even listening to it
source_reason: the Athenians concluded that what was not morally right was likewise not expedient
source_lesson: Let it be set down as an established principle, then, that what is morally wrong can never be expedient — not even when one secures by means of it that which one thinks expedient; for the mere act of thinking a course expedient, when it is morally wrong, is demoralizing.
source_verdict: Their attitude was better than ours; for we let pirates go scot free, while we make our allies pay tribute.
stoic_judgement: reported as highly expedient but not morally right, concluding what is not morally right is not expedient
stoic_reason: The rejection comes from a correct judgement: crushing Sparta's power is an external and no true good, while the wrong itself would harm their moral purpose (Discourses 1.29). An act that proceeds from correct judgements is well done (R1, Discourses 4.8). Refusing a treacherous attack on Greek partners is fair dealing, so justice is the main virtue (R8). Seeing that the wrong cannot be truly expedient is wisdom (R5, R8).

self: You, a statesman kept by armed treason from politics and the bar, turn your forced leisure and solitude to account, having learned that among evils one should extract any good they contain.
contested_note: The maxim he acts from calls his circumstances 'evils', which Epictetus denies (Handbook 5; Discourses 1.29). The source passage also shows Cicero regretting his lot and admitting he lacks the 'strength of mind' to forget his solitude, which would suggest a passion assented to (R2). Epictetus's framing praises making good use of externals but faults judging them evils. Cicero, writing as an Academic, approves his own conduct, though he ranks Africanus higher (R9).
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)

speaker: Cicero, writing to his son Marcus
source_quote: I am turning my leisure to account — though it is not such repose as the man should be entitled to who once brought the state repose from civil strife — and I am not letting this solitude, which necessity and not my will imposes on me, find me idle.
source_reason: But I have learned from philosophers that among evils one ought not only to choose the least, but also to extract even from these any element of good that they may contain.
source_lesson: But I have learned from philosophers that among evils one ought not only to choose the least, but also to extract even from these any element of good that they may contain.

stoic_judgement: turning his forced leisure and solitude to account, having learned that among evils one should extract any good they contain
stoic_reason: Exclusion from office and the forum is not up to him; it is material for his moral purpose (Discourses 1.29), and he uses it well by acting from a judgement about what to do with it (R1, R5). Calling it among 'evils' is loose, non-Stoic wording for a rejected indifferent, but the vignette shows no assented grief or anxiety (R2), so his use of circumstances counts as acting well.

other: You see a vendor who knows his house is unsanitary, vermin-ridden and built of unsound timber keep these facts from the purchaser for his own profit, selling it for far more than it is worth.
self: You know your house is unsanitary, vermin-ridden and built of unsound timber, and you keep these facts from the purchaser for your own profit, selling it for far more than it is worth.
contested_note: The Stoics disagree. Antipater holds that withholding the defects is unjust, since it deliberately leads the buyer astray. Diogenes of Babylon holds that a vendor who says nothing, and does not praise the house, commits no fraud, because the buyer uses his own judgement. Epictetus gives no rule on disclosure in a sale (R9, L5 Q41). His framing condemns deceit for profit, but on its own it does not settle whether mere silence is deceit. The label follows the vignette's 'for his own profit' and Epictetus's judgement-centred framing. Cicero, writing as an Academic, sides with Antipater.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, posing the case and deciding between the arguments of Antipater and Diogenes
source_quote: the vendor does not tell the purchaser these facts but sells him the house for far more than he could reasonably have expected to get for it
source_reason: trying for your own profit to keep others from finding out something that you know, when it is for their interest to know it
source_lesson: I think, then, that it was the duty of that grain-dealer not to keep back the facts from the Rhodians, and of this vendor of the house to deal in the same way with his purchaser.
source_verdict: And who fails to discern what manner of concealment that is and what sort of person would be guilty of it? At all events he would be no candid or sincere or straightforward or upright or honest man, but rather one who is shifty, sly, artful, shrewd, underhand, cunning, one grown old in fraud and subtlety.
stoic_judgement: keep these facts from the purchaser for his own profit, selling it for far more than it is worth
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement behind the act (R1): he treats profit, which is not up to him and not a good, as worth more than dealing fairly with his neighbour. A man who uses another's ignorance of a house that may collapse in order to gain money has made a wrong use of impressions, and this is the deceit for profit that Handbook 52 counts as acting badly. The failed virtue is justice, in its part of fair dealing (R8).

self: You, a shepherd of the king made invisible by turning a gold ring, murder your royal master with the queen's assistance, without anyone's being able to detect you.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, citing Plato
source_quote: And so, with the advantage which the ring gave him, he debauched the queen, and with her assistance he murdered his royal master and removed all those who he thought stood in his way, without anyone’s being able to detect him in his crimes. Thus, by virtue of the ring, he shortly rose to be king of Lydia.
source_lesson: Now, suppose a wise man had just such a ring, he would not imagine that he was free to do wrongly any more than if he did not have it; for good men aim to secure not secrecy but the right.
source_verdict: without anyone’s being able to detect him in his crimes
stoic_judgement: made invisible by turning a gold ring, murder his royal master ... without anyone's being able to detect him
stoic_reason: Murdering the master he serves, by stealth and with the queen's help, is an act 'reason deprecates' against his role as the king's shepherd (R6, DL 7.108). His reliance on invisibility shows that he treats escaping detection as what matters, not the right (R1). That is a moral purpose corrupted for externals such as power or the queen, which Epictetus places in bad judgement, so it is a vice against justice (R2, R8).

other: You see a leading Roman citizen, named joint-heir by forgers in a will he suspects is forged, accept the legacy meant for the dead man's nephew, being conscious of no personal guilt.
self: You, a leading Roman citizen named joint-heir by forgers in a will you suspect is forged, accept the legacy meant for the dead man's nephew, being conscious of no personal guilt.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, arguing in his own voice in On Duties Book III
source_quote: Although these men suspected that the will was a forgery, still, as they were conscious of no personal guilt in the matter, they did not spurn the miserable boon procured through the crime of others.
source_reason: as they were conscious of no personal guilt in the matter
source_lesson: For if he does wrong who does not ward off and repel injury when he can — as I explained in the course of the First Book — what is to be thought of the man who not only does not try to prevent wrong, but actually aids and abets it?
source_verdict: Is this excuse competent to acquit them of guilt? I cannot think so, although I loved the one while he lived, and do not hate the other now that he is dead.
stoic_judgement: named joint-heir by forgers in a will he suspects is forged, accept the legacy ... being conscious of no personal guilt
stoic_reason: Under R1, R2 and R9, he treats property, which is not up to him, as a good worth taking even from a suspected crime. He excuses himself because he did not forge the will himself, though the error lies in his own choice to accept (Discourses 1.29; Handbook 52, 'ready with the arguments'). Taking what is due to another is a failure of justice, the apportioning of what is due.

source_quote: There before the Roman People he accused his own general, an eminent man and one of our first citizens, of purposely protracting the war
source_reason: declared that if they would make him consul, he would within a short time deliver Jugurtha alive or dead into the hands of the Roman People
source_lesson: But for all cases we have one rule, with which I desire you to be perfectly familiar: that which seems expedient must not be morally wrong; or, if it is morally wrong, it must not seem expedient.

other: You see a man who asked the vendor of a farm to name his price definitely reply that he considers it worth more, and pay him 100,000 sesterces over and above what he asked.
self: You asked the vendor of a farm to name his price definitely, and you reply that you consider it worth more and pay him 100,000 sesterces over and above what he asked.
contested_note: The Stoics disagree. Hecaton of Rhodes, a pupil of Panaetius, could not approve of the act, since he holds a wise man should look after his private interests and abstain only from what the law forbids. Cicero, an Academic following Panaetius on good faith, calls it the act of an honest man; his praise is not by itself a Stoic verdict (R9). Epictetus gives no rule on paying more than the asking price (cf. R9, L5 Q41). His framing settles the case only if the motive is fairness and not display.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, in his philosophical treatise (later citing Hecaton's contrary opinion of the act)
source_quote: he replied that he considered it worth more, and paid him 100,000 sesterces over and above what he asked
source_reason: he replied that he considered it worth more
source_lesson: Here, then, is that mischievous idea — the world accounting some men upright, others wise; and it is this fact that gives Ennius occasion to say:
source_verdict: No one could say that this was not the act of an honest man; but people do say that it was not the act of a worldly-wise man, any more than if he had sold for a smaller amount than he could have commanded.
stoic_judgement: reply that he considers it worth more
stoic_reason: Under R1 his stated judgement is that the farm is worth more than the asking price. He treats money, which is not up to us (Handbook 1), as material for his moral purpose (Discourses 1.29), and he prefers fair dealing to gain. That reads as acting well from a correct judgement, labelled virtue as one making progress (R5). The virtue is justice, as fair dealing and good faith (R8).

other: You see a banker of Syracuse ask the fishermen to do their fishing in front of his villa, then tell a Roman knight seeking a country seat, "this is where all the fish in Syracuse are."
self: You, a banker of Syracuse, ask the fishermen to do their fishing in front of your villa, then tell a Roman knight seeking a country seat, "this is where all the fish in Syracuse are."
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero
source_quote: When this fact was spread abroad, one Pythius, a banker of Syracuse, informed him that he had such an estate; that it was not for sale, however, but Canius might make himself at home there, if he pleased; and at the same time he invited him to the estate to dinner next day. Canius accepted. Then Pythius, who, as might be expected of a moneylender, could command favours of all classes, called the fishermen together and asked them to do their fishing the next day out in front of his villa, and told them what he wished them to do. ... "No wonder," answered Pythius; "this is where all the fish in Syracuse are; here is where the fresh water comes from; the fishermen cannot get along without this estate." ... Inflamed with desire for it, Canius insisted upon Pythius's selling it to him. At first he demurred. To make a long story short, Canius gained his point. The man was rich, and, in his desire to own the country seat, he paid for it all that Pythius asked; and he bought the entire equipment, too. Pythius entered the amount upon his ledger and completed the transfer.
source_lesson: No act of theirs can be expedient, when what they do is tainted with so many vices.
source_verdict: Pythius, therefore, and all others who do one thing while they pretend another are faithless, dishonest, and unprincipled scoundrels.
stoic_judgement: ask the fishermen to do their fishing in front of his villa, then tell a Roman knight seeking a country seat, "this is where all the fish in Syracuse are."
stoic_reason: He stages a false appearance and then states a falsehood to a man he knows wants an estate. That is a deliberate lie, not mere silence, and it proceeds from the bad judgement that an external gain is worth more than good faith (R1, Handbook 52, Discourses 1.29). Deceiving a neighbour in a dealing fails justice, whose foundation is truth and fair dealing (R8, Cicero De Officiis 1.23). Self-restraint also fails, since his craving for an external drives the act.

other: You see a house owner, ordered by state religious officials to pull down the tall parts of his building, at once advertise it for sale and sell it without making the order known.
self: You, a house owner ordered by state religious officials to pull down the tall parts of your building, at once advertise it for sale and sell it without making the order known.
contested_note: Epictetus gives no rule on disclosure in a sale, and silence alone is not settled (R9, L5 Q41). In De Officiis 3.51, Diogenes of Babylon requires a seller to declare only the defects the civil law requires, while Antipater requires full disclosure. Here the civil law, as Cicero reports it, did require declaring known defects, so both would likely condemn the act. The source, Cato as reported by Cicero, a non-Stoic, also condemns it. The case is still flagged because Epictetus's framing settles it only through the inferred motive.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, citing the verdict of Marcus Cato
source_quote: Claudius at once advertised his block for sale, and Publius Calpurnius Lanarius bought it. ... since the augurs' mandate was known to the vendor at the time of making the transfer and since he had not made it known
source_lesson: With this verdict he established the principle that it was essential to good faith that any defect known to the vendor must be made known to the purchaser.
source_verdict: since the augurs' mandate was known to the vendor at the time of making the transfer and since he had not made it known, he was bound to make good the purchaser's loss.
modernised: [{"source": "the augurs", "vignette": "state religious officials", "why": "A reader today might take 'augurs' for private fortune-tellers and miss that their order bound the owner and lowered the house's value."}]
stoic_judgement: "at once advertise it for sale and sell it without making the order known": he sells straight after the order and hides it. This implies he treats keeping his property's value, an external not up to him, as a good worth getting by shifting a loss he knows of onto a buyer who does not know it.
stoic_reason: The judgement is inferred from the timing (R1). Selling at once to escape the order, and keeping silent about a defect he knows, treats property as the good and the buyer's loss as nothing. That is deceit for profit, an act from a bad judgement (Handbook 52; Discourses 1.29, 4.8), and a failure of justice and good faith (Arius 5b2; Cicero De Officiis 1.23; R8). Under R9, the label follows Epictetus's framing, but the silence question is flagged as contested.

other: You see a grain-dealer in famine-struck Rhodes who sighted other vessels laden with grain bound there keep his own counsel and sell at the highest market price, his price no higher than his competitors'.
self: You, a grain-dealer in famine-struck Rhodes who sighted other vessels laden with grain bound there, keep your own counsel and sell at the highest market price, your price no higher than your competitors'.
contested_note: The Stoics disagree. Antipater holds that all facts must be disclosed, so silence is wrong. Diogenes of Babylon holds that the seller need declare only what law requires and may sell to best advantage without misrepresentation, so this act is permissible. Cicero, writing as an Academic, sides with Antipater: concealing for profit is dishonest. Epictetus gives no sale-specific disclosure rule (L5, Q41). His framing condemns acting from the judgement that profit is a good, but silence alone is not settled by his texts. The 'vice' label rests on an inferred profit motive.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, posing a dilemma and staging the opposing arguments of the Stoics Diogenes of Babylonia and Antipater before deciding the case himself
source_quote: is he to report the fact to the Rhodians or is he to keep his own counsel and sell his own stock at the highest market price?
source_reason: "I have offered it for sale; I sell at a price no higher than my competitors — perhaps even lower, when the market is overstocked. Who is wronged?"
source_lesson: The fact is that merely holding one's peace about a thing does not constitute concealment, but concealment consists in trying for your own profit to keep others from finding out something that you know, when it is for their interest to know it.
source_verdict: I think, then, that it was the duty of that grain-dealer not to keep back the facts from the Rhodians
stoic_judgement: not shown: the vignette gives the outward act (he 'keep[s] his own counsel and sell[s] at the highest market price, his price no higher than his competitors'') but not what he takes to be good. Cicero, writing as an Academic, presents this with approval. Epictetus never addresses the case. His Handbook 30 tells the son to give way to his father in all things, while his role-ethics (Discourses 2.10) and his refusal to obey in a shameful act (Discourses 4.1) point toward the citizen's duty. His framing therefore does not clearly settle whether the son's role permits killing or betraying his father, as opposed to refusing complicity.

As a father he owes his son care, and wishing his death is the plain opposite of what that role asks (R6, DL 7.108 'to neglect one's parents' as the type of unbefitting act).

self: You, a paroled prisoner of war sworn to return to the enemy camp, go back on the pretext of forgetting something, then remain behind at Rome, explaining that your return released you from your oath.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, citing Polybius
source_quote: one of the ten, who, a little while after leaving the camp, had gone back on the pretext that he had forgotten something or other, remained behind at Rome
source_reason: he explained that by his return to the camp he was released from the obligation of his oath
source_lesson: He was wrong; for deceit does not remove the guilt of perjury — it merely aggravates it.
source_verdict: He was wrong; for deceit does not remove the guilt of perjury — it merely aggravates it. His cunning that impudently tried to masquerade as prudence was, therefore, only folly. And so the senate ordered that the cunning scoundrel should be taken back to Hannibal in chains.
stoic_judgement: go back on the pretext of forgetting something, then remain behind at Rome, explaining that his return released him from his oath
stoic_reason: The word 'pretext' shows a contrived return, so his explanation is an argument made to excuse breaking his oath, not a sincere mistake. Epictetus says 'we lie, indeed, but are ready with the arguments' (Handbook 52). He chooses an external, staying safe at Rome rather than captive, over keeping faith, and the act proceeds from a bad judgement (R1, Discourses 4.8). Good faith belongs to justice (R8, De Officiis 1.23).

other: You see a man say he does not in general agree with the philosopher Antisthenes and, when shown Antisthenes's essay on Sophocles and asked if it has any excellence, reply that he does not know.
self: You say you do not in general agree with the philosopher Antisthenes and, when shown Antisthenes's essay on Sophocles and asked if it has any excellence, you reply that you do not know.
contested_note: From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as virtue: Under R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45), until we learn the judgement behind 'I do not know' we can neither praise nor blame it. It may be an honest withholding of assent, which is the third field and acting well (wisdom). It may equally be a partisan refusal to grant an opponent any merit, which would be a vice. The label 'virtue' is provisional only, and R7 forbids defaulting to 'neutral'.

source_verdict: "Then are you not ashamed," quoth he, "to pick out and mention anything wrong said by Antisthenes, while you suppress his good things without giving them a thought?"
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: Under R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45) the vignette must show the judgement he speaks from. Read most plainly, he assents to a general verdict against Antisthenes while admitting he cannot say whether a work of his has any excellence. That is rashness in assent, the third field of Discourses 3.2, and an unfair dealing with his neighbour's merits, so it is labelled vice. But his 'I do not know' could also be an honest suspension of assent, so the label rests on our reading of the vignette, not on a fact it states.

Coercing another by terror is a failure of fair dealing, so the vice is against justice (R8).

The source says the pupil was 'so unwelcome' and that he finally went away, which suggests Zeno meant to be rid of him rather than to teach him. Driving him off in contempt would not show the teacher's role well done. Diogenes Laertius reports the act approvingly but writes as a reporter, so his approval is not by itself a Stoic verdict (R9).

stoic_reason: Under R1 and R6, the vignette shows the teacher acting from a judgement that arrogance is a fault and that a fine cloak and rank among beggars are indifferents. Teaching a pupil that these externals are not his good fits the teacher's role, so read this way it is acting well while making progress (R5). Under R8 it is nearest to temperance, the virtue that opposes vanity and arrogance.

stoic_reason: His reply shows that he values restraint in speech, which is his own doing, over making a display to win the king's notice, which is not up to him (Discourses 2.13, the singer who wants applause). His silence therefore proceeds from a correct judgement and is well done (R1, R5); restraint of the urge to show off is temperance, which here involves propriety and modesty (R8).

source_verdict: "I see," said he, "the imprints of your anger."
stoic_judgement: "I see the imprints of your anger." He reads the weals as the mark of the acquaintance's anger, a fault of moral purpose, rather than as a deserved punishment or the slave's own fault.
stoic_reason: Under R1, his words show the judgement he acts from: what is bad here is the master's assented passion (Handbook 5, 20; Discourses 1.18), not anything outside the master's control. Saying so plainly to an acquaintance is the frank correction that suits a philosopher's role (R6), so it is acting well as one making progress (R5).

He bears poverty and toil, which are externals not up to him, as materials for that purpose, and he works for his living without complaint. This is the man making progress of Discourses 1.4, and so acting well (R5). Taking up the endurance of hardship and industriousness is nearest to courage (Arius 5b2; R8).

contested_note: Diogenes Laertius praises the act, but he reports rather than judges as a Stoic (R9). Epictetus's framing does not settle the case. Dialectic belongs to the third field, assent, and Handbook 52 warns that we are 'ready with the arguments' while neglecting practice. On that reading, eagerness for clever sophisms could be display or a misplaced priority. If instead the learning is for the correct use of impressions, it is acting well.

source_quote: Being told a hundred drachmas, he promptly paid two hundred

stoic_judgement: promptly pay him two hundred in his love of learning
stoic_reason: R1: the vignette shows the motive. He treats money, which is not up to us and is only material for the moral purpose (Discourses 1.29), as worth less than training his judgement, and he pays more than was asked. That is acting well in one making progress (R5), nearest to wisdom. Whether the learning serves his moral purpose or mere skill with sophisms is not shown, so per R9 the source's praise does not settle it.

source_quote: He would often find fault with himself too ... he, laughing, said, "An old man with grey hairs and no wits."

stoic_judgement: finding fault with himself ... he laughs and says, "An old man with grey hairs and no wits."
stoic_reason: He puts the blame on his own judgement ('no wits'), the one thing up to him, and not on externals, as one making progress does (Discourses 1.4, 1.11; Handbook 1). His laughter shows the self-reproach is calm correction, not an assented passion of distress (R1, R2, R4, R5).

stoic_reason: The vignette shows his judgement: the poet's abuse is not an evil worth anger. That is the judgement Handbook 20 asks for, that it is not the reviler who insults you but your own judgement. By R1 and R2 he refuses assent to the passion of anger, and by R8 restraining anger is mainly temperance. Accepting the apology also gives the poet his due, as kindness and good fellowship (justice).

He answers with good humour rather than anger, turning the insult into a statement of his commitment to the work. The judgement is shown (R1), and it is acting well as one making progress (R5). The virtue is endurance under abuse, which is courage, with restraint of anger and a right view of what is up to him (R8).

stoic_reason: R1 and Handbook 45: he will not join in blame without knowing the judgement behind the man's acts. He looks to the deeds, which keep to duty, rather than to the words, which deny it, and so gives the other philosopher his due. This is an appropriate act done for a stated, sound reason, acting well as one making progress (R5).

He holds to health and the power to read and write as things naturally preferred, without craving them (Discourses 2.10). The act proceeds from correct judgements, so it is well done (Discourses 4.8; R1, R2, R5).

contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle the case because the judgement is not shown. Declining the court could come from indifference to externals and a preference for duty to kin, or from arrogance. The source's author (Diogenes Laertius, via Demetrius) frames the anecdote with 'He appears to have been a very arrogant man', which differs from the provisional 'virtue' label.

stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: The vignette shows only outward acts: declining a king's summons and educating his sister's sons. It gives no motive, so it does not show whether he spurned the court from right judgement (office and royal favour are not up to us) or from pride. Under R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45) we may neither praise nor blame until we know the judgement. The 'virtue' label is provisional: it rests only on the acts being appropriate to his role as kinsman (R6, Discourses 2.10), and R1 says not to default to 'neutral'.
also_in: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020)

Refusing to let appetite for luxury rule him is acting from a correct judgement (R1, Discourses 4.8), and restraint of appetite is temperance (R8, Arius 5b2). As one making progress, not a sage, his act counts as 'virtue' (R5).

stoic_judgement: answer with a smile, "Neither does he lend."
stoic_reason: Reproached by a hypocrite, he answers calmly and smiling. That reads as not judging the reproach an insult (Handbook 20) and not treating another's opinion of him as a good he must have, so no anger is assented to (R2). Under R1 this is only inferred from his outward manner, so 'virtue' rests on reading the smile as calm; restraint of anger falls under temperance (R8), with the wisdom of seeing that the reproach does not touch what is up to him.

self: You are buying goods from a seller who thinks he is selling brass when it is actually gold, and instead of buying for one shilling what is worth a thousand, you inform him that his stuff is gold.
contested_note: Cicero reports this as one of the disclosure questions disputed between Diogenes of Babylon and Antipater. On the parallel questions about spoiling wine and slaves' faults, Diogenes holds disclosure is not required and Antipater holds an honest man would disclose; Cicero sides with Antipater. Epictetus condemns deceit for profit (Handbook 52), but the checked sources contain no ruling from him on whether silence in a sale is wrong (R9). Disclosure is therefore praised on Antipater's and Cicero's view but not required on Diogenes'.

source_lesson: With this I think I have said enough about those actions which masquerade as expedient under the guise of prudence, while they are really contrary to justice.

stoic_judgement: "instead of buying for one shilling what is worth a thousand, he informs him that his stuff is gold". This only implies a judgement: that a fair deal matters more than the gain. The vignette states no motive.
stoic_reason: The profit is an external, not up to him. The fair treatment of his neighbour is his own moral purpose (Discourses 1.29). Giving up a thousandfold gain to tell the truth reads as an act that proceeds from the judgement that fair dealing is the good and the gain is not (R1, R5). It belongs under justice as fair dealing and good faith (R8, Arius 5b2; Cicero De Officiis 1.23). R1 warns that the motive should be shown before we praise, and R9 marks disclosure-in-sale cases as unsettled.

Comfort in words is allowed (Handbook 16), but he goes past it: in the role of a philosopher (R6) he takes away the one real good, a right moral purpose that sees the murder as the king's own wrong (Discourses 1.18, 1.29), and so encourages more such acts.

The sacrifice itself is not the fault; the fault is the judgement that his private occasion outweighs what he owes the city.

other: You see the Persian king, who believes everyone is his slave except his wife, assign one of his attendants to come to him at dawn and say, “Arise, O king, and attend to the matters that the great Ahuramazda wants you to attend to.”
self: You are the Persian king, believing everyone is your slave except your wife, and you assign one of your attendants to come to you at dawn and say, “Arise, O king, and attend to the matters that the great Ahuramazda wants you to attend to.”
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle it, because the judgement shown and the act shown come apart. The belief that all are his slaves is a vice-making judgement. The deed of arranging a reminder of duty to the god is, as a type, appropriate (cf. Discourses 1.4, rising in the morning to observe what one has learned), and its motive is not shown. If it came from a real wish to do his duty, the act could be well done even while the belief about his subjects is wrong. Plutarch's point differs again: an external voice stands in for a Reason the king lacks within. | From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as virtue: The morning reminder treats his office as a charge from the god, which is the recollection of role that Discourses 2.10 asks for. It is also the morning practice of Discourses 1.4 ('when he rises in the morning he proceeds to keep and observe'). So, read through R6 and R5, the act leans toward acting well. Against this, the vignette also shows a false judgement: that other people are his slaves, though no one owns another's moral purpose (Handbook 1). R1 is therefore not cleanly met.

source_quote: Now, the Persian king assigned to one of his attendants this task: to come to him at dawn and to say, “Arise, O king, and attend to the matters that the great Ahuramazda wants you to attend to.”

source_lesson: But this voice is always present within educated and self-controlled leaders, speaking out and exhorting them.

stoic_reason: The one judgement the vignette shows is false. It treats rule as mastery over others, and others as his slaves, when a ruler's role is to be a guardian (Discourses 2.10; R6) and others are not his to possess (Handbook 1). So under R1 the person is acting from a bad judgement. The vignette gives no motive for the dawn reminder itself. Taken alone, being reminded of one's duty each morning could be an appropriate act of a person making progress (Discourses 1.4).

Yet Epictetus holds that they are only 'materials for the moral purpose' (Discourses 1.29), and that a king's role, like any role, is where his own good or evil is found (Discourses 2.10). Assenting to this impression, and feeling weighed down by it, is a faulty judgement and so acting badly (R1, R2, R6).

source_verdict: But for a man to use the appearances presented to him rashly and foolishly and carelessly, and not to understand argument, nor demonstration, nor sophism, nor, in a word, to see in questioning and answering what is consistent with that which we have granted or is not consistent; is there no error in this?
stoic_judgement: reply, "I suppose that I have burnt the Capitol."
stoic_reason: His retort shows the judgement that a careless assent in reasoning is no real fault, as if only great outward crimes like burning the Capitol counted. But the use of impressions is the one thing up to him (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.1), and error in assent is the fault proper to it (Discourses 3.2, third field). An act that proceeds from this bad judgement is badly done (R1, Discourses 4.8).
also_in: Musonius Rufus, Lectures / Fragments (ancient; translator uncredited in 2015 anthology)

other: You see a father whose little daughter is sick and supposed to be in danger leave home, because he cannot endure to stay with her, till a person sends news she has recovered.
self: You leave home when your little daughter is sick and supposed to be in danger, because you cannot endure to stay with her, till a person sends news she has recovered.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.11.1–4,20–26 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with a visiting magistrate
source_quote: lately, when my little daughter was sick and was supposed to be in danger, I could not endure to stay with her, but I left home till a person sent me news that she had recovered.
source_reason: I acted naturally, the man replied. ... This is the case, said the man, with all or at least most fathers.
source_lesson: And in a word, neither death nor exile nor pain nor anything of the kind is the cause of our doing anything or not doing; but our own opinions and our wills \(δόγματα\).
source_verdict: Well then to leave your sick child and to go away is not reasonable, and I suppose that you will not say that it is ... But if this is so, it results that your behaviour was not at all an affec- tionate act.
stoic_judgement: because he cannot endure to stay with her
stoic_reason: He acts from the judgement that his daughter's danger, which is not up to him, is an evil too dreadful to bear (R1, R2; Handbook 5). That passion is assented to and acted on: he stays away until news comes, so this is no first movement (R3). It leads him to abandon what his role as father asks (R6; Handbook 30, Discourses 2.10). Affection that is not consistent with reason is not 'right and good' (Discourses 1.11; R4), so he acts badly.

other: You see a once rich man of rank, stripped of all, hand back the submissive letter written to Rome for him: "I wished for your help, not your pity: no evil has happened to me."
self: You, once a rich man of rank and now stripped of all, hand back the submissive letter written to Rome for you: "I wished for your help, not your pity: no evil has happened to me."
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.9.27–28 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How from the fact that we are akin to God a man may proceed to the consequences.
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse, recounting an episode from his own experience
source_quote: when he had read the letter, he gave it back to me and said, "I wished for your help, not your pity: no evil has happened to me."
source_reason: no evil has happened to me
source_lesson: But if he were anything more, lie would know that one man is not miserable through the means of another.
source_verdict: But when a man is cowardly and mean, what else must be done for him than to write letters as you would about a corpse.
stoic_judgement: "I wished for your help, not your pity: no evil has happened to me."
stoic_reason: He holds that the loss of rank and wealth, which is not up to him, is no evil (Handbook 5, Discourses 1.29), so he will not be pitied or plead submissively. He still asks for help with things naturally preferred, as is fitting (Discourses 2.10). An act that proceeds from correct judgement is well done (R1, R5). Bearing hardship with greatness of soul is mainly courage, and seeing what is and is not his own is wisdom (R8).

other: You see an old man, back from exile and vowing to pass the rest of his life in quiet and tranquillity, receive letters from Caesar before entering Rome, forget all, and add one piece of business to another.
self: You, an old man back from exile who vowed to pass the rest of your life in quiet and tranquillity, receive letters from Caesar before entering Rome, forget all, and add one piece of business to another.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.10.2–6 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: *Against those who eagerly seek preferment at Rome.*
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students, recounting his own exchange with the man
source_quote: Before he entered the city, he was met by letters from Caesar, and as soon as he received them, he forgot all, and ever after has added one piece of business to another.
source_verdict: I wish that I were now by his side to remind him of what he said when he was passing this way, and to tell him how much better a seer I am than he is.
stoic_judgement: vowing to pass the rest of his life in quiet and tranquillity ... receive letters from Caesar before entering Rome, forget all, and add one piece of business to another
stoic_reason: He drops his own stated resolve the moment Caesar's favour is offered. This reads as craving office and preferment, things not up to him, so that he is 'tossed to and fro' with externals and subordinates himself to those who can grant them (Discourses 1.4; R1, R2). The fault is not activity as such but neglecting his own moral purpose for business about grain and profits, so the main virtue failed is temperance (restraint of ambition), with wisdom (seeing what is up to us) also failed (R8).

other: You see a man declaring, as his settled choice, that he would rather be killed to-day than banished to-morrow.
self: You declare, as your settled choice, that you would rather be killed to-day than banished to-morrow.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.1.26–27 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: Of the things which are in our power, and not in our power.
speaker: Epictetus, lecturing, citing Thrasea's maxim and Rufus's reply to him
source_quote: Thrasea used to say, I would rather be killed to-day than banished to-morrow.
source_lesson: This it is to have studied what a man ought to study; to have made desire, aversion, free from hindrance, and free from all that a man would avoid.
source_verdict: If you choose death as the heavier misfortune, how great is the folly of your choice? But if, as the lighter, who has given you the choice? Will you not study to be content with that which has been given to you?
stoic_judgement: declaring, as his settled choice, that he would rather be killed to-day than banished to-morrow
stoic_reason: He sets his desire and aversion on death and exile, which are not up to him, and ranks them as misfortunes to choose between (Handbook 1, Discourses 3.2). By Rufus's dilemma this is faulty whichever way he ranks them: either he chooses the heavier misfortune, or he wants a lot other than the one given. So it is assent to a false judgement about externals, not a first movement (R1, R2, R3).

other: You see a senator, commanded by the emperor not to go into the senate and told he will be put to death if he speaks, reply that so long as he is a member he must go in and say what he thinks right.
self: You, a senator commanded by the emperor not to go into the senate and told you will be put to death if you speak, reply that so long as you are a member you must go in and say what you think right.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.2.19–21 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How a man on every occasion can maintain his proper character.
speaker: Epictetus, lecturing (as recorded by Arrian)
source_quote: "It is in your power not to allow me to be a member of the senate, but so long as I am, I must go in." ... And I must say what I think right. ... When then did I tell you that I am immortal? You will do your part, and I will do mine: it is your part to kill; it is mine to die, but not in fear: yours to banish me; mine to depart without sorrow.
source_reason: "It is in your power not to allow me to be a member of the senate, but so long as I am, I must go in."
source_lesson: Why, what else than this, that it is conspicuous in the toga as purple, and is displayed also as a fine example to all other things?
source_verdict: Priscus Helvidius also saw this, and acted conformably. ... Why, what else than this, that it is conspicuous in the toga as purple, and is displayed also as a fine example to all other things?
stoic_judgement: reply that so long as he is a member he must go in and say what he thinks right
stoic_reason: His reply shows the judgement he acts from: his duty as a councillor (Discourses 2.10, R6) is up to him and outweighs death, which is not up to him and is not an evil (Handbook 1, 5). An act from correct judgements is well done (Discourses 4.8, R1), and enduring the threat of death for it is courage (R8). This is progress-level acting well (R5), not a sage's right act.
also_in: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020); source: Epictetus (exchange); Suetonius (opposition named at line 2809)

other: You see a teacher laughing at the young man he set to read hypothetical arguments, though he did not prepare him nor ascertain whether he was able to understand these matters.
self: You laugh at the young man you set to read hypothetical arguments, though you did not prepare him nor ascertain whether he was able to understand these matters.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.26.13 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: What is the law of life.
speaker: Epictetus, speaking to the teacher who had arranged a young man's reading of hypothetical arguments
source_quote: the teacher who had suggested the reading was laughing at the reader
source_lesson: This then is the beginning of philosophy, a man's perception of the state of his ruling faculty; for when a man knows that it is weak, then he will not employ it on things of the greatest difficulty.
source_verdict: You are laughing at yourself: you did not prepare the young man nor did you ascertain whether he was able to understand these matters; but perhaps, you are only employing him as a reader.
stoic_judgement: laughing at the young man he set to read hypothetical arguments, though he did not prepare him nor ascertain whether he was able to understand these matters
stoic_reason: As teacher, his role (R6; Discourses 2.10) asked him to prepare the student and test his ability. He omitted this appropriate act, which is a wrong act by omission (Arius 11a). His mockery then treats the failure as the young man's, when it was his own doing, so he misjudges what is his. As Epictetus says, he is 'laughing at himself' (R1, R6).

other: You see a very rich man embracing the knees of a wealthy man, complaining that he has only one and a half million denarii, a vast fortune, remaining.
self: You embrace the knees of a wealthy man, complaining that you have only one and a half million denarii, a vast fortune, remaining.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.26.11–12 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: What is the law of life.
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students
source_quote: complained, as he embraced the knees of Epaphroditus, that he had only one hundred and fifty times ten thousand denarii remaining
source_reason: that he had only one hundred and fifty times ten thousand denarii remaining.
source_lesson: This is the reason why it is difficult for a man to be master of the appearances, where the things which disturb the judgment are great.
source_verdict: This is the reason why it is difficult for a man to be master of the appearances, where the things which disturb the judgment are great.
modernised: [{"source": "one hundred and fifty times ten thousand denarii", "vignette": "one and a half million denarii, a vast fortune", "why": "Readers today don't know what a denarius was worth and could take the sum for modest savings, missing that the complainer still has enormous wealth."}]
stoic_judgement: embracing the knees of a wealthy man, complaining that he has only one and a half million denarii, a vast fortune, remaining
stoic_reason: He grieves over property, which is not under our control (Handbook 1). By supplicating another man about it, he assents to the impression that its loss is an evil, so this is an assented passion and acting badly even with no further deed (R2; Handbook 5, Discourses 2.13). He has failed to be master of the appearances, in the field of desire and aversion (Discourses 3.2).

other: You see a man find his iron lamp carried off and say he will find an earthen lamp tomorrow, reflecting that the thief did nothing strange, for a man only loses that which he has.
self: You find your iron lamp carried off and say you will find an earthen lamp tomorrow, reflecting that the thief did nothing strange, for a man only loses that which he has.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.18.15; repeated 1.29.21 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: That we ought not to be angry with the errors \(faults\) of others.
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse, recounting his own experience to his listeners
source_quote: hearing a noise at the door, I ran down, and found that the lamp had been carried off. I reflected that he who had taken the lamp had done nothing strange. What then? To-morrow, I said, you will find an earthen lamp: for a man only loses that which he has.
source_reason: for a man only loses that which he has.
source_lesson: Why then are you troubled? for we only lose those things, we have only pains about those things which we possess.
source_verdict: Why then are you troubled? for we only lose those things, we have only pains about those things which we possess.
stoic_judgement: say he will find an earthen lamp tomorrow, reflecting that the thief did nothing strange, for a man only loses that which he has
stoic_reason: He judges the lamp to be an external, not his own, and the thief to be a man acting on what appears good to him (Handbook 1, 42; Discourses 1.18). So he assents to no anger, and he calmly provides for a preferred indifferent, a lamp tomorrow. This act proceeds from correct judgements and is well done (R1, R2 by contrast, R5).
also_in: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020)

other: You see a man who sold his shoemaker as good for nothing now, after the shoemaker has become Caesar's shoemaker, asking, “How does the good Felicion do, I pray?” and consulting with him about something.
self: You, having sold your shoemaker as good for nothing, now, after he has become Caesar's shoemaker, ask, “How does the good Felicion do, I pray?” and consult with him about something.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.19.19–23 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How we should behave to tyrants.
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students
source_quote: You should have seen what respect Epaphroditus paid to him: “How does the good Felicion do, I pray?” Then if any of us asked, “What is master \(Epaphroditus\) doing?” the answer was, “He is consulting about something with Felicion.”
source_lesson: This is an instance of valuing something else than the things which depend on the will.
source_verdict: Had he not sold the man as good for nothing? Who then made him wise all at once? This is an instance of valuing something else than the things which depend on the will.
stoic_judgement: sold his shoemaker as good for nothing now, after the shoemaker has become Caesar's shoemaker, asking, “How does the good Felicion do, I pray?” and consulting with him
stoic_reason: Nothing in the shoemaker changed except his office, which is not up to him. So the man's sudden respect comes from judging nearness to Caesar, an external, to be a good. That judgement makes him subordinate himself to whoever can procure it (R1, R2; Handbook 1, Discourses 1.4, 1.29). It is a failure of wisdom: he misjudges what is good and what is up to us. It also falls short of justice, since his esteem for the man is insincere flattery rather than fair dealing (R8).

other: You see an old man who has lost his strength, summoned by the magistrates he advises, hear boys say the inability to obey imposes a greater obligation than obeying one's master, and return home.
self: You have lost your strength, and when the magistrates you advise summon you, you hear boys say the inability to obey imposes a greater obligation than obeying one's master, and you return home.
source: Plutarch, How to Be a Leader (Jeffrey Beneker, 2019)
speaker: Plutarch, addressing Euphanes
source_quote: Menecrates reasoned, then, that he had reached the limit of his useful service, and he returned home.
source_reason: he met some young boys and asked them if they knew of anything that imposed a greater obligation than obeying one's master, to which they answered, "The inability to obey."
source_lesson: Our willingness to obey, therefore, should not give out before our ability, but once our willingness has been abandoned by our ability, we should not force ourselves to serve.
source_verdict: Our willingness to obey, therefore, should not give out before our ability, but once our willingness has been abandoned by our ability, we should not force ourselves to serve.
modernised: [{"source": "the ephors", "vignette": "the magistrates", "why": "Most readers do not know that ephors were Sparta's chief elected magistrates, so they could not tell who is summoning him or what his duty to them is."}]
stoic_judgement: hear boys say the inability to obey imposes a greater obligation than obeying one's master, and return home
stoic_reason: His body and its strength are not up to him (Handbook 1). In his role as an elder adviser (Discourses 2.10), he seems to accept the saying that inability releases him from the summons, and he goes home without anxiety. Read this way, he acts from a correct judgement about what is and is not his to do (R1, R5, R6). The vignette shows that judgement only by implication.

other: You see a man whom the ruler threatens with death say to him, "You threaten me with death, but nature threatens you," for beyond the poor body no one has any power over him.
self: When the ruler threatens you with death, you say to him, "You threaten me with death, but nature threatens you," for beyond the poor body no one has any power over you.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.25.22 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a lecture, citing Demetrius's reply to Nero
source_quote: Demetrius said to Nero, "You threaten me with death, but nature threatens you."
source_reason: and as to the last garment, that is the poor body, no one has any power over me beyond this
source_lesson: If I set my admiration on the poor body, I have given myself up to be a slave: if on my little possessions, I also make myself a slave: for I immediately make it plain with what I may be caught; as if the snake draws in his head, I tell you to strike that part of him which be guards; and do you be assured that whatever part you choose to guard, that part your master will attack.
source_verdict: If I set my admiration on the poor body, I have given myself up to be a slave: if on my little possessions, I also make myself a slave ... Remembering this whom will you still flatter or fear?
stoic_judgement: for beyond the poor body no one has any power over him
stoic_reason: He judges that death and the body are not up to him and so not evils, and that only his own moral purpose is his. So he does not fear the threat, does not flatter, and answers freely. This act proceeds from correct judgement (R1, Handbook 1 and 5, Discourses 1.25) and shows no assent to fear (R2). It counts as acting well under the progress convention (R5).

other: You see the foremost Greek warrior at Troy begin to be angry and weep for a girl, forgetting that he is at Troy not to get mistresses, but to fight.
self: You, the foremost Greek warrior at Troy, begin to be angry and weep for a girl, forgetting that you are at Troy not to get mistresses, but to fight.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.28.24; repeated 2.24.18–23 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: That we ought not to be angry with men; and what are the small and the great things among men.
speaker: Epictetus, in discourse with an interlocutor
source_quote: when he began to be angry, when he wept for a girl, when he forgot that he was at Troy not to get mistresses, but to fight
source_lesson: These things are the ruin of men, this is being besieged, this is the destruction of cities, when right opinions are destroyed, when they are corrupted.
source_verdict: When was Achilles ruined? Was it when Patroclus died? Not so. But it happened when he began to be angry, when he wept for a girl, when he forgot that he was at Troy not to get mistresses, but to fight.
stoic_judgement: begin to be angry and weep for a girl, forgetting that he is at Troy not to get mistresses, but to fight
stoic_reason: Achilles assents to the impression that losing the girl, an external not up to him, is an evil, and that she is a good he must have. That is an assented passion (R2, Handbook 5 and 19), not a first movement (R3), and it is shown by his forgetting what his role as a warrior asks (R6, Discourses 2.10). His tears are not the fault by themselves (R4); the fault is the judgement behind the anger, so he acts badly, failing to restrain anger and appetite.

other: You see a man who has proved to the judges that his case is just in a little suit about a bit of land end his speech: 'I will neither intreat you nor do I care what judgment you will give; it is you rather than I who are on your trial.'
self: You have proved to the judges that your case is just in a little suit about a bit of land, and you end your speech: 'I will neither intreat you nor do I care what judgment you will give; it is you rather than I who are on your trial.'
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.2.17–18 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in discourse to a student who may have to plead a case in court
source_quote: my friend Heraclitus, who had a little suit in Rhodes about a bit of land, and had proved to the judges (δικασταῖς) that his case was just, said when he had come to the peroration of his speech, I will neither intreat you nor do I care what judgment you will give, and it is you father than I who are on your trial. And thus he ended the business.
source_lesson: Only do not intreat; but do not also say, ‘I do not intreat;’ unless there is a fit occasion to irritate purposely the judges, as was the case with Socrates.
source_verdict: What need was there of this? Only do not intreat; but do not also say, ‘I do not intreat;’ unless there is a fit occasion to irritate purposely the judges, as was the case with Socrates.
stoic_judgement: 'I will neither intreat you nor do I care what judgment you will give; it is you rather than I who are on your trial.'
stoic_reason: Not caring about the verdict, which is not up to him, is a correct judgement (Handbook 1). But having chosen to plead his case, announcing his indifference only provokes the judges with no fit occasion. That does not fit the role he took up (R6), so it is badly done, a failure to see what the situation asks (R1, R6; R9: the label follows Epictetus's own framing).

other: You see a philosopher refuse a man asking for letters of recommendation, saying the recipient will know whether he is good or bad if by experience skilful to distinguish them, and never otherwise, though he write ten thousand times.
self: You refuse a man asking you for letters of recommendation, saying the recipient will know whether he is good or bad if by experience skilful to distinguish them, and never otherwise, though you write ten thousand times.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.3.1–2 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: To those who recommend persons to philosophers.
speaker: Epictetus, recounting Diogenes' reply to a man who asked him for a letter of recommendation
source_quote: DIOGENES said well to one who asked from him letters of recommendation, “That you are a man, he said, he will know as soon as he sees you; and he will know whether you are good or bad, if he is by experience skilful to distinguish the good and the bad; but if he is without experience, he will never know, if I write to him ten thousand times.”
source_reason: he will know whether you are good or bad, if he is by experience skilful to distinguish the good and the bad; but if he is without experience, he will never know, if I write to him ten thousand times.
source_lesson: We ought then in life also to have some skill as in the case of silver coin that a man may be able to say like the judge of silver, Bring me any drachma and I will test it.
source_verdict: DIOGENES said well to one who asked from him letters of recommendation
stoic_judgement: saying the recipient will know whether he is good or bad if by experience skilful to distinguish them, and never otherwise, though he write ten thousand times
stoic_reason: The refusal comes from a correct judgement. A man's goodness is his own moral purpose and shows itself to anyone skilled in testing, like a drachma. A letter is an external that cannot make anyone known as good or bad, so writing one would vouch for what the writer cannot vouch for. R1 applies because the judgement is stated, so the act may be praised; R5 lets us call it acting well; R8 places it chiefly under wisdom (soundness of judgement), with justice (honest dealing, no empty testimony) also fitting.

other: You see a philosopher facing trial, reminded by a friend to prepare for it, reply that he has been preparing for it all his life, for he has never done anything unjust in his private or public life.
self: You are facing trial, and when a friend reminds you to prepare for it, you reply that you have been preparing for it all your life, for you have never done anything unjust in your private or public life.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.2.8–9 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse, citing Socrates
source_quote: I have maintained that which was in my own power. ... I have never done anything unjust either in my private or in my public life.
source_lesson: For if you wish to maintain a will conformable to nature, you have every security, every facility, you have no troubles.
source_verdict: Only do not intreat; but do not also say, ‘I do not intreat;’ unless there is a fit occasion to irritate purposely the judges, as was the case with Socrates.
stoic_judgement: reply that he has been preparing for it all his life, for he has never done anything unjust in his private or public life
stoic_reason: He treats his own just conduct, which is up to him, as his preparation, and does not treat the verdict, which is not up to him, as the thing to secure (Handbook 1; Discourses 1.29). Under R1 and R5, the act proceeds from a correct judgement and is acting well, with no assented fear of the outcome (R2, Discourses 2.13).

other: You see a man on trial for his life using pleasantry in court, asking his accuser who can believe there are mules but not asses, with chains, banishment, a draught of poison and his children's orphaning at stake.
self: You are on trial for your life and use pleasantry in court, asking your accuser who can believe there are mules but not asses, with chains, banishment, a draught of poison and your children's orphaning at stake.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.5.18–20 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How magnanimity is consistent with care.
speaker: Epictetus, discoursing to his students
source_quote: Socrates then knew how to play at ball. How? By using pleasantry in the court where he was tried.
source_lesson: So we should do: we must employ all the care of the players, but show the same indifference about the ball.
source_verdict: but still he did play and threw the ball skilfully.
stoic_judgement: using pleasantry in court, asking his accuser who can believe there are mules but not asses, with chains, banishment, a draught of poison and his children's orphaning at stake
stoic_reason: Read as Epictetus reads it, he is calm and playful while life, chains and his children's orphaning are at stake. That calm suggests he does not judge these externals to be evils (Handbook 5; Discourses 1.29). His pointed refutation of the charge shows care in the use, which is up to him (Discourses 2.10), so this is acting well as one making progress (R1, R2 by contrast, R5) and comes nearest to courage, with the wisdom of knowing what is and is not up to us (R8).

other: You see a condemned philosopher, about to drink the poison, excuse the jailor who had charge of him in prison and is weeping, and say, "How generously he laments over us."
self: You, a condemned philosopher about to drink the poison, excuse the jailor who has charge of you in prison and is weeping, and say, "How generously he laments over us."
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.29.65–66 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students
source_quote: For Socrates also excused the jailor, who had the charge of him in prison and was weeping when Socrates was going to drink the poison, and said, How generously he laments over us.
source_lesson: No, but we ought to accommodate ourselves to the ignorant \(τοῖς ἰδιώταις\) and to say: “This man recommends to me that which he thinks good for himself: I excuse him.”
source_verdict: For Socrates also excused the jailor, who had the charge of him in prison and was weeping when Socrates was going to drink the poison, and said, How generously he laments over us.
stoic_judgement: excuse the jailor ... and say, "How generously he laments over us."
stoic_reason: He excuses the weeping jailor and calls the tears generous. That is the judgement of Handbook 42: the man acts on what seems good to him, and his goodwill is to be met kindly, not blamed or corrected. This is an act from correct judgement, so it is well done (Discourses 4.8, R1, R5). It is kindness and fair dealing suited to his role toward a well-meaning man (R6), and his tears are not mistaken for a fault (R4).

self: You, a man of letters who had once been detected in adultery in the city, say, "What then, are not women common by nature? I am a man of letters and understand Archedemus."
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.4.1–3 (Long; file edition 1890)
