speaker: Epictetus, addressing a man of letters present in his audience who had once been detected in adultery
source_quote: had once been detected in adultery in the city
source_reason: What then, are not women common by nature? ... But I am a man of letters and understand Archedemus.
source_lesson: Understand Archedemus then, and be an adulterer, and faithless, and instead of a man, be a wolf or an ape: for what is the difference?
source_verdict: They do not, because you are bad and useless.
stoic_judgement: "What then, are not women common by nature? I am a man of letters and understand Archedemus."
stoic_reason: He offers a school doctrine to excuse taking a woman who, by the distribution of the laws, belongs to another. Epictetus places the fault in that judgement, not in the outward deed (R1, Discourses 1.11; R2): he treats an external, another's wife, as his to seize. In his role as neighbour and citizen this overthrows fidelity, the mark of a man (R6), and his learning only arms the wrong (Handbook 52).

other: You see a woman indulging her passion and taking vengeance on her husband rather than sparing her children, because she thinks this more profitable.
self: You indulge your passion and take vengeance on your husband rather than sparing your children, because you think this more profitable.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.28.7–9; repeated 2.17.19–22 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: *That we ought not to be angry with men; and what are the small and the great things among men.*
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his hearers
source_quote: to indulge her passion and take vengeance on her husband ... than to spare her children
source_reason: She thought that to indulge her passion and take vengeance on her husband was more profitable than to spare her children.
source_lesson: Why then are you angry with the unhappy woman that she has been bewildered about the most important things, and is become a viper instead of human creature? And why not, if it is possible, rather pity, as we pity the blind and the lame, so those who are blinded and maimed in the faculties which are supreme?
source_verdict: It was so; but she was deceived.
stoic_judgement: indulging her passion and taking vengeance on her husband rather than sparing her children, because she thinks this more profitable
stoic_reason: She acts from an assented passion: the judgement that vengeance on her husband, something outside her control, is a good worth more than her children's lives. By Discourses 4.8 an act that proceeds from bad judgements is badly done, and by Handbook 42 the one deceived is the one who suffers (R1, R2). Handbook 30 and Discourses 2.10 hold that a mother's role asks her to spare her children (R6).

other: You see a warrior who, when he was going to strike the enemy, checks himself when he hears the trumpet sounding a retreat, because it seems better to him to obey the general's command than to follow his own inclination.
self: You are going to strike the enemy and check yourself when you hear the trumpet sounding a retreat, because it seems better to you to obey the general's command than to follow your own inclination.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.6.15 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students
source_quote: when he was going to strike the enemy checked himself when he heard the trumpet sounding a retreat
source_reason: it seemed better to him to obey the general's command than to follow his own inclination.
source_lesson: But not one of us chooses, even when necessity summons, readily to obey it, but weeping and groaning we suffer what we do suffer, and we call them 'circumstances.'
source_verdict: But not one of us chooses, even when necessity summons, readily to obey it, but weeping and groaning we suffer what we do suffer, and we call them 'circumstances.'
stoic_judgement: checks himself when he hears the trumpet sounding a retreat, because it seems better to him to obey the general's command than to follow his own inclination
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a correct judgement (R1, Discourses 4.8): he ranks his duty as a soldier under the general's command above his own impulse to strike, so he acts in an orderly fashion upon good reasons in his role (R6, Discourses 2.10, 3.2). Self-restraint governs impulses, so the chief virtue is temperance (R8, Arius 5b2), and by R5 this counts as acting well for a person making progress.

other: You see a woman intending to send by a vessel a month's provisions to her friend in banishment, saying she would rather the emperor should seize all than that she should not send it.
self: You intend to send by a vessel a month's provisions to your friend in banishment, saying you would rather the emperor should seize all than that you should not send it.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.7.8 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How we ought to use divination.
speaker: Epictetus, in discourse to his students
source_quote: who intended to send by a vessel a month's provisions to Gratilla in her banishment
source_reason: I would rather, she replied, that Domitian should seize all than that I should not send it.
source_lesson: If then I must expose myself to danger for a friend, and if it is my duty even to die for him, what need have I then for divination?
source_verdict: made a good answer to him who said that Domitian would seize what she sent
stoic_judgement: saying she would rather the emperor should seize all than that she should not send it
stoic_reason: Her words show she treats the provisions, which the emperor may seize and which are not up to her, as indifferent, and treats her duty to a banished friend, which is up to her, as what matters. The act proceeds from a correct judgement and fits her role as a friend, so it is well done (R1, R6, R5). She does not consult whether the external will be lost; she acts for what reason urges.

other: You see one of a teacher's companions, on the third day of abstaining from food, holding to his resolve, made for no reason, to starve himself to death, saying, 'We ought to keep to our determinations.'
self: You are on the third day of abstaining from food, having resolved for no reason to starve yourself to death, and when your teacher asks why, you say, 'We ought to keep to our determinations.'
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.15.4–13 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: To or against those who obstinately persist in what they have determined.
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse, recounting how he went to confront his companion
source_quote: resolved to starve himself to death
source_reason: We ought to keep to our determinations.
source_lesson: We ought to keep not to all our determinations, but to those which are right
source_verdict: Then while you are committing murder and destroying a man who has done no wrong, do you say that you ought to abide by your determinations?
stoic_judgement: holding to his resolve, made for no reason, to starve himself to death, saying, 'We ought to keep to our determinations.'
stoic_reason: He acts from the judgement that a resolution must be kept because it was made, not because it is sound. That is a rash assent in the third field and a failure of duty in the second: firmness built on a rotten foundation is 'atony', not tone. The judgement is shown (R1) and it is false, so the act proceeds from a bad judgement and is badly done (Discourses 4.8). A sincere judgement can still be wrong (Handbook 42).

other: You see a philosopher lying down with a beautiful young man and mocking the young man's beauty.
self: You lie down with a beautiful young man and mock his beauty.
contested_note: The labeller calls this label tentative:  The judgement is only implied, so the label is tentative under R1 and R5.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.18.22 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How we should struggle against appearances.
speaker: Epictetus, in discourse to his students
source_quote: lying down with Alcibiades, and mocking his beauty
source_lesson: By placing these objects on the other side you will conquer the appearance: you will not be drawn away by it.
source_verdict: consider what a victory he at last found that he had gained over himself; what an Olympian victory; in what number he stood from Hercules; so that, by the Gods, one may justly salute him, Hail, wondrous man, you who have conquered not these sorry boxers and pancratiasts, nor yet those who are like them, the gladiators.
stoic_judgement: mocking the young man's beauty
stoic_reason: The mockery suggests he judges the young man's beauty, an external not up to us, to be no good worth craving. So he is not carried off by the appearance, which Epictetus counts as restraint of appetite and as acting well (R1, R2 reversed, R8 temperance). The judgement is only implied, so the label is tentative under R1 and R5.

other: You see a king anxious when he is going to meet a philosopher, for he wishes to please the philosopher.
self: You are a king, and you are anxious when you are going to meet a philosopher, for you wish to please him.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.13.14–15 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse, with an interlocutor answering him in the application that follows the case
source_quote: But Antigonus was anxious when he was going to meet Zeno
source_reason: for he wished to please Zeno
source_lesson: But Zeno did not want to please Antigonus; for no man who is skilled in any art wishes to please one who has no such skill.
source_verdict: no good man laments or groans or weeps, no good man is pale and trembles, or says, How will he receive me, how will he listen to me?
stoic_judgement: anxious when he is going to meet a philosopher, for he wishes to please the philosopher
stoic_reason: The king's anxiety comes from wanting something outside his control: whether the philosopher is pleased belongs to the philosopher (Discourses 2.13, the singer who wants applause). The vignette gives this want as the cause of a lasting anxiety, not a sudden unwilled start, so it is an assented passion and counts as acting badly even with no outward deed (R1, R2; not R3). The failure lies mainly in not discerning what is his own and what is another's (wisdom), with a craving for approval that self-restraint would check (R8).

other: You see a man who is a guest in another man's house carry off his host's wife, as it appeared to him to do, and she follows him.
self: You, a guest in another man's house, carry off your host's wife, as it appears to you to do, and she follows you.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.28.12,23; repeated 2.22.23 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: That we ought not to be angry with men; and what are the small and the great things among men.
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with an interlocutor (his Discourse)
source_quote: It appeared to Alexander to carry off the wife of Menelaus: it appeared to Helene to follow him.
source_lesson: So then all these great and dreadful deeds have this origin, in the appearance (opinion)? Yes, this origin and no other.
source_verdict: now the ruin of Alexander was when he lost the character of modesty, fidelity, regard to hospitality, and to decency.
modernised: [{"source": "the wife of Menelaus", "vignette": "his host's wife", "why": "A reader today would not know that Menelaus was Alexander's host. Without that, the breach of hospitality and fidelity on which the author's verdict turns would be lost."}]
stoic_judgement: carry off his host's wife, as it appeared to him to do
stoic_reason: He acts on the impression that taking his host's wife, something not his own and not up to him, is good to do. By Discourses 4.8 and Handbook 42 an act that proceeds from a bad judgement is badly done, even if sincerely held, and he is the one deceived and harmed. As a guest (R6) he breaks fidelity and hospitality, so under R1, R2 and R6 this is acting badly; Epictetus's counsel not to be angry with him does not make the act good.

other: You see a philosopher, when an earthquake happens, imagine that the city is going to fall on him.
self: When an earthquake happens, you, a philosopher, imagine that the city is going to fall on you.
contested_note: Fragment 9 names the collapse of a building and sudden word of peril as cases where even the wise man is briefly disturbed without fault. On that reading the reaction is neutral (R3). Epictetus in the source treats this very reaction as opinion added through want of discipline, which is acting badly. The vignette's word 'imagine' does not settle which case it is. | From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as neutral: "Imagine that the city is going to fall on him" reports an impression of sudden peril, the kind fragment 9 says disturbs even the wise man 'before the action of the intellect and the reason'. The vignette shows no assent that being crushed is an evil, which Long §9.4 says dread requires, so read as a first movement this is neither (R3, R7). R1 forbids treating an unknown judgement as neutral by default, so the row is flagged.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.16.23 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: That we do not strive to use our opinions about good and evil.
speaker: Epictetus, speaking to his students, using his own reactions as the example
source_quote: when an earthquake shall happen, I imagine that the city is going to fall on me
source_lesson: What then are the things which are heavy on us and disturb us? What else than opinions?
source_verdict: Consequently through want of discipline we are always adding something to the appearance and representing things to be greater than what they are.
stoic_judgement: imagine that the city is going to fall on him
stoic_reason: Picturing the whole city falling on him goes beyond the bare shock of the quake. It is 'adding something to the appearance', a judgement that a looming external (death or injury) is terrible, which is dread and is in his control (Handbook 5, Discourses 2.13; R1, R2). A swift, unwilled start at the quake would be only a first movement and not a fault (fragment 9, R3), but the vignette shows him elaborating the danger, not merely blenching.

other: You see a man seeking the costly priesthood of Augustus because those who draw up agreements will write his name, his name will remain, and he will wear a crown of gold.
self: You seek the costly priesthood of Augustus because those who draw up agreements will write your name, your name will remain, and you will wear a crown of gold.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.19.26–29 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How we should behave to tyrants.
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with a man who is interested in the priesthood of Augustus
source_quote: A person was talking to me to-day about the priesthood of Augustus ... But he replies, "Those who draw up agreements will write my name." ... My name will remain. ... But I shall wear a crown of gold.
source_reason: "Those who draw up agreements will write my name." ... My name will remain. ... But I shall wear a crown of gold.
source_lesson: This is an instance of valuing something else than the things which depend on the will.
source_verdict: "Man, let the thing alone: you will spend much for no purpose." ... If you desire a crown at all, take a crown of roses and put it on, for it will be more elegant in appearance.
stoic_judgement: because those who draw up agreements will write his name, his name will remain, and he will wear a crown of gold
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement behind the act (R1): he treats reputation, a lasting name and a gold crown, which are not up to him (Handbook 1), as goods worth great cost. That misplaced desire is acting badly (R2, Handbook 19). Seeking office is not wrong in itself, but this motive is vanity unrestrained (R8 temperance), resting on a failure to see what is and is not his own (wisdom).

other: You see a man on a voyage look down on the deep sea and round on it, seeing no land, and he is out of his mind, imagining he must drink up all this water if wrecked.
self: You are on a voyage, look down on the deep sea and round on it and see no land, and you are out of your mind, imagining you must drink up all this water if you are wrecked.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.16.22 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: That we do not strive to use our opinions about good and evil.
speaker: Epictetus, speaking in his own person in a lecture
source_quote: when I am on a voyage and look down on the deep sea, or look round on it and see no land, I am out of my mind and imagine that I must drink up all this water if I am wrecked, and it does not occur to me that three pints are enough
source_lesson: What then disturbs me? The sea? No, but my opinion.
source_verdict: Consequently through want of discipline we are always adding something to the appearance and representing things to be greater than what they are.
stoic_judgement: he is out of his mind, imagining he must drink up all this water if wrecked
stoic_reason: He is not just startled. He goes on to assent to an enlarged impression, judging drowning (an external, not up to him) a great looming evil, and 'adding something to the appearance'. By R2 (Handbook 5; Discourses 2.13) an assented fear is acting badly even with no outward deed, and the sustained, reasoned-out imagining is more than a fragment 9 first movement (R3).

other: You see a provincial governor, Caesar's friend and deputy, cry out and spring up from his seat in the theatre, his slaves calling out, because he wishes an actor to be crowned.
self: You, a provincial governor and Caesar's friend and deputy, cry out and spring up from your seat in the theatre, your slaves calling out, because you wish an actor to be crowned.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.4.1–12 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: Against a person who showed his partizanship in an unseemly way in a theatre.
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with the governor of Epirus
source_quote: having shown his favour to an actor in an unseemly way ... and that he was vexed at those who blamed him
source_reason: But I wish Sophron to be crowned.
source_lesson: But in public do not claim more than your due, nor attempt to appropriate to yourself what belongs to all.
source_verdict: for if it is not right to show partizanship in this way, do not do so yourself; and if it is right, why are you angry if they followed your example?
stoic_judgement: cry out and spring up from his seat in the theatre, his slaves calling out, because he wishes an actor to be crowned
stoic_reason: He sets his desire on something not up to him, which actor is crowned, and is carried away by it. Like the singer who wants applause (Discourses 2.13), he treats an external as a good he must secure. That is an assented passion (R2, the first field of desire and aversion). As Caesar's deputy he is also an example to the crowd, so the outburst fails his role and claims more than his due in a public matter (R6).

other: You see a man, born of the same mother and father as his brother and brought up together with him, quarrel with him about the royal power and tell him, 'I will place myself opposite and try to kill you.'
self: You, born of the same mother and father as your brother and brought up together with him, quarrel with him about the royal power and tell him, 'I will place myself opposite and try to kill you.'
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.22.13–14 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, discoursing to his pupils
source_quote: But when a quarrel rose between them about the royal power, as between dogs about a bit of meat ... I will place myself opposite and try to kill you. ... I also wish to do the same. Such are the wishes that they utter.
source_reason: about the royal power
source_lesson: For universally, be not deceived, every animal is attached to nothing so much as to its own interest.
source_verdict: If in externals, do not name them friends, no more than name them trustworthy or constant, or brave or free: do not name them even men, if you have any judgment.
stoic_judgement: quarrel with him about the royal power and tell him, 'I will place myself opposite and try to kill you.'
stoic_reason: He treats royal power, an office not under his control (Handbook 1), as a good great enough to kill his own brother for. This is an assented passion carried into a declared intent (R1, R2, Handbook 19), and it fails the duty his role as brother asks of him (R6, Discourses 2.10; DL 7.108: 'to be indifferent to one's brothers' is contrary to duty).

other: You see a ruler, when his dear friend died, order the temples of Aesculapius, the god of healing, to be burned.
self: When your dear friend dies, you, a ruler, order the temples of Aesculapius, the god of healing, to be burned.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.22.17 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his hearers
source_quote: Alexander ordered the temples of Aes- culapius to be burned
source_reason: when his dear friend died
source_lesson: For this reason if a man put in the same place his interest, sanctity, goodness, and country, and parents, and friends, all these are secured: but if he puts in one place his interest, in another his friends, and his country and his kinsmen and justice itself, all these give way being borne down by the weight of interest.
source_verdict: For this reason if a man put in the same place his interest, sanctity, goodness, and country, and parents, and friends, all these are secured: but if he puts in one place his interest, in another his friends, and his country and his kinsmen and justice itself, all these give way being borne down by the weight of interest.
modernised: [{"source": "Aesculapius", "vignette": "Aesculapius, the god of healing", "why": "A reader today may not know Aesculapius was the god of healing, and so would miss that the ruler is striking at the god he holds to blame for the friend's death."}]
stoic_judgement: "when his dear friend died, order the temples of Aesculapius, the god of healing, to be burned". The motive is not stated in words. It is implied by the timing (the friend's death) and the target (the healing god): he treats the death, which is not up to him, as an evil, and the god as the one who failed him.
stoic_reason: Under R2, his passion (grief turned to anger at the gods) rests on the false judgement that a friend's death, an external, is an evil. Under R1, the act proceeds from that bad judgement and is badly done. Against piety, a part of justice, he burns the temples, as Epictetus says men do 'when the gods appear to us to be an impediment' to what they place their interest in (Discourses 2.22).

other: You see a sophist, at whom the philosopher Diogenes has pointed by stretching out his middle finger, wild with rage.
self: You are a sophist, and when the philosopher Diogenes points you out by stretching out his middle finger at you, you are wild with rage.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.2.11–12 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: *In what a man ought to be exercised who has made proficiency; and that we neglect the chief things.*
speaker: Epictetus, addressing a pupil
source_quote: when the man was wild with rage
source_lesson: For a man is not shown by the finger, as a stone or a piece of wood; but when any person shows the man's principles, then he shows him as a man.
source_verdict: For a man is not shown by the finger, as a stone or a piece of wood; but when any person shows the man's principles, then he shows him as a man.
stoic_judgement: wild with rage
stoic_reason: Under R2 and Handbook 20, it is not Diogenes's finger that insults the sophist but his own judgement that it does. Being 'wild with rage' is full anger: he has assented to the view that his reputation, which is not up to him, has been harmed. That is not the brief, involuntary blench of fragment 9 (R3), so he acts badly. In the passage's own words, the rage itself 'shows the man's principles'.

other: You see the most reputed philosopher among the Romans, vexed with his own friends as if suffering something intolerable, cry, "I cannot bear it, you are killing me: you will make me such as that man is," pointing to another philosopher.
self: You, the most reputed philosopher among the Romans, vexed with your own friends as if suffering something intolerable, cry, "I cannot bear it, you are killing me: you will make me such as that man is," pointing to another philosopher.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.8.7 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How we must exercise ourselves against appearances (φαντασίας).
speaker: Epictetus, telling his audience of an incident at which he was present
source_quote: being vexed with his own friends and as if he was suffering something intolerable said, "I cannot bear it, you are killing me: you will make me such as that man is;" pointing to me
source_lesson: Hear how the Romans feel towards philosophers, if you would like to know.
source_verdict: Affliction is a thing which depends on the will: it is an evil.
stoic_judgement: vexed with his own friends as if suffering something intolerable, cry, "I cannot bear it, you are killing me: you will make me such as that man is"
stoic_reason: His friends' conduct, and what others make of him, are not up to him. Yet he assents to the impression that they are intolerable evils, saying "I cannot bear it, you are killing me." That is a passion assented to: vexation with others and a failure to endure. Under R2 this is acting badly, and his outcry is a fully formed judgement, not a passing first movement (R3).

other: You see a wife who has lived long with her husband and is the mother of his many children let a necklace come between them, through her opinion about such things.
self: You, a wife who has lived long with your husband and are the mother of his many children, let a necklace come between you, through your opinion about such things.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.22.32–33 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse on friendship, answering an imagined objection about a wife of long standing
source_quote: But a necklace came between them:
source_reason: and what is a necklace? It is the opinion about such things.
source_lesson: And let every man among you who has seriously resolved either to be a friend himself or to have another for his friend, cut out these opinions, hate them, drive them from his soul.
source_verdict: That was the bestial principle, that was the thing which broke asunder the friendship between husband and wife, that which did not allow the woman to be a wife nor the mother to be a mother.
stoic_judgement: let a necklace come between them, through her opinion about such things
stoic_reason: She acts from the judgement that a necklace, an external not up to her, is a good worth more than her bond as wife and mother. Her own opinion, not the necklace, breaks the friendship (Handbook 5; Discourses 1.29), so this is acting badly (R1, R2). It also fails what the roles of wife and mother ask (R6).

other: You see a philosopher, half asleep, answer a king who stands by him quoting Homer's line 'A man a councillor should not sleep all night' with 'The people's guardian and so full of cares.'
self: You, half asleep, answer a king who stands by you quoting Homer's line 'A man a councillor should not sleep all night' with 'The people's guardian and so full of cares.'
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.22.92 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in discourse with a young man who is considering the Cynic life
source_quote: in reply to Alexander, who stood by him when he was sleeping, and quoted Homer's line ... he answered, when he was half asleep, ... The people's guardian and so full of cares.
source_lesson: There ought also to belong to the Cynic much natural grace and sharpness; and if this is not so, he is a stupid fellow, and nothing else; and he must have these qualities that he may be able readily and fitly to be a match for all circumstances that may happen.
source_verdict: There ought also to belong to the Cynic much natural grace and sharpness; and if this is not so, he is a stupid fellow, and nothing else; and he must have these qualities that he may be able readily and fitly to be a match for all circumstances that may happen.
stoic_judgement: half asleep, answer a king ... with 'The people's guardian and so full of cares.' (the reply implies that sleepless care belongs to the one whose role is guarding the people, and that a king's rebuke, which is not up to him, does not disturb him)
stoic_reason: Under R1 and R6, the reply treats the duty of sleepless care as measured by role. Under R2, he shows no fear or anxiety at a king's censure, since another's opinion is not under his control. So he acts from a correct judgement with fitting sharpness, which under R5 counts as acting well for one making progress.

other: You see a man vexed that a flatterer, free from shame, has become rich, saying the unjust man has the advantage in money, though he himself would never lie with Sura for it and admits modesty is better than riches.
self: You are vexed that a flatterer, free from shame, has become rich, saying the unjust man has the advantage in money, though you would never lie with Sura for it and admit modesty is better than riches.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.17.4–5 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, recounting how he questioned a man vexed at Philostorgus's good fortune
source_quote: was vexed because Philostorgus was fortunate
source_reason: the unjust man has the advantage ... In money.
source_lesson: Remember then always and have in readiness the truth, that this is a law of nature, that the superior has an advantage over the inferior in that in which he is superior; and you will never be vexed.
source_verdict: Why are you vexed then, man, when you possess the better thing?
stoic_judgement: vexed that a flatterer ... has become rich, saying the unjust man has the advantage in money
stoic_reason: His vexation is an assented passion (R2). He judges the flatterer's money, which is not up to him, a good he lacks. That is envy (Handbook 19), and it contradicts his own admission that modesty, which he has, is the better thing (Discourses 1.29: the good lies only in moral purpose). His refusal to sell his modesty is to his credit, but the feeling the vignette shows is a faulty judgement, not a first movement, since he holds it and argues for it (R3 does not apply).

other: You see a Cynic in a fever, convinced that whatever he suffers it is Zeus who is exercising him, call to passers-by going to Olympia to see athletes fight, 'Miserable wretches, will you not stay and see the combat between a fever and a man?'
self: You, a Cynic in a fever, convinced that whatever you suffer it is Zeus who is exercising you, call to passers-by going to Olympia to see athletes fight, 'Miserable wretches, will you not stay and see the combat between a fever and a man?'
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.22.58–59 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, replying to a pupil inclined to Cynicism who asked what kind of person a Cynic ought to be
source_quote: Hear what Diogenes says to the passers by when he is in a fever, Miserable wretches, will you not stay? but are you going so long a journey to Olympia to see the destruction or the fight of athletes; and will you not choose to see the combat between a fever and a man?
source_reason: Is he not convinced that whatever he suffers, it is Zeus who is exercising him?
source_lesson: And is he who is trained to the contest and exercised by Zeus going to call out and to be vexed, he who is worthy to bear the sceptre of Diogenes?
source_verdict: Would such a man accuse God who sent him down as if God were treating him unworthily, a man who gloried in his circumstances, and claimed to be an example to those who were passing by?
stoic_judgement: convinced that whatever he suffers it is Zeus who is exercising him
stoic_reason: He judges the fever, which is not up to him, to be no evil but a contest he has been set, so his conduct proceeds from a correct judgement and is well done (R1, R5). He neither assents to grief nor accuses God; he endures the hardship and offers himself as an example, which is acting well as a person in the Cynic's role (R2, R6).

other: You see a Cynic philosopher, asked by a man, 'Are you the one who does not believe that there are gods?', reply, 'How can this be when I think that you are odious to the gods?'
self: You, a Cynic philosopher, are asked by a man, 'Are you the one who does not believe that there are gods?', and you reply, 'How can this be when I think that you are odious to the gods?'
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle this vignette. If the retort comes from undisturbed frankness fitting the Cynic's role, it is acting well (wisdom, with courage in plain speech). If it comes from anger at the accusation, or from contempt for the man, it is an assented passion and acting badly (R2). Epictetus himself, in the source, praises it as the 'grace and sharpness' a Cynic needs. Under R9, his praise of the type of reply does not decide this token. | From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as vice: The vignette shows only the outward act, a retort that calls the questioner 'odious to the gods'. It does not show whether the Cynic speaks from anger at a judged insult (Handbook 20; a passion, R2) or from a frank, well-meant rebuke in the Cynic's role (R6). By R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45) we can neither praise nor blame until the judgement is known. The provisional `vice` rests on the retort's surface: it repays a question with abuse, which falls short of fair dealing with one's neighbour. | The labeller calls this label tentative:  Read in his Cynic role (R6), the reply refuses the impression of being insulted (Handbook 20) and fitly meets the circumstance, so it is tentatively labelled acting well; but the vignette does not show this.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.22.91 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse on the Cynic character, answering a young man who is considering the Cynic life
source_quote: So Diogenes replied to one who said, Are you the Diogenes who does not believe that there are gods? And, how, replied Diogenes, can this be when I think that you are odious to the gods?
source_reason: when I think that you are odious to the gods
source_lesson: There ought also to belong to the Cynic much natural grace and sharpness; and if this is not so, he is a stupid fellow, and nothing else; and he must have these qualities that he may be able readily and fitly to be a match for all circumstances that may happen.
source_verdict: There ought also to belong to the Cynic much natural grace and sharpness; and if this is not so, he is a stupid fellow, and nothing else; and he must have these qualities that he may be able readily and fitly to be a match for all circumstances that may happen.
stoic_judgement: not shown (the vignette gives only the retort 'How can this be when I think that you are odious to the gods?', which shows that he believes in the gods but not whether he answers from calm frankness or from anger and contempt)
stoic_reason: Under R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45) we cannot praise or blame until we know the judgement behind the act. Read in his Cynic role (R6), the reply refuses the impression of being insulted (Handbook 20) and fitly meets the circumstance, so it is tentatively labelled acting well; but the vignette does not show this.

other: You see a man sail as far as Cassiope in winter with his son, and accompany him.
self: You sail as far as Cassiope in winter with your son, and accompany him.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.7.3 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: To the administrator of the free cities who was an Epicurean.
speaker: Epictetus, questioning the visiting administrator of the free cities, who was an Epicurean
source_quote: Maximus sailed as far as Cassiope in winter \(or bad weather\) with his son, and accompanied him
source_lesson: For this reason Maximus acted foolishly if he made the voyage for any other reason than for the sake of the flesh, that is, for the sake of the best.
source_verdict: For this reason Maximus acted foolishly if he made the voyage for any other reason than for the sake of the flesh, that is, for the sake of the best.
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: The vignette shows only the outward act. Until we learn the judgement behind it, Epictetus says we may neither praise nor blame it (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45; R1), and unknown judgement is not grounds for 'neutral' (R7). The label 'virtue' is provisional: a father attending to his son is the kind of act his role calls for (Handbook 30, Discourses 2.10; R6), and enduring a winter voyage for it points to care for something other than the flesh. It stands only if the rewrite shows he acted from affection joined with reason (Discourses 1.11).

other: You see a far-traveled man, parted from his wife, feeling a desire for his wife and weeping as he sits on a rock.
self: You are parted from your wife, and you feel a desire for her and weep as you sit on a rock.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.24.18–20 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: *That we ought not to be moved by a desire of those things which are not in our power.*
speaker: Epictetus, discoursing, answering an objection raised by an imagined student who quotes Homer
source_quote: Ulysses felt a desire for his wife and wept as he sat on a rock.
source_lesson: To desire then things which are impossible is to have a slavish character, and is foolish: it is the part of a stranger, of a man who fights against God in the only way that he can, by his opinions.
source_verdict: Or if Ulysses really wept, what was he else than an unhappy man? and what good man is unhappy? ... and if Ulysses did weep and lament, he was not a good man.
stoic_judgement: feeling a desire for his wife and weeping as he sits on a rock
stoic_reason: He desires something not under his control (his wife's presence) and sits weeping over its absence. Epictetus treats this as the passion of the first field, where desire fails of its object, and not as a first movement (R2, R3) or as reasonable affection (R4). He has forgotten that what is made is perishable and that no one can be with another always, so his 'opinions fight against God' (R1, R2).

other: You see a man, sent by the tyrants to seize another man, refuse without even deliberating about the matter, because he thinks it a base action, knowing he must die for his refusal if it so happens.
self: You are sent by the tyrants to seize a man, and you refuse without even deliberating about the matter, because you think it a base action, knowing you must die for your refusal if it so happens.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 4.1.160–161 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students
source_quote: when he was sent by the tyrants to seize Leon, he did not even deliberate about the matter
source_reason: because he thought that it was a base action ... for he intended to preserve something else, not his poor flesh, but his fidelity, his honourable character.
source_lesson: These are things which could not be assailed nor brought into subjection.
source_verdict: Socrates will not save his life by a base act; ... he who refused to obey the tyrants, ... It is not possible to save such a man's life by base acts, but he is saved by dying, not by running away.
stoic_judgement: refuse without even deliberating about the matter, because he thinks it a base action, knowing he must die for his refusal if it so happens
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a correct judgement (R1, Discourses 4.8): that doing a base act is the real evil, while death, which is not up to him, is not. So he will not buy his body at the price of his fidelity, and acts well as one making progress (R5). An order from those in power does not make a shameful act appropriate for him (R6). Courage is the virtue most at stake, since he endures the threat of death (R8).

other: You see a veteran who has seen much military service sending presents to a girl who hates him, and intreating her and weeping.
self: You, a veteran who has seen much military service, send presents to a girl who hates you, and intreat her and weep.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 4.1.19–23 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, addressing an interlocutor who claims to be free
source_quote: first of all went out by night, when Geta \(a slave\) does not venture out ... he sends presents to her who hates him, and intreats and weeps, and on the other hand having had a little success he is elated
source_lesson: Unhappy man, who are the slave even of a girl, and a worthless girl.
source_verdict: Unhappy man, who are the slave even of a girl, and a worthless girl.
stoic_judgement: sending presents to a girl who hates him, and intreating her and weeping
stoic_reason: Entreating and weeping before someone who hates him shows that he craves her favour, which is not up to him. Craving it makes him subordinate himself to the one who can grant or withhold it (Discourses 1.4, 2.13). That is an assented passion, and so acting badly (R2). This is our reading of his conduct, not a stated motive (R1). The persistent entreaty is not a mere first movement (R3), and the tears are not the fault in themselves (R4).

other: You see a man cast out shipwrecked go off to the young women to beg for necessaries, which is considered most shameful, relying on his opinions about the things which are in our power and those which are not.
self: You are cast out shipwrecked and go off to the young women to beg for necessaries, which is considered most shameful, relying on your opinions about the things which are in our power and those which are not.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.26.33–34 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, discoursing to a pupil (addressed as 'you') who fears want and is ashamed of begging or of menial ways of getting food
source_quote: And when Ulysses was cast out shipwrecked, did want humiliate him, did it break his spirit? but how did he go off to the virgins to ask for necessaries, to beg which is considered most shameful?
source_reason: Not on reputation nor on wealth nor on the power of a magistrate, but on his own strength, that is, on his opinions about the things which are in our power and those which are not.
source_lesson: For these are the only things which make men free, which make them escape from hindrance, which raise the head (neck) of those who are depressed, which make them look with steady eyes on the rich and on tyrants.
source_verdict: And when Ulysses was cast out shipwrecked, did want humiliate him, did it break his spirit?
modernised: [{"source": "the virgins", "vignette": "the young women", "why": "Today 'virgins' points to sexual status, but the source only means unmarried young women. Readers might wrongly think that status matters to the act of begging."}]
stoic_judgement: relying on his opinions about the things which are in our power and those which are not
stoic_reason: He acts from the correct judgement that reputation, and the shame others attach to begging, are not up to him and are not evils. So he does not let want break his spirit, and he seeks necessaries, which are naturally to be preferred (Discourses 2.10; Handbook 1). The act proceeds from correct judgements and is well done (R1, R5), and enduring hardship without humiliation is chiefly courage (R8).

other: You see a philosopher, taken prisoner by pirates, reprove them for feeding their captives badly, for he has said that he can no longer be enslaved by any man.
self: You, taken prisoner by pirates, reprove them for feeding their captives badly, for you have said that you can no longer be enslaved by any man.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 4.1.115; related 3.24.66 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with a visitor
source_quote: when he was taken prisoner, how did he behave to the pirates? ... How did he reprove them for feeding badly their captives?
source_reason: he said that he could no longer be enslaved by any man
source_lesson: for this is really freedom.
source_verdict: And what was strange in this? for if his master had bought an exercise master, would he have employed him in the exercises of the palaestra as a servant or as a master? and sc if he had bought a physician or an architect. And so in every matter, it is absolutely necessary that he who has skill must be the superior of him who has not. Whoever then generally possesses the science of life, what else must he be than master?
stoic_judgement: for he has said that he can no longer be enslaved by any man
stoic_reason: He treats the pirates' power over his body as not up to him and not an evil, so he does not fear them. He acts as a free man and reproves them as one who has the skill of life (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.29; R1, R5). The reproof, done without fear of externals, comes nearest to courage (intrepidness), and it also serves the captives' due treatment (R8).

other: You see a philosopher, taken prisoner by pirates and sold as a slave, immediately tell his master that he ought not to be dressed or shaved as he is, and how to bring up his children.
self: You, a philosopher taken prisoner by pirates and sold as a slave, immediately tell your master that he ought not to be dressed or shaved as he is, and how to bring up his children.
contested_note: The labeller calls this label tentative:  So the label rests on the source's framing and is flagged.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 4.1.116 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with an interlocutor
source_quote: when he was taken prisoner, how did he behave to the pirates? Did he call any of them master? ... How did he reprove them for feeding badly their captives? How was he sold? Did he seek a master? no; but a slave. And when he was sold how did he behave to his master? Immediately he disputed with him and said to his master that he ought not to be dressed as he was, nor shaved in such a manner; and about the children he told them how he ought to bring them up.
source_lesson: And so in every matter, it is absolutely necessary that he who has skill must be the superior of him who has not. Whoever then generally possesses the science of life, what else must he be than master?
source_verdict: And what was strange in this? for if his master had bought an exercise master, would he have employed him in the exercises of the palaestra as a servant or as a master?
stoic_judgement: not shown. The vignette gives only the outward act: 'immediately tell his master that he ought not to be dressed or shaved as he is, and how to bring up his children.' 'Immediately' after capture and sale hints that he does not treat slavery, an external, as an evil. But it does not state his judgement.
stoic_reason: Read as the source frames it, this is acting well. He treats his body, freedom and status as not his own, so he is not cowed by the master. He uses what is up to him, his skill in the science of life, to offer the master and his children their good (R1, R2, R6, R8). Under R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45), though, the vignette alone gives no judgement, and the same words could come from arrogance or contempt. So the label rests on the source's framing and is flagged.

other: You see a Lacedaemonian, blinded in one eye by a young fellow-citizen the people turned over to him for whatever vengeance he desires, refrain, and bring him up and make a good man of him.
self: You, blinded in one eye by a young fellow-citizen the people turned over to you for whatever vengeance you desire, refrain, and bring him up and make a good man of him.
source: Epictetus, Fragment 5 (Oldfather, 1928; private seed)
speaker: Epictetus, as recorded by Rufus in notes on friendship
source_quote: this he refrained from doing, but brought him up and made a good man of him, and presented him in the theatre
source_verdict: What man among us does not admire the saying of Lycurgus the Lacedaemonian?
stoic_judgement: refrain, and bring him up and make a good man of him
stoic_reason: Offered vengeance, he does not treat the lost eye as an evil to be repaid. He acts for the young man's moral purpose, making him good, as in Discourses 1.18, where a man deprived of right moral purpose gives no ground for anger. Under R1 the judgement is shown by the act's stated aim. Under R2 no anger is assented to. Under R5 this is acting well, and under R8 the act is kindness, which is 'a knowledge which is disposed to do good' and falls under justice, with restraint of anger (temperance) also at stake.
also_in: Musonius Rufus, Lectures / Fragments (ancient; translator uncredited in 2015 anthology)

other: You see a man striving a long time to be a philosopher without people knowing it, doing well for himself and God, not spectators, so that if he does anything base, philosophy is not endangered.
self: You strive a long time to be a philosopher without people knowing it, doing well for yourself and God, not spectators, so that if you do anything base, philosophy is not endangered.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 4.8.17–20 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: *Against those who hastily rush into the use of the philosophic dress.*
speaker: Epictetus, citing Euphrates
source_quote: A long time I strove to be a philosopher without people knowing it;
source_reason: for first I knew that when I did any thing well, I did not do it for the sake of the spectators, but for the sake of myself: I ate well for the sake of myself; I had my countenance well composed and my walk: all for myself and for God. Then, as I struggled alone, so I alone also was in danger: in no respect through me, if I did anything base or unbecoming, was philosophy endangered; nor did I injure the many by doing any thing wrong as a philosopher.
source_lesson: First strive that it be not known what you are: be a philosopher to yourself \(or, philosophize to yourself\) a short time.
source_verdict: For this reason Euphrates used to say well, A long time I strove to be a philosopher without people knowing it; and this, he said, was useful to me:
stoic_judgement: doing well for himself and God, not spectators, so that if he does anything base, philosophy is not endangered
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement behind the act (R1). He does not treat spectators' approval, which is not up to him, as his good (Handbook 1; Discourses 2.13, the singer who wants applause). He also takes care that his faults should not harm philosophy or others. This is acting well as one making progress (R5; Discourses 1.4), and it chiefly restrains vanity (R8).

other: You see a man endure his very ill-tempered wife, who pours water on his head and tramples on the cake sent to him, remembering that no man has in his power another man's ruling principle.
self: You endure your very ill-tempered wife, who pours water on your head and tramples on the cake sent to you, remembering that no man has in his power another man's ruling principle.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 4.5.33 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students
source_quote: Remembering this Socrates managed his own house and endured a very ill tempered wife and a foolish \(ungrateful?\) son.
source_reason: For he remembered well that no man has in his power another man's ruling principle.
source_lesson: for this power of being free from check \(hindrance\) is given by God to every man.
source_verdict: And an example of this as well as of all other things is proposed to us in the life of Socrates, who not only himself on all occasions avoided fights \(quarrels\), but would not allow even others to quarrel. ... how he tolerated his wife, and how he tolerated his son who attempted to confute him and to cavil with him.
stoic_judgement: remembering that no man has in his power another man's ruling principle
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement behind the act (R1): his wife's temper and her treatment of him are not up to him, only his own ruling principle is (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.29). So he does not take her insults as an evil (Handbook 20), and he endures them without strife; an act from correct judgement is well done (Discourses 4.8, R5), and as husband he keeps his own part whatever she does (R6).

other: You see a philosopher, to whom persons come and ask to be recommended by him to philosophers, taking them to philosophers.
self: You are a philosopher, and when persons come to you and ask to be recommended by you to philosophers, you take them to philosophers.
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 46; related Discourses 4.8.22–23 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, instructing a student (Arrian's Enchiridion, Oldfather translation)
source_quote: persons used to come to him and ask to be recommended by him to philosophers, and he used to take them to philosophers: so easily did he submit to being overlooked
source_lesson: For remember that in this way Socrates also altogether avoided ostentation
source_verdict: For remember that in this way Socrates also altogether avoided ostentation
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: Epictetus (Handbook 46) praises this act because it comes from not treating reputation, which is not up to us, as a good: Socrates 'so easily did he submit to being overlooked'. Read with that judgement, it is acting well and is restraint of vanity (R1, R5, R8). But the vignette shows only the outward act, and Discourses 4.8 says we may not praise it until we know the judgement behind it (R1).

other: You see a man ordered to drink the poison refuse to escape prison for his children's sake, choosing not to save his poor body but that which is saved by doing what is just.
self: You are ordered to drink the poison and refuse to escape prison for your children's sake, choosing not to save your poor body but that which is saved by doing what is just.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 4.1.162–165 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a lecture to his students
source_quote: when he was sent by the tyrants to seize Leon, he did not even deliberate about the matter... And what did he do when he was \(ordered\) to drink the poison, and when he had the power of escaping from prison, and when Crito said to him, Escape for the sake of your children, what did Socrates say? did he consider the power of escape as an unexpected gain? By no means: he considered what was fit and proper; but the rest he did not even look at or take into the reckoning.
source_reason: because he thought that it was a base action ... For he did not choose, he said, to save his poor body, but to save that which is increased and saved by doing what is just, and is impaired and destroyed by doing what is unjust.
source_lesson: Think of these things, these opinions, these words: look to these examples, if you would be free, if you desire the thing according to its worth.
source_verdict: Socrates will not save his life by a base act; he who would not put the Athenians to the vote when they clamoured that he should do so, he who refused to obey the tyrants, he who discoursed in such a manner about virtue and right behaviour. It is not possible to save such a man's life by base acts, but he is saved by dying, not by running away.
stoic_judgement: choosing not to save his poor body but that which is saved by doing what is just
stoic_reason: Under R1 the act shows its judgement: the body is not up to him, and what he guards is his moral purpose, 'that which is saved by doing what is just'. That is an act proceeding from correct judgement (Discourses 4.8), which counts as acting well in the sense of R5. His role as father does not require a base act, since duties follow roles only within what is just (R6), and Epictetus's own framing settles the case (R9).
also_in: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009) || David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)

other: You see a man who does not assist his friend when the friend is being murdered, and does not share his friend's danger.
self: You do not assist your friend when he is being murdered, and do not share your friend's danger.
contested_note: The labeller calls this label tentative:  R1 forbids blame on the outward act alone, so the label is provisional and flagged; by R1 and R7 it is not `neutral` by default.
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 32 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, instructing the reader
source_quote: did not assist his friend when he was being murdered
source_lesson: Therefore attend to the greater diviner, the Pythian God, who ejected from the temple him who did not assist his friend when he was being murdered.
source_verdict: But reason prevails that even with these risks we should share the dangers of our friend and of our country. Therefore attend to the greater diviner, the Pythian God, who ejected from the temple him who did not assist his friend when he was being murdered.
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: The vignette shows only an omission: he does not help his friend or share his danger. It does not say why or whether he could have helped. Epictetus's own verdict in Handbook 32 is that 'reason prevails' that we share a friend's danger even at the risk of death, so omitting this appropriate act is a wrong act (Arius 11a), most plausibly from judging death or injury, which are not up to us, to be evils (R2, R6). R1 forbids blame on the outward act alone, so the label is provisional and flagged; by R1 and R7 it is not `neutral` by default.

other: You see a philosopher, whom a ruler sends for to make him rich, send back the answer: "At Athens four quarts of barley-meal can be bought for a small coin, and there are running springs of water."
self: When a ruler sends for you to make you rich, you send back the answer: "At Athens four quarts of barley-meal can be bought for a small coin, and there are running springs of water."
source: Epictetus, Fragment 11 (Oldfather, 1928; private seed)
chapter: From the homilies of Arrian, exhorting to virtue
speaker: Epictetus, in a homily recorded by Arrian exhorting to virtue
source_quote: the latter bade the messenger take back the following answer: "At Athens four quarts of barley-meal can be bought for an obol, and there are running springs of water."
source_reason: if what I have is not sufficient for me, still, I am sufficient for it, and so it too is sufficient for me
source_lesson: And then shall the man of noble nature make a poorer showing than Polus, and not play well any role to which the Deity assigns him? And will he not follow the example of Odysseus, who was no less pre-eminent in his rags than in his rich and purple cloak?
source_verdict: And then shall the man of noble nature make a poorer showing than Polus, and not play well any role to which the Deity assigns him?
modernised: [{"source": "an obol", "vignette": "a small coin", "why": "Most readers would not know an obol was a tiny sum, so they would miss that the philosopher's bare needs cost next to nothing."}]
stoic_judgement: send back the answer: "At Athens four quarts of barley-meal can be bought for a small coin, and there are running springs of water."
stoic_reason: His reply treats riches, which are not up to him, as not needed: what he has is cheaply enough, so he does not crave the ruler's gift and will not subordinate himself to the one who can grant it (Discourses 1.4; Handbook 1, 19). The act proceeds from a correct judgement about externals (R1), and acting well as one making progress counts as virtue (R5). It comes nearest to restraint of the desire for wealth (R8).

other: You see a governor trying to persuade those he sentences that it is proper for them to be sentenced, since he votes against them not as an enemy but as a guardian, like a physician.
self: You, as governor, try to persuade those you sentence that it is proper for them to be sentenced, since you vote against them not as an enemy but as a guardian, like a physician.
source: Epictetus, Fragment 22 (Oldfather, 1928; private seed)
speaker: Epictetus, quoting Agrippinus (the fragment is headed 'From Agrippinus')
source_quote: When Agrippinus was governor, he used to try to persuade the persons whom he sentenced that it was proper for them to be sentenced.
source_reason: it is not as an enemy or as a brigand that I record my vote against them, but as a curator and guardian; just as also the physician encourages the man upon whom he is operating, and persuades him to submit to the operation.
source_verdict: For this reason it is right to praise Agrippinus, because, although he was a man of the very highest worth, he never praised himself, but used to blush even if someone else praised him.
stoic_judgement: he votes against them not as an enemy but as a guardian, like a physician; trying to persuade those he sentences that it is proper for them to be sentenced
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a correct judgement (Discourses 4.8, R1). As governor (R6, Discourses 2.10) he sentences for the condemned man's own good, as curator and guardian, not from anger or enmity (Discourses 1.18). He treats them as rational beings to be persuaded, as a physician persuades his patient. This is acting well in his role while making progress (R5).

other: You see a man, sure that as a wise man with true knowledge he will not be misled by mere opinions, give money deposited for safekeeping to the depositor's twin, who pretends to be the depositor.
self: You, sure that as a wise man with true knowledge you will not be misled by mere opinions, give money deposited with you for safekeeping to the depositor's twin, who pretends to be the depositor.
source: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020); source: Diogenes Laërtius
speaker: Holiday & Hanselman, citing Diogenes Laertius
source_quote: stupidly gave the money to the wrong brother
source_reason: being a wise man and having true knowledge, would therefore not be misled by mere opinions
source_lesson: It was a simple case where a rule—like checking for identification—was vastly superior than relying on your gut.
source_verdict: Aristo, who had so arrogantly claimed that he could make a wise decision in any circumstance, stupidly gave the money to the wrong brother.
stoic_judgement: sure that as a wise man with true knowledge he will not be misled by mere opinions
