stoic_reason: He treats exile, which is not up to him, as material for his moral purpose rather than an evil (Handbook 5; Discourses 1.29). From that correct judgement he does not grieve but acts for others' preferred indifferent, water, which is a well-done act of a person making progress (R1, R5). Bearing the hardship of exile without assenting to it as an evil is courage as endurance; providing for fellow exiles adds kindness under justice (R2 inverse, R8).
also_in: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)

other: You see an eighty-five-year-old senator take to the floor of the Senate to protest his own president's overreaches in the name of "security," because he stands for the Constitution and for the institution.
self: You take to the floor of the Senate at eighty-five years old to protest your own president's overreaches in the name of "security," because you stand for the Constitution and for the institution.
source: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020)
speaker: Holiday & Hanselman, quoting Senator Robert Byrd
source_quote: would take to the floor of the Senate at eighty-five years old to protest the overreaches in the name of "security" of his own president
source_reason: I stood for the Constitution. I stood for the institution. If it isn't heard today, there'll be some future member who will come through and will comb these tomes.
source_lesson: When asked why he gave this speech, Byrd managed to unintentionally provide the perfect lesson from Helvidius Priscus's life and those of the brave Stoics who had died opposing the reigns of Nero and his successors
source_verdict: Byrd managed to unintentionally provide the perfect lesson from Helvidius Priscus's life and those of the brave Stoics who had died opposing the reigns of Nero and his successors
stoic_judgement: because he stands for the Constitution and for the institution
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement behind the act (R1): he acts from what his role as a senator asks, fidelity to his country's laws and institution, not from wanting the president's favour (R6, *Discourses* 2.10: 'if you sit in the town council... remember that you are a councillor'). An act that proceeds from a correct judgement about what is his to do is well done (*Discourses* 4.8), so by our progress convention it is labelled virtue (R5).

other: You see a former slave kiss the orphan he adopted and raised good night, whispering to himself, "He may be dead in the morning," because he knows life is cruel and his son is not his possession.
self: You, a former slave, kiss the orphan you adopted and raised good night, whispering to yourself, "He may be dead in the morning," because you know life is cruel and your son is not your possession.
source: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020)
speaker: Holiday & Hanselman
source_quote: he adopted a young orphan and raised him to adulthood ... practicing steeling himself against the loss even of the joy being a father brought him
source_reason: he knew from experience that life was cruel. He wished to remind himself that his precious son was not his *possession*, nor were his friends or his students or his health.
source_lesson: Which for a Stoic means only one thing: Cherish them while we have them, but accept that they belong to us only in trust, that they can depart at any moment. Because they can. And so can we.
source_verdict: Which for a Stoic means only one thing: Cherish them while we have them, but accept that they belong to us only in trust, that they can depart at any moment.
stoic_judgement: whispering to himself, "He may be dead in the morning," because he knows ... his son is not his possession
stoic_reason: He kisses his son with affection while reminding himself that the boy's life is not under his control. That is affection that is also reasonable, which Epictetus calls 'right and good' (Discourses 1.11; Handbook 1), so it is acting well as one making progress (R1, R4, R5). Seeing what is and is not up to him is wisdom; holding firm against a loss he foresees also touches courage, and not craving an external touches temperance (R8).

other: You see an emperor, his treasury exhausted by plague and war, take the imperial ornaments to the Forum and sell them for gold, saying even the house he lives in is the Senate's.
self: You, an emperor whose treasury is exhausted by plague and war, take the imperial ornaments to the Forum and sell them for gold, saying even the house you live in is the Senate's.
source: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020); source: Dio Cassius
speaker: Holiday & Hanselman
source_quote: Marcus "took all the imperial ornaments to the Forum and sold them for gold. When the barbarian uprising had been put down, he returned the purchase price to those who voluntarily brought back the imperial possessions, but used no compulsion in the case of those who were unwilling to do so."
source_reason: "we are so far from possessing anything of our own that even the house in which we live is yours."
source_lesson: Even though as emperor he technically had unfettered control over Rome's budget, he never acted as such.
source_verdict: Even though as emperor he technically had unfettered control over Rome's budget, he never acted as such.
stoic_judgement: saying even the house he lives in is the Senate's
stoic_reason: Under R1, his words show the judgement he acts from: the imperial property is not his own but held for others. Under R6, he acts in his role as a steward of what belongs to the Senate and people, giving up externals (ornaments, property, which are not up to us, Handbook 1) rather than taking from his subjects. This is acting well as one making progress (R5) and comes nearest to justice, the apportioning of what is due (R8).
also_in: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009) || Donald J. Robertson, How to Think Like a Roman Emperor (2019; modern retelling)

other: You see a Roman emperor, returning to Rome after eight years away at the wars, forgive countless debts owed to the emperor's private treasury, burning the documents in the Forum so they could never be recovered.
self: You, a Roman emperor returning to Rome after eight years away at the wars, forgive countless debts owed to the emperor's private treasury, burning the documents in the Forum so they could never be recovered.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle it. Generosity from kindness, holding money as an indifferent, would be acting well. Generosity aimed at popular adoration, or done publicly for show, would be acting from a wrong judgement about externals. The source (Holiday & Hanselman, via Dio) praises it as generosity and gratitude, but per R9 the source's praise is not by itself a Stoic verdict.
source: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020); source: Dio Cassius (return narrative)
speaker: Holiday & Hanselman, citing Dio Cassius
source_quote: he would distribute to them eight hundred sesterces apiece, the largest gift from the emperor to the people ever given. ... On his return, he forgave countless debts owed to the emperor’s private treasury, actually burning the documents in the Forum so they could not ever be recovered.
source_reason: As a token of his gratitude and beneficence
source_lesson: Marcus may have lived humbly, but no one could say he was not generous to others.
source_verdict: Marcus may have lived humbly, but no one could say he was not generous to others. In fact, his policies as emperor perfectly adhered to the principles he jotted down one day in his diary: “Be tolerant with others and strict with yourself.”
stoic_judgement: not shown (only "burning the documents in the Forum so they could never be recovered" bears on intent: it shows he meant the remission to be irrevocable, but not why he did it)
stoic_reason: By R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45), we cannot praise the act until we know the judgement it comes from. The vignette shows the outward deed but not whether he gave from kindness proper to his role as ruler (R6, justice) or for the crowd's applause, which is not up to him (Discourses 2.13, a public burning in the Forum). The type of act is appropriate for an emperor, and its irrevocability points to real goodwill, so 'virtue' is a provisional label only.

other: You see a young slave, his master twisting his leg with all his might, calmly warn him not to take it too far; when it snaps, he makes no sound, smiles, and says, "Didn't I warn you?"
self: You are a young slave whose master twists your leg with all his might; you calmly warn him not to take it too far, and when it snaps, you make no sound, smile, and say, "Didn't I warn you?"
source: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020); source: Later Christian writers (not individually named here)
speaker: Holiday & Hanselman, citing later Christian writers
source_quote: All we hear is that Epictetus calmly warned him about taking it too far. When the leg snapped, Epictetus made no sound and cried no tears. He only smiled, looked at his master, and said, "Didn't I warn you?"
source_lesson: The Stoics believed we decided how we would react to what happened to us. Epictetus, as we each hold the power to do, *chose* to see his disability as only a physical impairment, and in fact it was that idea of *choice*, we shall see, that defined the core of his philosophical beliefs.
source_verdict: Why does this make us shudder? Empathy or pain? A horror at the senselessness? Or is it at the sheer self-mastery? With Epictetus it is all this and more.
stoic_judgement: calmly warn him not to take it too far; when it snaps, he makes no sound, smiles
stoic_reason: He treats his leg, which is not up to him, as material for his moral purpose, not as a good to cling to (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.29). He keeps calm before and after the injury, warns his master plainly, and shows no assented grief or anger, so this is endurance from a correct judgement (R1, R2 by contrast, R8). It is read as acting well while making progress, not as a sage's right act (R5).
also_in: Donald J. Robertson, How to Think Like a Roman Emperor (2019; modern retelling)

other: You see an emperor whose most trusted general attempted a coup treat each collaborator, including senators, with leniency, calling it a chance "to forgive a man who has wronged one, to remain a friend to one who has transgressed friendship."
self: Your most trusted general has attempted a coup against you, and you, the emperor, treat each collaborator, including senators, with leniency, calling it a chance "to forgive a man who has wronged one, to remain a friend to one who has transgressed friendship."
source: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020); source: Dio Cassius
speaker: Holiday & Hanselman, citing Dio Cassius
source_quote: Marcus decided the attempted coup was an *opportunity.* They could, he said to his soldiers, go out and "settle this affair well and show to all mankind there is a right way to deal even with civil wars." It was a chance "to forgive a man who has wronged one, to remain a friend to one who has transgressed friendship, to continue faithful to one who has broken faith." ... Marcus "was so greatly grieved at the death of Cassius that he could not bring himself even to look at the severed head of his enemy, but before the murderers drew near gave orders that it should be buried." He proceeded to treat each of Avidius's collaborators with leniency, including several senators who had actively endorsed this attempted coup. "I implore you, the senate, to keep my reign unstained by the blood of any senator," Marcus later appealed to those who wanted vengeance on his behalf. "May it never happen."
source_reason: It was a chance "to forgive a man who has wronged one, to remain a friend to one who has transgressed friendship, to continue faithful to one who has broken faith."
source_lesson: His dictum in life and in leadership was simple and straightforward: "Do the right thing. The rest doesn't matter."
source_verdict: Incredibly, Marcus decided the attempted coup was an *opportunity.* ... An assassin would soon enough take down Avidius, hoping almost certainly to impress himself to Marcus, and in the process revealing just how different a plane Marcus Aurelius was operating on.
stoic_judgement: calling it a chance "to forgive a man who has wronged one, to remain a friend to one who has transgressed friendship."
stoic_reason: The quoted words show he treats the coup as material for his own moral purpose rather than as an evil done to him. He finds no ground for anger at men who have harmed only themselves (Discourses 1.18, Handbook 42), and he keeps faith in his role as ruler (R1, R2 by contrast, R6). As a progressing man's act from correct judgement, it is acting well (R5).

other: You see a Stoic philosopher, condemned to death by the emperor he once tutored, chastise the friends weeping over his fate at his execution, asking what had become of their Stoicism.
self: You, a Stoic philosopher condemned to death by the emperor you once tutored, chastise the friends weeping over your fate at your execution, asking what has become of their Stoicism.
contested_note: Handbook 16 tells one to sympathize in words with those who weep, even to groan with them, and only to refuse the judgement inwardly. Under that framing the outward rebuke may lack the kindness owed to friends (justice), and their tears might be unwilled first movements, not assented grief (R3, R4). On the other side, Epictetus often rebukes students who lapse from their principles, and the friends are addressed as Stoics. His framing does not settle whether the rebuke, as distinct from Seneca's own calm, was rightly done.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine, recounting Seneca's life and death
source_quote: When the friends who were present at his execution wept over his fate, Seneca chastised them.
source_reason: What, he asked, had become of their Stoicism?
source_verdict: He never feels grief, since he realizes that grief is an “irrational contraction of the soul.”
stoic_judgement: chastise the friends weeping over his fate at his execution, asking what had become of their Stoicism
stoic_reason: His rebuke shows the judgement behind it (R1). He treats his coming death, which is not up to him, as no evil, and their weeping as a lapse from the teaching that 'the judgement that death is dreadful, *this* is the dreadful thing' (Handbook 5). Facing an execution from that judgement is acting well as one making progress (R5), and it comes nearest to courage, which endures what others fear (R8).
also_in: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)

other: You see a man whose neck is covered with wens and whose feet are diseased joking about his own deformities so much that others have nothing to add.
self: You, whose neck is covered with wens and whose feet are diseased, joke about your own deformities so much that others have nothing to add.
contested_note: The labeller calls this label tentative:  On that tentative reading he acts well, using the wisdom to see what is his own, with endurance and freedom from vanity.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: Irvine, citing Seneca's description of Vatinius
source_quote: joked about his own deformities so much that others had nothing to add
source_lesson: Of the kinds of humor we might use in response to an insult, self-deprecating humor can be particularly effective.
source_verdict: self-deprecating humor can be particularly effective
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: Under Handbook 45 and Discourses 4.8 (R1), we cannot praise or blame an act until we know the judgement it comes from. The vignette shows only the outward act of joking about his wens and diseased feet. The most natural reading is that he does not treat his body, which is not up to him (Handbook 1), as an evil or a disgrace, and that he lets no reviler insult him (Handbook 20). On that tentative reading he acts well, using the wisdom to see what is his own, with endurance and freedom from vanity. But the text does not establish this.

other: You see a Stoic judge, holding the power of the state, order that a Christian philosopher who refused to sacrifice to the gods be scourged and put to death, seeing a threat to public order and his power.
self: You, a Stoic judge holding the power of the state, order that a Christian philosopher who refused to sacrifice to the gods be scourged and put to death, seeing a threat to public order and your power.
source: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020); source: The Acts of Justin
speaker: Holiday & Hanselman
source_quote: Holding the immense power of the state in his hands, Rusticus chose to use it. “Let those who have refused to sacrifice to the gods and to obey the command of the emperor,” he ordered, “be scourged and led away to suffer capital punishment according to the ruling of the laws.”
source_reason: All he saw was a threat to the public order, a threat to his power. ... Duty-bound, Rusticus had done what he believed he had needed to do.
source_lesson: We think we are doing the right thing. We think we are protecting the status quo. We do terrible things in the process.
source_verdict: It would be a stain on two otherwise flawless reputations. ... For the former's failure to see a bigger picture, he would be a villain to millions of Christians for the rest of history.
stoic_judgement: seeing a threat to public order and his power
stoic_reason: By R1 and R2, he sentences from the judgement that his own power, which is not up to him (Handbook 1), is a good he must defend, and that a man's dissent is an evil to be put down. Epictetus says that a man who craves externals 'must end by subordinating himself' to them, and that we should not be angry at one who is deceived (Discourses 1.18; Handbook 42). So by R6 this is not the judge as 'curator and guardian' acting in his role but an error against justice; mercy and fair dealing were owed.

other: You see a woman, three years after her son's death, as grief-stricken as on the day she buried him, spending her days thinking bitterly about the happiness she has been deprived of by his death.
self: You, three years after your son's death, are as grief-stricken as on the day you buried him, spending your days thinking bitterly about the happiness you have been deprived of by his death.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: Irvine, relaying Seneca's consolation and advice to Marcia
source_quote: a woman who, three years after the death of her son, was as grief-stricken as on the day she buried him... spending her days thinking bitterly about the happiness she has been deprived of by the death of her son
source_lesson: By engaging in retrospective negative visualization, Seneca thinks, we can replace our feelings of regret at having lost something with feelings of thanks for once having had it.
source_verdict: Rather than spending her days thinking bitterly about the happiness she has been deprived of by the death of her son, Marcia should, says Seneca, think about how much worse off she would be today if she had never been able to enjoy his company.
stoic_judgement: as grief-stricken as on the day she buried him, spending her days thinking bitterly about the happiness she has been deprived of by his death
stoic_reason: Her bitter dwelling on 'the happiness she has been deprived of' shows that she judges her son's death, which was not up to her, to be an evil done to her. That makes it an assented passion of grief (Handbook 5; Discourses 3.2: an aversion that has fallen into what it would avoid), not unwilled first tears (R3, R4), so it is acting badly even with no outward deed (R2). The fault is in misjudging what is and is not up to her, so the main virtue is wisdom; her failure to restrain the passion and to endure the loss touches temperance and courage (R8).
also_in: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)

other: You see a Roman statesman go out in public without shoes or tunic, to accustom himself to be ashamed only of what is really shameful, and to ignore men's low opinion of other things.
self: You, a Roman statesman, go out in public without shoes or tunic, to accustom yourself to be ashamed only of what is really shameful, and to ignore men's low opinion of other things.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: Irvine, citing Plutarch on Cato
source_quote: Cato made a point of ignoring the dictates of fashion: When everyone was wearing light purple, he wore dark, and although ancient Romans normally went out in public wearing shoes and a tunic, Cato wore neither.
source_reason: not because he "sought vainglory"; to the contrary, he dressed differently in order to accustom himself "to be ashamed only of what was really shameful, and to ignore men's low opinion of other things."
source_lesson: In other words, Cato consciously did things to trigger the disdain of other people simply so he could practice ignoring their disdain.
source_verdict: Another way to overcome our obsession with winning the admiration of other people is to go out of our way to do things likely to trigger their disdain.
stoic_judgement: to accustom himself to be ashamed only of what is really shameful, and to ignore men's low opinion of other things
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement behind the act (R1). Others' opinion is reputation, which is not up to us (Handbook 1), and he treats only what is really shameful as worth shame. That is training desire and aversion in the way Discourses 1.4 counts as progress, so it is acting well for one making progress (R5). The main virtue is restraint of the craving for approval, which is temperance (R8). Seeing what is and is not up to him is wisdom, and enduring public disdain is courage.

other: You see an academic, having fallen under the influence of the Stoics, answer a colleague who is trying to decide whether to characterize him in print as evil or merely misguided: "Why can't you portray me as being both evil and misguided?"
self: You, having fallen under the influence of the Stoics, answer a colleague who is trying to decide whether to characterize you in print as evil or merely misguided: "Why can't you portray me as being both evil and misguided?"
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine
source_quote: having fallen under the influence of the Stoics, I had the presence of mind to respond to this insult in a Stoically acceptable manner, with self-deprecating humor: “Why can’t you portray me as being both evil and misguided?” I asked.
source_lesson: Self-deprecating humor has become my standard response to insults.
source_verdict: But on that particular day, having fallen under the influence of the Stoics, I had the presence of mind to respond to this insult in a Stoically acceptable manner, with self-deprecating humor
stoic_judgement: "having fallen under the influence of the Stoics" ... answer ... "Why can't you portray me as being both evil and misguided?" (a joking reply in place of anger or a counter-insult, which implies he does not judge the remark to be a harm)
stoic_reason: By Handbook 20 it is our own judgement that insults us. Answering the put-down with self-deprecating humour, not anger, shows he does not treat the colleague's opinion of him, which is not up to him, as a good or an evil (R1, R2). It is restraint of anger and vanity, acted on with reason, so it counts as acting well for a person making progress (R5, R8).
also_in: Massimo Pigliucci, How to Be a Stoic (2017)

other: You see a man, left sitting nearly an hour in a doctor's waiting room because the doctor is woefully behind schedule, find it impossible to get angry because he is thinking about anger during that hour.
self: You are left sitting nearly an hour in a doctor's waiting room because the doctor is woefully behind schedule, and you find it impossible to get angry because you are thinking about anger during that hour.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine, the author, narrating his own experience as a practicing Stoic
source_quote: I found it impossible to get angry.
source_reason: because I was thinking about anger during that hour
source_lesson: But one thing I have found is that the more you think about and understand anger, the easier it is to control it.
source_verdict: But one thing I have found is that the more you think about and understand anger, the easier it is to control it.
stoic_judgement: find it impossible to get angry because he is thinking about anger during that hour
stoic_reason: The vignette shows him not assenting to the impression that the doctor's delay is an injury to him. He gets there by examining anger itself, training in the first field (Discourses 3.2), so the absent passion comes from his own use of impressions and not from the delay (Handbook 20). Under R1, R2 (inverted) and R5 this counts as acting well as a person making progress, applying his principles 'as the runner does' (Discourses 1.4).

other: You see a man, exiled after he or his father adulterated Sinope's coinage, respond to someone shaming him that the people of Sinope sentenced him to exile, but he sentenced them to remain in Sinope.
self: When someone brings up how you or your father adulterated Sinope's coinage, to shame you, you respond that the people of Sinope sentenced you to exile, but you sentenced them to remain in Sinope.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: Irvine, citing Musonius
source_quote: when someone later brought up this incident in an attempt to shame him, Diogenes, with typical Cynic wit, responded that although it was true that the people of Sinope had sentenced him to exile, he in turn had sentenced them to remain in Sinope.
source_lesson: Musonius also reminds us that exile has changed people for the better. ... It has also transformed ordinary people, such as Diogenes of Sinope, into philosophers.
source_verdict: Diogenes, with typical Cynic wit, responded
stoic_judgement: respond to someone shaming him that the people of Sinope sentenced him to exile, but he sentenced them to remain in Sinope
stoic_reason: The retort shows he does not judge exile, which is not up to him, to be an evil. He also does not take the reproach as an insult (Handbook 20; Discourses 1.29, externals are only material for the moral purpose). So he acts from a correct judgement and acts well as one making progress (R1, R2, R5). It is courage, the knowledge of what need not be feared and can be endured, together with seeing what is up to us (R8).

other: You see a man experimenting with a simplified lifestyle, asked where he had gotten the T-shirt he is wearing, answer that he bought it at a thrift store and find himself feeling a bit ashamed.
self: You, experimenting with a simplified lifestyle, are asked where you got the T-shirt you are wearing, answer that you bought it at a thrift store, and find yourself feeling a bit ashamed.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle the case. If the shame is a passing first motion that he then works against, as the source goes on to say he does by emulating Cato, it is neutral (fragment 9). If he assents that being seen in thrift-store clothes is truly shameful, it is acting badly (Handbook 5, 20). Fragment 9 concerns sudden shocks, and it is unclear whether mild social shame fits that class. | From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as vice: Shame at others' possible opinion of a thrift-store shirt treats reputation, which is not up to us (Handbook 1), as a good he lacks. Read as an assented passion, this is acting badly even with no outward deed (R2; Discourses 2.13, the singer who wants applause). He answers honestly and is making progress, but the feeling itself is the fault (R5). | The source's author judges it badly (inferred); Epictetus's framing gives neutral
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine, the author, recounting his own experience
source_quote: When, for example, someone asked me where I had gotten the T-shirt I was wearing and I answered that I had bought it at a thrift store, I found myself feeling a bit ashamed.
source_lesson: He wanted to teach himself "to be ashamed only of what was really shameful."
source_verdict: He therefore went out of his way to do things that would trigger inappropriate feelings of shame in himself, simply so he could practice overcoming such feelings. I have lately been trying to emulate Cato in this respect.
stoic_judgement: find himself feeling a bit ashamed
stoic_reason: The shame touches reputation, which is not up to him (Handbook 1). Assented to, it would be the judgement that others' opinion of his shirt is an evil, and so a passion (R2, Handbook 20). But 'find himself feeling a bit ashamed' reads as an unwilled first motion, and the vignette shows no assent (R3, fragment 9). His honest answer is an outward act whose judgement is not shown (R1).

other: You see a Roman emperor whose citizens tell jokes at his expense, and he does not punish them for doing so.
self: You are a Roman emperor, and when citizens tell jokes at your expense, you do not punish them for doing so.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: Irvine, recounting the life and reign of the emperor Marcus Aurelius
source_quote: Citizens told jokes at his expense and were not punished for doing so.
source_lesson: It is therefore with good reason that Marcus observed, in his Meditations, that "the art of living is more like wrestling than dancing."
source_verdict: As Roman emperors go, Marcus was exceptionally good. For one thing, he exercised great restraint in his use of power.
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: The vignette shows only an outward act, an emperor not punishing jokes. Under R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45) we cannot praise or blame it until we know the judgement behind it. He may refuse to count mockery as an insult (Handbook 20) and refuse anger (Discourses 1.18), or he may simply be indifferent or calculating. Under R7 unknown judgement is not neutral, so 'virtue' is provisional: forbearance fits a ruler's role (R6), but the row must be rewritten or flagged.

other: You see a Stoic who took up competitive rowing working through his fears of flipping, of rowing in the predawn darkness, and of being out in a tiny boat hundreds of yards from shore, choosing activities that give him butterflies simply so he can practice dealing with them.
self: You, having taken up competitive rowing as a Stoic, work through your fears of flipping, of rowing in the predawn darkness, and of being out in a tiny boat hundreds of yards from shore, choosing activities that give you butterflies simply so you can practice dealing with them.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine, the author, recounting his own practice of Stoicism
source_quote: It took me considerable effort to overcome my fear of flipping \(by successfully surviving three flips\). From there, I went on to work through other fears, including a fear of rowing in the predawn darkness, a fear of pushing off from the dock while standing up in the boat, and a fear of being out in the middle of a lake, hundreds of yards from the nearest shore, in a tiny boat \(that has thrice betrayed me\).
source_reason: I like to engage in activities, such as competitive rowing, that give me butterflies simply so I can practice dealing with them.
source_lesson: These feelings are, after all, an important component of the fear of failure, so that by dealing with them I am working to overcome my fear of failure.
source_verdict: I like to engage in activities, such as competitive rowing, that give me butterflies simply so I can practice dealing with them.
stoic_judgement: choosing activities that give him butterflies simply so he can practice dealing with them
stoic_reason: The act comes from a correct judgement (R1): he treats his fears as his own to train, which is the first field of Discourses 3.2 (aversions), and he deliberately seeks out that training, which is the mark of progress in Discourses 1.4. The fears he works through are not counted against him as passions endorsed (R2). They are the material of his training, and the vignette shows him working against them, so under R5 this is acting well as one making progress.

other: You see a man feeling a bit depressed taking a trip to cheer himself up, thinking a change of scenery might help to improve his mood.
self: You are feeling a bit depressed and take a trip to cheer yourself up, thinking a change of scenery might help to improve your mood.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle the verdict. If the man treats the change of place as the cure for his distress, he places the remedy in externals, which is an error. If he takes the trip as a reasonable rest, a preferred indifferent, while still working on his judgements, that is appropriate. Seneca himself approved of travel for relaxation and disapproved only of using it to escape oneself. 'Might help' is tentative and fits either reading.
source: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)
chapter: Wherever You Go, There You Are: You Can't Escape Yourself
speaker: David Fideler, recounting Seneca's comment to Lucilius
source_quote: LUCILIUS WAS FEELING A BIT DEPRESSED and wanted to cheer himself up by taking a trip, as many people do today.
source_reason: He thought a change of scenery might help to improve his mood.
source_lesson: But as Seneca commented, "You must change the mind, not the location," because "your faults will travel with you wherever you go."
source_verdict: Unfortunately, the project was a failure: Lucilius's depression was not cured.
stoic_judgement: thinking a change of scenery might help to improve his mood
stoic_reason: By Handbook 5 it is judgements, not things, that disturb us. A man who looks to a place, which is not up to him, to cure his mood has misjudged where his trouble and its remedy lie: a failure in the field of assent (R1, R2). Travel itself is an indifferent, and a rest may be preferred (Discourses 2.10), so the fault is only in the judgement as shown (R8: wisdom).

other: You see a novice banjo player, asked by his teacher to play in the students' recital, agree to take part because it is a wonderful opportunity to cause himself psychological discomfort and to confront his fear of failing.
self: You, a novice banjo player asked by your teacher to play in the students' recital, agree to take part because it is a wonderful opportunity to cause yourself psychological discomfort and to confront your fear of failing.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine, narrating his own experience as a Stoic practitioner
source_quote: I initially rejected the offer; it sounded like no fun at all to risk public humiliation trying to play banjo in front of a bunch of strangers. But then it occurred to me that this was a wonderful opportunity to cause myself psychological discomfort and to confront—and hopefully vanquish—my fear of failing. I agreed to take part.
source_reason: this was a wonderful opportunity to cause myself psychological discomfort and to confront—and hopefully vanquish—my fear of failing.
source_lesson: By taking part in the recital, in other words, I immunized myself against a fair amount of future anxiety.
source_verdict: Not at all. In causing myself anxiety by, for example, giving a banjo recital, I have precluded much future anxiety in my life.
stoic_judgement: agree to take part because it is a wonderful opportunity to cause himself psychological discomfort and to confront his fear of failing
stoic_reason: He acts from the judgement that public failure, a matter of reputation and so not up to him, is not something to flee, and he deliberately trains his aversion. This is the first field of training (Discourses 3.2), the work of a man making progress (Discourses 1.4). An act proceeding from that correct judgement is well done (R1, R5); the fear he means to face is the thing to be worked on, not the fault in this act (R2 applies only to a passion he assents to).

other: You see a father whose little son has just fallen down the steep stairs and scraped his back respond calmly, with concern but without panic, feeling no shock or surprise because he had anticipated it.
self: When your little son falls down the steep stairs and scrapes his back, you respond calmly, with concern but without panic, feeling no shock or surprise because you had anticipated it.

speaker: David Fideler, the author, recounting his own experience with his son Benjamin
source_quote: Since this was a serious concern, I would imagine Benjamin falling down the stairs and hurting himself. That way, if it actually happened, at least I'd be fully prepared for it. ... The Stoic training I had used allowed me to respond to the misfortune calmly—with concern, but without panic.
source_reason: There was no sense of shock or surprise when it happened, because I had anticipated it.
source_lesson: Rehearsing a potential disaster in advance increases your ability to cope and think clearly should the imagined disaster ever take place.
source_verdict: While this sounds like a slightly unpleasant exercise, I'm glad I did it
stoic_judgement: respond calmly, with concern but without panic, feeling no shock or surprise because he had anticipated it
stoic_reason: He does not assent to the impression that his son's fall is a dreadful evil (no panic, Handbook 5; R2 not met). His concern is the reasonable caution and affection of a father toward his son (Discourses 1.11, DL 7.116; R4), shown in his role (Handbook 30, Discourses 2.10; R6). The vignette shows the judgement he acts from, his prepared expectation that such a fall could happen, so it is acting well for one making progress (R1, R5).

other: You see a wealthy company owner walk over to his next-door neighbor's house after the neighbor's personal tragedy, to see how he is doing, and tell him, "I think you can only put it in God's hands."
self: When your next-door neighbor experiences a personal tragedy, you, a wealthy company owner, walk over to his house to see how he is doing and tell him, "I think you can only put it in God's hands."
source: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)
speaker: David Fideler, the author, recounting his wealthy next-door neighbor Fred as an example of Seneca's point
source_quote: Once, when I experienced a personal tragedy, Fred walked over to my house to see how I was doing. When we talked, he said, "When something like that happens, I think you can only put it in God's hands."
source_lesson: In any case, Fred is a perfect example of what Seneca had in mind when saying that if you possess wealth, you have a fabulous opportunity to practice virtue.
source_verdict: he was also down-to-earth, easy to talk with, and never once showed the least bit of arrogance or extravagance
stoic_judgement: walk over to his next-door neighbor's house after the neighbor's personal tragedy, to see how he is doing, and tell him, "I think you can only put it in God's hands."
stoic_reason: He visits out of concern for his neighbor and sympathizes in words without calling the loss an evil. He points the grieving man to what is not up to us and leaves it to God. That is affection joined with reason (Handbook 16; Discourses 1.11; Handbook 1), shown by his judgement, not only his outward act (R1, R4, R5). His duty as a neighbor is one of good fellowship (R6), and the main virtue is justice in its forms of kindness and good fellowship (R8).

other: You see a man, grieving a recent breakup, go to stay in a Palladian villa, since it is a once-in-a-lifetime chance and costs almost nothing, and break down in tears alone in his room.

chapter: Wherever You Go, There You Are: You Can't Escape Yourself
speaker: David Fideler, the author, telling a story from his own life
source_quote: I decided to go on the trip, which was unforgettable. But when I was alone in my room, I sometimes broke down into tears, because of the grief and disappointment that had followed me there.
source_reason: since it was a once-in-a-lifetime chance to stay in a Palladian villa \(and cost almost nothing\)
source_lesson: Whatever problems we suffer from internally, they do follow us
source_verdict: If you want to escape your troubles, you don't need to be somewhere else: you need to be someone else.
stoic_judgement: grieving a recent breakup ... break down in tears alone in his room
stoic_reason: Under R2, grief that persists and returns, carried with him to the villa, is the passion of distress: the judgement that losing the relationship, which is not up to him, is an evil (Handbook 5, 16; Discourses 3.2, a desire that failed to get its object). This is not tears at the first blow (R3, R4). Choosing the trip for a preferred indifferent is not the fault (Discourses 2.10).

other: You see a son who, after enduring his stroke-weakened mother's pleas for a glass of water she cannot safely drink, asks the nurse and, on her advice, pops an ice cube into his mother's mouth.
self: You, after enduring your stroke-weakened mother's pleas for a glass of water she cannot safely drink, ask the nurse and, on her advice, pop an ice cube into your mother's mouth.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine, the author, recounting his own experience caring for his mother
source_quote: I became my mother’s personal ice man, bringing a cup on each visit. ... I would pop a cube into her mouth, and she would, while sucking it, tell me how wonderful the ice was.
source_reason: After enduring my mother’s pleas for a time, I asked the nurse what to do. ... As a result of this advice
source_lesson: Nevertheless, watching her suck on ice cubes has been quite instructive. It has made me cognizant of yet another thing that I take utterly for granted: my ability to gulp down a big glass of cold water on a hot summer day.
source_verdict: Watching her suck appreciatively on ice cubes, I felt a tinge of envy. Wouldn’t it be wonderful, I thought, to be able to derive this much pleasure from a simple ice cube?
stoic_judgement: after enduring his stroke-weakened mother's pleas for a glass of water she cannot safely drink, asks the nurse and, on her advice, pops an ice cube into his mother's mouth
stoic_reason: In his role as a son (Handbook 30; Discourses 2.10; R6), he cleaves to what is naturally more fit to be chosen, her safety and her relief. He bears her pleas rather than give the dangerous water, and he deliberates by asking the nurse, so he acts 'upon good reasons, and not carelessly' (Discourses 3.2). Read as the judgement of someone making progress, this is acting well (R1, R5), and wisdom is the virtue most at stake (R8).

other: You see a wealthy company owner train thirty people to get off welfare and give them all permanent jobs, because he loves working on projects to make things better.
self: You are a wealthy company owner, and you train thirty people to get off welfare and give them all permanent jobs, because you love working on projects to make things better.
source: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)
speaker: David Fideler, recounting the example of his former next-door neighbor Fred to illustrate Seneca's point about wealth
source_quote: His family's foundation had given millions to the local community. But one program he created, and was understandably proud of, trained thirty people with the skills they needed to get off welfare. When they completed the training, he gave them all permanent jobs—a feat the government had been unable to accomplish.
source_reason: I love working on these projects to make things better. The most interesting problem, which I think about often, is how to eliminate poverty.
source_lesson: Fred is a perfect example of what Seneca had in mind when saying that if you possess wealth, you have a fabulous opportunity to practice virtue.
source_verdict: Fred is a perfect example of what Seneca had in mind when saying that if you possess wealth, you have a fabulous opportunity to practice virtue.
stoic_judgement: because he loves working on projects to make things better
stoic_reason: Under R1, the vignette shows his motive. He uses his wealth, which is not up to him, as material for his moral purpose (Discourses 1.29). He acts for what is by nature preferable for others, their livelihood and independence (Discourses 2.10), from affection joined with reason, which Epictetus calls 'right and good' (Discourses 1.11; R4). He is acting well as a person making progress (R5), and it comes nearest to justice in its parts, kindness and good fellowship (R8).

other: You see a Roman lover of luxury, finding he has "only" ten million sesterces (still a fortune) left, kill himself, afraid he might die in "poverty" and without his extravagant meals.
self: You, a Roman lover of luxury, finding you have "only" ten million sesterces (still a fortune) left, kill yourself, afraid you might die in "poverty" and without your extravagant meals.

speaker: Fideler, relaying Seneca's story of Apicius
source_quote: After he spent one hundred million Roman sesterces (an astronomically huge amount of money) on his addiction to fine dining, he discovered that he had "only" ten million left. Afraid that he might die in "poverty" and without his extravagant meals, Apicius killed himself instead.
source_reason: Afraid that he might die in "poverty" and without his extravagant meals
source_lesson: One of the greatest dangers of extreme wealth is that it encourages some people to become addicted to luxury, excess, and living beyond their means.
source_verdict: Offering a case study of out-of-control excess
modernised: [{"source": "ten million left", "vignette": "ten million sesterces (still a fortune) left", "why": "Readers today do not know the value of sesterces and might take the ironic \"only\" and \"poverty\" at face value, missing that the source treats the remaining sum as vast wealth."}]
stoic_judgement: afraid he might die in "poverty" and without his extravagant meals
stoic_reason: He kills himself from fear, judging the loss of wealth and fine dining, which are not up to him, to be a great evil and luxury a good he cannot live without. This is an assented passion acted on, the judgement that disturbs men (Handbook 5; Discourses 2.13; R1, R2). Craving externals has subordinated him to them (Discourses 1.4), so the act fails temperance first (R8).

other: You see a philosopher weeping so excessively for his dear friend, much younger than he, because he had never imagined it possible for his friend's death to precede his own.
self: You weep so excessively for your dear friend, much younger than you, because you had never imagined it possible for his death to precede yours.
source: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)
speaker: David Fideler, recounting Seneca’s confession to Lucilius about grieving for his friend Serenus
source_quote: Even Seneca failed to follow his own advice about this with his close friend Annaeus Serenus, who died at a young age. As Seneca confided to Lucilius, “I wept so excessively for my dear friend.”
source_reason: That’s because Serenus was so much younger, and, as Seneca said, “I had never imagined it possible for his death to precede mine.”
source_lesson: That’s why it’s helpful to remind ourselves from time to time that it could take place. ... He concluded, “Let us continually think as much about our own mortality as about all of those we love. . . . Whatever can happen at any time can happen today.”
source_verdict: Even Seneca failed to follow his own advice about this with his close friend Annaeus Serenus, who died at a young age.
stoic_judgement: weeping so excessively ... because he had never imagined it possible for his friend's death to precede his own
stoic_reason: The weeping is called excessive, so it is not a first movement at the first blow (R3, R4). It comes from a wrong assent: he counted on keeping something not up to him, his friend's life, and treated losing it as an evil. That is a desire falling short of an external, the source of strong emotion in Discourses 3.2, so it is an assented passion and acting badly (R2, R1).

other: You see a man drinking a lot of alcohol and using other mind-altering substances to cope with breakup grief.
self: You drink a lot of alcohol and use other mind-altering substances to cope with breakup grief.
source: Einzelgänger, Stoicism for Inner Peace (2021; quoted translators unspecified)
speaker: Einzelgänger, the author, recounting his own past way of coping with breakup grief
source_quote: I used to drink a lot of alcohol and used other mind-altering substances to cope with breakup grief, which eventually led to hangovers, increased sadness, and doing very stupid things.
source_reason: to cope with breakup grief
source_lesson: From my personal experience, I can say the ideal way to deal with grief is a balance of active engagement with the world and moments in solitude to 'sit with it.'
source_verdict: These were just quick fixes that wouldn't help in the long run.
stoic_judgement: drinking a lot of alcohol and using other mind-altering substances to cope with breakup grief
stoic_reason: The vignette names the judgement behind the drinking (R1, Handbook 45): it is not mere 'drinking a good deal' but numbing a grief he has assented to. Repeated intoxication to escape it shows he treats the loss of the partner, a thing not up to him, as an evil he cannot bear (Handbook 5, 16). That is a passion, not a first movement or involuntary tears (R2, R3, R4). He also fails at the restraint of appetite, so the act is acting badly, chiefly against temperance (R8).

other: You see a man look in the mirror one morning, as he has every morning for thirty-three years since reading a quote at seventeen, and ask himself: "If today were the last day of my life, would I want to do what I am about to do today?"
self: You look in the mirror one morning, as you have every morning for thirty-three years since reading a quote at seventeen, and ask yourself: "If today were the last day of my life, would I want to do what I am about to do today?"
contested_note: Fideler and Seneca (Letters 61.1, 'settle our accounts with life every day') praise the practice. Epictetus's framing does not settle it, because the test is 'would I want to do', which is desire, not what reason or one's role asks (R6). If what he wants is externals such as success, the practice could serve a faulty judgement (R1, R9).
source: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)
chapter: LIVING EACH DAY AS IF IT'S YOUR LAST
speaker: Steve Jobs, in a speech to college students, quoted by Fideler
source_quote: for the past thirty-three years, I have looked in the mirror every morning and asked myself: "If today were the last day of my life, would I want to do what I am about to do today? And whenever the answer has been "No" for too many days in a row, I know I need to change something.
source_reason: When I was seventeen, I read a quote that went something like: "If you live each day as if it was your last, someday you'll most certainly be right." It made an impression on me
source_lesson: As a daily meditation, it encourages a person to reflect on his or her life as a whole, including the quality of one's life at that very moment.
source_verdict: But regardless of that, it's undoubtedly a good practice.
stoic_judgement: ask himself: "If today were the last day of my life, would I want to do what I am about to do today?"
stoic_reason: Each morning he examines his own coming actions, which are up to him (Handbook 1), in the light of death. This is the morning practice of one making progress (Discourses 1.4), so it is labelled acting well (R5, R1), with wisdom as the main virtue (R8). But the vignette shows only the question. It does not show whether his measure of a day worth living is a right moral purpose or something outside his control.

other: You see a father, whose young son performed badly at school today by biting a girl's foot, say of him, "My son acted poorly today."
self: When your young son performs badly at school today by biting a girl's foot, you say of him, "My son acted poorly today."
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle the case. Read as a calm, correct assent about an act within the boy's choice, it is acting well. But Handbook 45 warns against saying someone acts 'badly' without knowing the judgement that prompted him, and the vignette does not show whether the father inwardly treats the incident as an evil to himself. The source (Fideler) approves the remark as a mere observation, not a complaint. | From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as vice: Handbook 45 and Discourses 4.8 (R1) warn against saying someone acts badly before learning the judgement that prompts him. The father reports not the act ('my son bit a girl's foot') but a verdict on it, which reads as hasty assent, a fault in the third field. But as a father (R6) he may have to judge and correct his son, and may know his son's motive, so the verdict is tentative.
source: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)
speaker: David Fideler (the author), giving an example from his son Benjamin's behavior at school
source_quote: performed badly at school today by biting a girl's foot—yes, that happened when he was in first grade
source_lesson: In the end, complaining involves expressing emotional dissatisfaction.
source_verdict: If my son performed badly at school today by biting a girl's foot—yes, that happened when he was in first grade!—I could say, "Benjamin acted poorly today," and it would not be a complaint.
stoic_judgement: say of him, "My son acted poorly today." (the plain description is shown, but not what he feels or treats as good or bad)
stoic_reason: The father places the fault in his son's act, which comes from the boy's own choice, and adds no cry that this is an evil befallen himself. That fits Discourses 1.29 and Handbook 5, and correcting a child's conduct is what a father's role asks (R6). But R1 and Discourses 4.8 forbid praising an act whose judgement is not shown. The label is therefore a provisional, low-confidence 'virtue' (R5), flagged rather than defaulted to neutral (R1, R7).

other: You see a farmer murder his brother, a shepherd, after God accepted the brother's offerings and rejected his, envious of his brother's virtue and the consequences of that virtue.

speaker: Einzelgänger, retelling the story of Cain and Abel from the *Old Testament* and the *Quran*
source_quote: Cain murdered his brother
source_reason: Thus we could say that Cain was envious of Abel’s virtue and the consequences of that virtue.
source_lesson: Instead of killing his brother, Cain could have used the spark of envy to realize that Abel was doing a better job than him. He could have seen his brother as an inspiration for becoming more virtuous himself.
source_verdict: Unfortunately, some people are so envious that they engage in immoral behavior like stealing, infidelity, and even murder.
stoic_judgement: envious of his brother's virtue and the consequences of that virtue
stoic_reason: Under R1 and R2, the act comes from envy, an assented passion: a judgement that his brother's being accepted, which is not up to the farmer, is a good he lacks. Handbook 19 says that if the good lies in what is up to us, 'there is no place for either envy or jealousy'. Envy of virtue misses that his own virtue was in his own power. Acting on that judgement by murder is the plainest failure of justice, the knowledge of what is due to others and especially to a brother (R6, the role of brother).

other: You see a man thank his wife for the cup of black tea with milk she brings to his bedside table, then, sipping it, feel grateful for the tea, his warm bed, and clean air.

source_quote: when she brings me a cup of tea, I'm very grateful to her as a person, and I always thank her. But then, as I sip the tea, I usually feel other kinds of gratitude, too, which is a perfect way to start the day.
source_lesson: Sometimes these different kinds of gratitude can intermingle with one another.
source_verdict: But then, as I sip the tea, I usually feel other kinds of gratitude, too, which is a perfect way to start the day.

stoic_reason: Thanking his wife fits his role as husband (R6) and is fair dealing toward her. His gratitude is a good feeling, which Epictetus endorses (Long §9.3: 'gratitude, cheerfulness, joy'). It is not a passion, because he does not treat the tea or the bed as goods he must have; he treats them as preferred things he has received with appreciation (R4, R5).

other: You see a Stoic teacher, in the middle of teaching, send home one of his students who has told him that he wants to go home because he is sick.

source: Einzelgänger, Stoicism for Inner Peace (2021; quoted translators unspecified)
speaker: Einzelgänger (the author), retelling an episode from Epictetus’ teaching recorded in the Discourses
source_quote: When Epictetus was teaching, one of his students told him that he wanted to go home, because he was sick. Epictetus then sent him home.
source_reason: because he was sick
source_lesson: The lesson we take from this is that it’s wise to do what the current situation asks of us.
source_verdict: The lesson we take from this is that it’s wise to do what the current situation asks of us.

stoic_reason: Per R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45), only the outward act is shown: a teacher sends home a sick student who asked to leave. Without the judgement behind it we can neither praise nor blame. Releasing a sick student is an appropriate act for a teacher's role (R6), so 'virtue' is a provisional label for a row that must be rewritten to show the judgement, not a verdict. R7 rules out 'neutral' by default.

other: You see a writer fasting for seventy-two hours, refraining from eating and only consuming water.

contested_note: From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as neutral: The vignette shows only an outward act, a 72-hour water fast. Under Handbook 45 and Discourses 4.8 we must say only that he fasts long, neither praising nor blaming it, until we know the judgement it proceeds from (R1). Under R7, an unknown judgement is not positive evidence for neutral, so the label below is a placeholder pending a rewrite, not a verdict.
source: Einzelgänger, Stoicism for Inner Peace (2021; quoted translators unspecified)
speaker: Einzelgänger (the author), recounting his own experience in first person
source_quote: I fasted for seventy-two hours (meaning that I refrained from eating and only consumed water)
source_lesson: What I learned from fasting is that many of the desires that we may perceive as 'bodily needs' are created by ideas we have in regards to those desires.
source_verdict: I've become less prone to fear of not eating, knowing that I'll be fine and that I'm perfectly able to function when I don't eat for a while. As a consequence, I worry less about food.
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: The vignette shows only an outward act, fasting on water for seventy-two hours. By Discourses 4.8 and Handbook 45 (R1) we can neither praise nor blame it until we know the judgement behind it. The label is provisional: the source gives the motive as training self-control and testing the belief that he would faint without food, which is restraint of desire and correction of a false impression (R2, R8). On that reading it is temperance, but the vignette itself must show this before the label stands. Unknown judgement is not neutral (R7).

other: You see a young boy with a bad temper hammer about thirty nails into the fence in one day, a nail for every time he lost his temper, as his father told him to.
self: You are a young boy with a bad temper, and in one day you hammer about thirty nails into the fence, a nail for every time you lost your temper, as your father told you to.
source: Einzelgänger, Stoicism for Inner Peace (2021; quoted translators unspecified)
speaker: Einzelgänger, retelling a Buddhist story
source_quote: He told him to hammer a nail into the fence every time he lost his temper. After the first day, the boy hammered about thirty nails in the fence.
source_lesson: Even when we may seem to have a very good reason to be angry, which is a sense of being wronged and violated, we only risk doing further damage if we throw our ability to reason in the gutter and let our emotions take over.
source_verdict: Even when we may seem to have a very good reason to be angry, which is a sense of being wronged and violated, we only risk doing further damage if we throw our ability to reason in the gutter and let our emotions take over.
stoic_judgement: a young boy with a bad temper ... a nail for every time he lost his temper
stoic_reason: Thirty losses of temper in one day are outbursts, not a sudden blench, so they are anger assented to: the judgement that someone has wronged him, which Handbook 20 says is his own judgement (R2, not R3). Hammering the nails 'as his father told him' is an appropriate act toward a father (Handbook 30, R6), but the vignette does not show from what judgement he does it, so it cannot be praised (R1, Discourses 4.8). What the vignette does show of his judgement is the anger.

other: You see a thirteen-year-old boy, totally unprepared for his father's death from lung cancer, become angry and depressed.
self: You are thirteen, totally unprepared for your father's death from lung cancer, and you become angry and depressed.
source: Donald J. Robertson, How to Think Like a Roman Emperor (2019; modern retelling)
speaker: Donald J. Robertson, the author, narrating his own teenage years
source_quote: I coped with it badly. I became angry and depressed.
source_reason: I was totally unprepared for his death
source_lesson: I didn’t know it at the time, but that sort of existential anxiety is a common experience that drives people to the study of philosophy.
source_verdict: I coped with it badly.
stoic_judgement: totally unprepared for his father's death ... become angry and depressed
stoic_reason: Anger and depression (grief) that he 'becomes', as a lasting state rather than a sudden shrinking, are assented passions. Each is the judgement that an external, his father's death, is an evil, and that is acting badly even with no outward deed (R2, Handbook 5). They are not unwilled first movements (R3), and they go beyond the tears that R4 excuses. Being 'totally unprepared' points to a failure to see that his father's life was not up to him (Handbook 1).

contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not fully settle it. Good reputation is a preferred indifferent, and he says we should 'cleave to that which is naturally more fit to be chosen' (Discourses 2.10). He also measures duties by role (R6): here, a student before his professors. Outside Part 1, he asks young men to be clean and decent in appearance rather than slovenly (Discourses 4.11), and warns that training exercises should not be done for display (Discourses 3.12). The deliberate lowering of reputation is the Cynic practice the source cites (Diogenes of Sinope), and Epictetus reserves that calling for few (Discourses 3.22). On that reading the act could be an error against his role. Read as training the judgement and not as courting disrepute, it is acting well.

It comes nearest to temperance, the restraint of vanity and the craving for approval (R8).

contested_note: The calm contemplation is settled, but refusing food to hasten death is not. The earlier Stoics (Diogenes Laertius 7.130) allow a reasonable departure from life, for instance under incurable disease. Epictetus says 'the door is open' but warns against leaving before the god gives the signal (Discourses 1.9, 1.29). Since he is already dying, most readers would allow it, but Epictetus's framing as given in Part 1 does not settle the refusal itself.

source_quote: Now he *voluntarily* rejects food and drink to hasten his own demise. ... He therefore asks his physicians to describe patiently and in detail what's happening inside his body, so that he may contemplate his own symptoms with the studied indifference of a natural philosopher.

He still sheds tears and mourns losses, but as a wise man does. He no longer adds to his natural grief by complaining and shaking his fist at the universe.

Studying his own symptoms calmly is an act that proceeds from a correct judgement and is done well by one making progress (R1, R5). Facing death without dread is endurance, so the main virtue is courage (R8).

Like the citharoede who wants applause (Discourses 2.13), he subordinates himself to those who can procure or prevent what he craves or shuns (Discourses 1.4). This is an assented fear of externals and a giving up of his own purpose, so it is acting badly (R1, R2). It fails courage chiefly, with wisdom (confusing what is up to him) and justice (good faith in speech) also at stake (R8).

An act that proceeds from this correct judgement is well done (R1, R5), and seeing what is and is not up to us is chiefly wisdom (R8).

He simply carried on doing what he loved: discussing philosophy with his friends.
source_lesson: Marcus quotes this letter and then exhorts himself always to act as Epicurus did: remain focused on the pursuit of wisdom even in the face of illness, pain, or any other hardship. This advice, he says, is common not only to Epicureanism and Stoicism but to all other schools of philosophy. Our main concern should always remain the use we are making right now, from moment to moment, of our own mind.

stoic_reason: He treats the body's illness as not up to him and keeps attending to his own moral purpose and his proper work. Epictetus would say he 'eats as a self-respecting man' while sick (Discourses 1.4) and makes correct use of impressions (R1, R2 not triggered, R5). Endurance of hardship without assenting to the impression that it is an evil comes nearest to courage (R8).

contested_note: The deferral itself proceeds from correct judgement and is acting well. But the vignette says he is 'angry'. If that anger is an assented passion (the judgement that the slave's fault is an evil done to him, Handbook 20, Discourses 1.18), R2 counts the feeling itself as acting badly, even though he does not act on it. If it is only a first movement (fragment 9; Seneca, De ira 2.2-4) that he then checks, there is no fault in it. Seneca's text ('at the moment, he corrected himself') suggests the second reading, but this does not fully settle the verdict on the whole person.

Under R1 and R5 this is acting well as one making progress.
