other: You see a general, when a soldier condemned as his comrade's murderer is brought back with the comrade alive, order both and the centurion executed: for being condemned, for causing the condemnation, for disobeying his general.
self: You are a general, and when a soldier condemned as his comrade's murderer is brought back with the comrade alive, you order both and the centurion executed: for being condemned, for causing the condemnation, for disobeying his general.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 1.18 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise On Anger, writing to Novatus
source_quote: In his anger he ordered a soldier to be led off to execution because he had returned from furlough without his comrade, as though he must have murdered him if he could not show him. ... Piso mounted the tribunal in a fury and ordered them both to be executed, both him who had not murdered and him who had not been slain. ... Piso even added a third: for he actually ordered the centurion, who had brought back the condemned man, to be put to death.
source_reason: “You,” it says, “I order to be executed, because you have been condemned to death: you, because you have been the cause of your comrade’s condemnation, and you, because when ordered to put him to death you disobeyed your general.”
source_lesson: O, how clever is anger at inventing reasons for its frenzy\!
source_verdict: What could be more unworthy than this? Because one was proved to be innocent, two perished.
stoic_judgement: order both and the centurion executed: for being condemned, for causing the condemnation, for disobeying his general
stoic_reason: The reasons he gives are his judgement (R1). He treats a condemnation already shown false, and obedience to himself, as grounds to kill three innocent men, ranking his authority and the appearance of consistency (externals, not up to him) above justice. Even if he holds these reasons sincerely, the judgement is wrong and the act is done badly (Handbook 42; Discourses 4.8). As general he is a guardian of his soldiers, not their enemy (R6). Executing the innocent is what reason forbids (Arius 11a).

other: You see a man, rather angry at some fault of his slave, ask his associate to correct the slave with stripes for him, because in his rage he would beat him more than he ought.
self: You, rather angry at some fault of your slave, ask your associate to correct the slave with stripes for you, because in your rage you would beat him more than you ought.
contested_note: The act of delegating is well done, since it comes from the correct judgement that his anger unfits him to punish. But the anger itself, if assented to, is a passion and so acting badly (R2, Discourses 1.18: 'what ground is left for you to be angry at him?'). On the strict view he still has a punishment carried out while he is angry, against Seneca's own lesson that 'while you are angry, you ought not to be allowed to do anything.' Seneca praises the act. Epictetus's framing settles the act but not the feeling.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.12 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca
source_quote: He therefore denied himself the exercise of authority over his own household, and once, being rather angry at some fault, said, "Speusippus, will you please to correct that slave with stripes; for I am in a rage." He would not strike him, for the very reason for which another man would have struck him.
source_reason: "I am in a rage," said he; "I should beat him more than I ought: I should take more pleasure than I ought in doing so: let not that slave fall into the power of one who is not in his own power."
source_lesson: While you are angry, you ought not to be allowed to do anything.
source_verdict: Can anyone wish to grant the power of revenge to an angry man, when Plato himself gave up his own right to exercise it?
stoic_judgement: because in his rage he would beat him more than he ought
stoic_reason: He judges his own rage to be what is wrong here, not the slave's fault. He refuses to let the slave 'fall into the power of one who is not in his own power', so the act of handing over the correction comes from a correct judgement about his own moral purpose. That is acting well as one making progress (R1, R5), and it is self-restraint of anger (R8). Correcting a household member is a duty of his role as master (R6).

other: You see a philosopher who, when he is given a box on the ear by a man, merely says that it is a pity a man cannot tell when he ought to wear his helmet out walking.
self: You, when you are given a box on the ear by a man, merely say that it is a pity a man cannot tell when he ought to wear his helmet out walking.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.11 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, advising the reader how to check anger
source_quote: when he was given a box on the ear, merely said that it was a pity a man could not tell when he ought to wear his helmet out walking
source_lesson: It does not so much matter how an injury is done, as how it is borne; and I do not see how moderation can be hard to practise, when I know that even despots, though success and impunity combine to swell their pride, have sometimes restrained their natural ferocity.
source_verdict: It does not so much matter how an injury is done, as how it is borne; and I do not see how moderation can be hard to practise, when I know that even despots, though success and impunity combine to swell their pride, have sometimes restrained their natural ferocity.
stoic_judgement: merely says that it is a pity a man cannot tell when he ought to wear his helmet out walking
stoic_reason: Struck, he treats the blow as a mere bodily accident, like weather one should dress for, not as an insult. By Handbook 20 it is only one's own judgement that insults one, and he makes no such judgement. He gives no assent to anger (R2), and the jest shows the correct judgement behind his reply (R1). That is acting well as one making progress (R5), and it falls under restraint of anger (R8).
also_in: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)

other: You see a man, struck in the public bath by someone who did not know him, reply to his apology, "I do not remember being struck," thinking it better to ignore the insult than to revenge it.
self: You, struck in the public bath by someone who did not know you, reply to his apology, "I do not remember being struck," thinking it better to ignore the insult than to revenge it.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 2.32 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, citing Cato
source_quote: Afterwards when he was apologizing, Cato replied, "I do not remember being struck."
source_reason: He thought it better to ignore the insult than to revenge it.
source_lesson: It is the part of a great mind to despise wrongs done to it; the most contemptuous form of revenge is not to deem one's adversary worth taking vengeance upon.
source_verdict: He thought it better to ignore the insult than to revenge it.
stoic_judgement: thinking it better to ignore the insult than to revenge it
stoic_reason: Cato does not assent to the impression that he has been harmed. It is not the striker who insults a man but his judgement that he is insulted (Handbook 20), and there is no ground for anger at someone who erred in ignorance (Discourses 1.18). His refusal to retaliate comes from a correct judgement, so it is acting well (R1, R2 in reverse, R5), and restraining anger falls under temperance (R8).
also_in: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)

other: You see a distinguished Roman knight, whose son the emperor has just had executed, dine at the emperor's banquet with a countenance which betrays no ill will, shedding no tear, because he has another son.
self: You, a distinguished Roman knight whose son the emperor has just had executed, dine at the emperor's banquet with a countenance which betrays no ill will, shedding no tear, because you have another son.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not fully settle the case. Read one way, the father acts with rational caution for a preferred indifferent within his role, which is acting well. Read another way, he acts from fear, treating the second son's life, which is not up to him, as a good he must keep, and that is a passion (Discourses 2.13). Some Stoic exemplars, such as Agrippinus and Helvidius, refuse to play the tyrant's part, though they do so when only their own lives are at stake. Seneca, who is of the same school, approves: 'love for his son quenched his anger.'
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 2.33 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise On Anger
source_quote: Pastor came with a countenance which betrayed no ill will. ... he shed no tear the while; he did not permit his grief to betray itself by the slightest sign; he dined just as though his entreaties had gained his son's life.
source_reason: he had another son. ... he would have lost his second son had he proved an unacceptable guest to the murderer of his eldest.
source_lesson: It is often so far from expedient to avenge our wrongs, that it will not do even to admit them.
source_verdict: The wrongs of the powerful must not only be borne, but borne with a cheerful countenance: they will repeat the wrong if they think they have inflicted it.
stoic_judgement: dine at the emperor's banquet with a countenance which betrays no ill will, shedding no tear, because he has another son
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement behind the act: he bears the tyrant's wrong for the sake of his living son. That fits what his role as father asks (R6, Handbook 30, Discourses 2.10) and cleaves to what is naturally to be preferred, his son's life (Discourses 2.10). He endures hardship and holds back anger, which is acting well as one making progress (R1, R5, R8). Shedding no tear is not itself the fault, nor the merit (R4).

other: You see a citizen of Sybaris, watching a man digging and vigorously brandishing a mattock, complain that the sight makes him weary, and forbid the man to work where he can see him.
self: You see a man digging and vigorously brandishing a mattock, complain that the sight makes you weary, and forbid him to work where you can see him.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 2.25 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise On Anger
source_quote: complained that the sight made him weary, and forbade the man to work where he could see him. The same man complained that he had suffered from the rose-leaves upon which he lay being folded double.
source_reason: the sight made him weary ... he had suffered from the rose-leaves upon which he lay being folded double
source_lesson: Nothing, therefore, nourishes anger more than excessive and dissatisfied luxury: the mind ought to be hardened by rough treatment, so as not to feel any blow that is not severe.
source_verdict: When pleasures have corrupted both the body and the mind, nothing seems endurable, not indeed because it is hard, but because he who has to bear it is soft
stoic_judgement: complain that the sight makes him weary, and forbid the man to work where he can see him
stoic_reason: He treats the mere sight of another's labour, an external not up to him, as an evil done to him. He assents to that aversion: he complains and acts on it by stopping another man's work. Under R1 and R2 this is a passion acted on, a failure in the first field of desire and aversion (Discourses 3.2, Handbook 5), so it is acting badly; it is not a first movement (R3).

other: You see a king's closest friend, who had advised him to drink more sparingly, look at his son shot through the heart by the drunken king and reply that Apollo himself could not have taken better aim.
self: You, the king's closest friend who advised him to drink more sparingly, look at your son shot through the heart by the drunken king and reply that Apollo himself could not have taken better aim.
contested_note: Seneca, a Stoic, is split. He condemns the praise ('a slave in mind ... it was worse to praise that arrow-shot than to shoot it') but says the father 'may be said to have done well in choking down his words', since he did not curse the king and so held back his anger. On an Epictetan reading, holding back anger would be acting well, but flattering a tyrant out of fear is acting badly. The vignette shows only the praise, not the inner judgement. If he spoke from a correct judgement (for example, to protect others, without assenting that his life was a good), Epictetus's framing would not condemn him. So the verdict depends on a motive the text does not give.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.14 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, telling the story as an example that anger can be suppressed
source_quote: He replied, that Apollo himself could not have taken better aim.
source_reason: He thought that the breast of his son being torn asunder, and his heart quivering with its wound, gave him an opportunity of making a complimentary speech.
source_lesson: the matter which we are now discussing, has been proved, I mean, that anger can be suppressed.
source_verdict: He actually praised an act which he ought not to have endured to witness. ... it was worse to praise that arrow-shot than to shoot it.
stoic_judgement: not shown: the vignette gives only his words, "Apollo himself could not have taken better aim", spoken over his son's body to the king who killed him. It does not say whether he speaks from fear of the king, flattery, or some other judgement.
stoic_reason: Under R1, the words alone are a false and flattering praise of a murder. Read as the fear of a man who treats his life and the king's favour, things not up to him, as goods worth buying with a lie, this is acting badly: he 'must end by subordinating himself to others, those who are able to procure or prevent these things that he craves or shuns' (Discourses 1.4; Handbook 52 on lying). Because the vignette never states that judgement, the verdict rests on our reading (R1, R2, R9).

other: You see a conqueror, never violent in anger, burn letters to his civil-war rival from men thought neutral or hostile, to put it out of his power to be angry, thinking the kindest pardon was not knowing their offence.
self: You, a conqueror never violent in anger, burn letters to your civil-war rival from men thought neutral or hostile, to put it out of your power to be angry, thinking the kindest pardon is not knowing their offence.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 2.23 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise On Anger
source_quote: he burned a packet of letters addressed to Gnaeus Pompeius by persons who had been thought to be either neutrals or on the other side.
source_reason: he preferred to put it out of his power to be angry: he thought that the kindest way to pardon each of them was not to know what his offence had been.
source_lesson: but the rarer moderation is among kings, the more it deserves to be praised.
source_verdict: Though he was never violent in his anger, yet he preferred to put it out of his power to be angry: he thought that the kindest way to pardon each of them was not to know what his offence had been.
stoic_judgement: to put it out of his power to be angry, thinking the kindest pardon was not knowing their offence
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement he acts from (R1). He treats anger as a fault to be kept from his own moral purpose, and pardon as the kind thing to do, rather than counting the letter-writers' disloyalty as a harm done to him (Handbook 20; Discourses 1.18). For a man making progress (R5), and in a conqueror's role, where clemency toward the defeated is what reason urges (R6), this is acting well. It comes nearest to temperance, the restraint of anger, with the justice of kindness and pardon also at stake (R8).

other: You see a king, hearing his soldiers curse him for bringing them into impassable mud, extricate the worst-stuck without their knowing their helper, and say, "Now curse the king, but bless the man who has brought you out of this slough."
self: You, a king hearing your soldiers curse you for bringing them into impassable mud, extricate the worst-stuck without their knowing their helper, and say, "Now curse the king, but bless the man who has brought you out of this slough."
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.22 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, addressing the reader
source_quote: He also on one night, hearing some of his soldiers invoking everything that was evil upon their king for having brought them along that road and into that impassable mud, went to those who were in the greatest difficulties, and having extricated them without their knowing who was their helper, said, "Now curse Antigonus, by whose fault you have fallen into this trouble, but bless the man who has brought you out of this slough."
source_lesson: These should be regarded as examples to be avoided, and what I am about to relate, on the contrary, to be followed, being examples of gentle and lenient conduct in men who both had reasons for anger and power to avenge themselves.
source_verdict: what I am about to relate, on the contrary, to be followed, being examples of gentle and lenient conduct in men who both had reasons for anger and power to avenge themselves.
stoic_judgement: hearing his soldiers curse him ... extricate the worst-stuck without their knowing their helper, and say, "Now curse the king, but bless the man who has brought you out of this slough."
stoic_reason: He does not take the soldiers' curses as an insult (Handbook 20), so no anger is assented to (R2). In his role as their king he helps those in greatest need without claiming credit, and his remark treats the abuse lightly. His act proceeds from correct judgements about what is and is not up to him, and about what his role asks (R1, R6), so it is acting well as one making progress (R5). The main virtue at stake is restraint of anger under insult, with kindness to his men also present (R8).

other: You see a king hurrying to besiege Babylon, enraged that a river washed away one of his chariot's white horses, devote all his army's resources to cutting channels until its bed is dry.
self: You, a king hurrying to besiege Babylon, enraged that a river washed away one of your chariot's white horses, devote all your army's resources to cutting channels until its bed is dry.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.21 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, addressing the reader
source_quote: he swore to reduce the river which had carried off his royal retinue to so low an ebb that even women should walk across it and trample upon it. He thereupon devoted all the resources of his army to this object, and remained working until by cutting one hundred and eighty channels across the bed of the river he divided it into three hundred and sixty brooks, and left the bed dry, the waters flowing through other channels.
source_reason: one of the white horses which drew the royal chariot was washed away, and his loss moved the king to such violent rage
source_lesson: Thus he lost time, which is very important in great operations, and lost, also, the soldiers’ courage, which was broken by useless labour, and the opportunity of falling upon his enemy unprepared, while he was waging against the river the war which he had declared against his foes.
source_verdict: This frenzy, for what else can you call it, has befallen Romans also
stoic_judgement: enraged that a river washed away one of his chariot's white horses, devote all his army's resources to cutting channels until its bed is dry
stoic_reason: He judges the loss of a horse, an external not up to him, to be an evil and the senseless river to have wronged him. That is an assented passion (R2, Handbook 5 and 20). It is no first movement (R3), since he acts on it at length, and as king and commander he neglects what his role asks (R6) by spending his army on a war against a river.

other: You see a poor pupil, whose fellow pupils each give their teacher large presents, say he can find nothing worthy of him, and so present him with the only thing he possesses, himself.
self: You are a poor pupil whose fellow pupils each give your teacher large presents; finding nothing to give him which is worthy of him, you present him with the only thing you possess, yourself.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 1.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise on benefits
source_quote: Therefore I present you with the only thing I possess, myself.
source_reason: I can find nothing to give you which is worthy of you; I feel my poverty in this respect alone.
source_lesson: We must not consider how great presents are, but in what spirit they are given.
source_verdict: By this present Aeschines outdid Alcibiades, whose mind was as great as his Wealth, and all the splendour of the most wealthy youths of Athens.
stoic_judgement: say he can find nothing worthy of him, and so present him with the only thing he possesses, himself
stoic_reason: He judges that externals he lacks are not what matters and gives what is truly his own, himself and his moral purpose, to his teacher's care. Under R1 and R6 this is a pupil acting well in his role from a correct judgement (Discourses 1.29: externals are only materials for the moral purpose), and under R5 it counts as acting well while making progress.

other: You see a king, hearing two common soldiers leaning against his tent speak evil of him, gently raise the cloth and say, "Go a little further off, for fear the king should hear you."
self: You are a king, and hearing two common soldiers leaning against your tent speak evil of you, you gently raise the cloth and say, "Go a little further off, for fear the king should hear you."
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.22 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca
source_quote: Antigonus heard all they said, as was likely, since there was only a piece of cloth between the speakers and the listener, who gently raised it, .and said "Go a little further off, for fear the king should hear you."
source_lesson: These should be regarded as examples to be avoided, and what I am about to relate, on the contrary, to be followed, being examples of gentle and lenient conduct in men who both had reasons for anger and power to avenge themselves.
source_verdict: what I am about to relate, on the contrary, to be followed, being examples of gentle and lenient conduct in men who both had reasons for anger and power to avenge themselves
stoic_judgement: gently raise the cloth and say, "Go a little further off, for fear the king should hear you."
stoic_reason: The king hears himself reviled, has the power to punish, and answers gently and with a jest. This shows he did not assent to the impression that he was insulted (Handbook 20), so no anger arose: his own moral purpose was not harmed (Discourses 1.18). This is acting well while making progress (R1, R2, R5). The main virtue at stake is the restraint of anger (R8).

other: You see a man pleading a case, spat upon the forehead by a demagogue, wipe his face and say, "I shall declare to all the world that men are mistaken when they say that you are wanting in cheek."
self: When a demagogue spits upon your forehead while you are pleading a case, you wipe your face and say, "I shall declare to all the world that men are mistaken when they say that you are wanting in cheek."
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.38 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in an essay addressed to Novatus
source_quote: Cato wiped his face, and said, "Lentulus, I shall declare to all the world that men are mistaken when they say that you are wanting in cheek."
source_verdict: Yet how much better did our Cato behave?
stoic_judgement: wipe his face and say, "I shall declare to all the world that men are mistaken when they say that you are wanting in cheek."
stoic_reason: Under Handbook 20, the insult lies in one's own judgement. Cato calmly wipes his face and answers with a jest instead of retaliating, which shows he did not assent to the impression that being spat on harmed him. The deed belongs to Lentulus and is not up to Cato, so he has no ground for anger (Discourses 1.18). This is restraint of anger while making progress (R1, R2 by contrast, R5, R8).
also_in: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)

other: You see an emperor, shocked that his friend and host ordered a slave thrown to his fish for breaking a crystal goblet, order the slave let go, the crystal broken, and the tank filled.
self: You, an emperor shocked that your friend and host ordered a slave thrown to his fish for breaking a crystal goblet, order the slave let go, the crystal broken, and the tank filled.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.40 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, writing to Novatus
source_quote: Caesar was shocked at this novel form of cruelty, and ordered him to be let go, and, in his place, all the crystal ware which he saw before him to be broken, and the tank to be filled up.
source_reason: Caesar was shocked at this novel form of cruelty
source_lesson: This was the proper way for Caesar to reprove his friend: he made a good use of his power.
source_verdict: he made a good use of his power.
stoic_judgement: shocked that his friend and host ordered a slave thrown to his fish for breaking a crystal goblet
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the emperor judging that a man's life outweighs a broken goblet, an external, and he acts in his role as the one with power to stop the cruelty. By saving the slave and removing the crystal and the tank that served the cruelty, he does the appropriate act from a correct judgement, so it is acting well (R1, R5, R6). His shock reads as rational aversion to injustice, not an assented passion (R4).

other: You see a king, told "Hang yourself" by an Athenian ambassador, bid his indignant bystanders be silent and let him depart safe, saying those who say such things are more arrogant than those who hear them unrevenged.
self: You, a king told "Hang yourself" by an Athenian ambassador, bid your indignant bystanders be silent and let him depart safe, saying those who say such things are more arrogant than those who hear them unrevenged.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.23 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, addressing the reader
source_quote: Philip bade them be silent, and let this Thersites depart safe and sound. ... he allowed a man to curse him with impunity.
source_reason: "But do you," said he, "you other ambassadors, tell the Athenians that those who say such things are much more arrogant than those who hear them without revenging themselves."
source_lesson: Let everyone, then, say to himself, whenever he is provoked, "Am I more powerful than Philip? yet he allowed a man to curse him with impunity.
source_verdict: it was an especial virtue of Philip's to endure insults patiently, and was a great safeguard of his kingdom.
stoic_judgement: saying those who say such things are more arrogant than those who hear them unrevenged
stoic_reason: Philip judges that the insult shows a fault in the speaker and is no harm to himself. This is the judgement of Handbook 20 ('it is your judgement that these men are insulting you') and Discourses 1.18, so he gives no assent to anger (R1, R2). He also keeps his role as a king receiving an embassy by restraining his court and sending the envoy away safe (R6). That is acting well as one making progress (R5), chiefly as restraint of anger (R8).

other: You see the worst-tempered orator, dining in his own chamber with a client who agrees to whatever he says, unable to bear it, exclaim, "Do contradict me in something, that there may be two of us!"
self: You, the worst-tempered orator, dining in your own chamber with a client who agrees to whatever you say, cannot bear it and exclaim, "Do contradict me in something, that there may be two of us!"
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, advising the reader
source_quote: Caelius could not bear his obsequious agreement, and exclaimed, "Do contradict me in something, that there may be two of us\!" Yet even he, who was angry at not being angry, soon recovered his temper, because he had no one to fight with.
source_reason: The other thought it best to agree to whatever he said, and to play second fiddle
source_lesson: If, then, we are conscious of an irascible disposition, let us especially choose for our friends those who will look and speak as we do: they will pamper us and lead us into a bad habit of listening to nothing that does not please us, but it will be good to give our anger respite and repose.
source_verdict: If, then, we are conscious of an irascible disposition, let us especially choose for our friends those who will look and speak as we do: they will pamper us and lead us into a bad habit of listening to nothing that does not please us, but it will be good to give our anger respite and repose.
stoic_judgement: "the worst-tempered orator ... unable to bear it, exclaim, 'Do contradict me in something, that there may be two of us!'"
stoic_reason: He treats the client's agreement, which is the client's doing and not up to him, as something he cannot bear, and he voices it. This is an assented passion of irritation, not a first movement, so by R2 (Handbook 5, 20; Discourses 1.18) and R1 he acts badly, failing in restraint of anger.

other: You see a conqueror willingly accept a city's citizenship from its envoys, thinking not of who offered it but that he was made equal to Hercules, the only stranger they had enrolled before.
self: You willingly accept a city's citizenship from its envoys, thinking not of who offered it but that you are made equal to Hercules, the only stranger they had enrolled before.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 1.13 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise On Benefits, addressing Liberalis
source_quote: Alexander willingly accepted the proffered honour, invited the ambassadors to his table, and showed them other courtesies.
source_reason: He did not think of who offered the citizenship, but to whom they had granted it; and being altogether the slave of glory ... fancied that the heaven to which his vanity aspired was indeed opening before him when he was made equal to Hercules.
source_verdict: In what indeed did that frantic youth, whose only merit was his lucky audacity, resemble Hercules? Hercules conquered nothing for himself; he travelled throughout the world, not coveting for himself but liberating the countries which he conquered, an enemy to bad men, a defender of the good, a peacemaker both by sea and land; whereas the other was from his boyhood a brigand and desolator of nations, a pest to his friends and enemies alike, whose greatest joy was to be the terror of all mankind, forgetting that men fear not only the fiercest but also the most cowardly animals, because of their evil and venomous nature.
stoic_judgement: thinking not of who offered it but that he was made equal to Hercules
stoic_reason: Accepting a city's citizenship is in itself an indifferent act. What decides the verdict is the judgement behind it (R1): he takes reputation and rank, which are 'not under our control' (Handbook 1), as a good worth having, so his mind is fixed on being equal to Hercules rather than on the givers. Assenting to that judgement is a craving for externals, the vanity of one who 'wishes to be a consul' rather than free (Handbook 19), so it is acting badly (R2), and the vice is chiefly a failure of restraint over vanity (R8).

other: You see a slave draw the ring bearing the emperor's portrait from his drunken master's finger as the master takes up a chamber-pot, then show it on his own finger when an informer accuses his master.
self: You are a slave, and you draw the ring bearing the emperor's portrait from your drunken master's finger as he takes up a chamber-pot, then show it on your own finger when an informer accuses your master.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 3.26 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca
source_quote: drew the ring from the finger of his drunken master... the slave showed the ring upon his own finger
source_lesson: After so many instances, can we doubt that a master may sometimes receive a benefit from a slave?
source_verdict: Such a man no more deserves to be called a slave, than Maro deserved to be called a guest.
stoic_judgement: not shown (the vignette gives only the acts; their timing, "as the master takes up a chamber-pot" and "when an informer accuses his master", suggests a protective purpose but does not state it)
stoic_reason: Under R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45), we should neither praise nor blame an act until we know the judgement it comes from. The likeliest reading of the acts' timing is a slave who foresees the danger and keeps faith with his master's good. That would be acting well in his role (R6) through foresight and fidelity, so it is labelled virtue provisionally, with the missing motive flagged.

other: You see an emperor, asked by a praetorian guardsman for help to pay his debts, order the money paid and add offensive reproaches, not wishing more friends to come with the same request.
self: You, an emperor asked by a praetorian guardsman for help to pay his debts, order the money paid and add offensive reproaches, not wishing more friends to come with the same request.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 2.7 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, writing to Liberalis
source_quote: When Marius Nepos of the praetorian guard asked Tiberius Caesar for help to pay his debts, Tiberius asked him for a list of his creditors; this is calling a meeting of creditors, not paying debts. When the list was made out, Tiberius wrote to Nepos telling him that he had ordered the money to be paid, and adding some offensive reproaches.
source_reason: Tiberius, however, had some design in doing so; I imagine he did not wish more of his friends to come to him with the same request.
source_lesson: His mode of proceeding was, perhaps, successful in restraining men’s extravagant desires by shame, but he who wishes to confer benefits must follow quite a different path.
source_verdict: In all ways you should make your benefit as acceptable as possible by presenting it in the most attractive form; but the method of Tiberius is not to confer benefits, but to reproach. ... This is not an act of generosity, but a reprimand.
stoic_judgement: add offensive reproaches, not wishing more friends to come with the same request
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a judgement shown in the vignette (R1): to keep further requests away, which is an external and not up to him, he chooses to shame a friend while helping him. That fails the kindness and good fellowship that his role as benefactor and friend asks (R6, Arius 5b2), so it is badly done even though the payment itself is a preferred act.
also_in: Seneca, On Benefits (c. 56-64 CE; Miriam Griffin and Brad Inwood, 2011)

other: You see a slave physician, ordered by his besieged master to give him poison, give a harmless drug and ask the master's son to keep him in custody till the result shows whether it was poison.
self: You, a slave physician ordered by your besieged master to give him poison, give a harmless drug and ask the master's son to keep you in custody till the result shows whether it was poison.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle it. The earlier Stoics allowed a reasonable exit from life, so Domitius's request might be a rational choice that his slave thwarted. The slave also outwardly assented and then deceived his master, and Handbook 52 counts lying as acting badly. Against this, Discourses 4.1 holds that one's role does not oblige a shameful deed, and Domitius's wish to die under siege may come from fear of Caesar, a passion. Seneca, the source, praises the slave outright.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 3.24 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca
source_quote: Then the slave assented, and gave him a harmless drug to drink. When Domitius fell asleep after drinking this, the slave went to his son, and said, “Give orders for my being kept in custody until you learn from the result whether I have given your father poison or no.”
source_lesson: After so many instances, can we doubt that a master may sometimes receive a benefit from a slave? Why need the person of the giver detract from the thing which he gives?
source_verdict: Domitius lived, and Caesar saved his life; but his slave had saved it before.
stoic_judgement: give a harmless drug and ask the master's son to keep him in custody till the result shows whether it was poison
stoic_reason: Read from his acts (R1), he chose to preserve his master's life rather than kill him, and he offered his own body to custody and judgement. That suggests he treated his safety, an external, as indifferent and fair dealing as what mattered. As a physician and a member of the household (R6), he refused a deed he would not do, as Socrates refused Leon. This reads as acting well while making progress (R5), nearest to justice (kindness, fair dealing), with wisdom and courage also present (R8).

self: You, a Lacedaemonian amid courtiers flattering the Persian king, alone tell him his unwieldy multitude is a danger to its chief, because an army too large cannot be governed, and cannot long exist.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 6.31 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, addressing the reader who wants to repay a prosperous benefactor
source_quote: Demaratus, the Lacedaemonian, alone told him that the disorganized and unwieldy multitude in which he trusted, was in itself a danger to its chief
source_reason: because it possessed only weight without strength; for an army which is too large cannot be governed, and one which cannot be governed, cannot long exist.
source_lesson: He deserved his reward before he asked for it, but how wretched must the nation have been, in which there was no one who would speak the truth to the king except one man who did not speak it to himself.
source_verdict: He deserved his reward before he asked for it
stoic_judgement: amid courtiers flattering the Persian king, alone tell him his unwieldy multitude is a danger to its chief, because an army too large cannot be governed, and cannot long exist
stoic_reason: He gives a reasoned, true assessment where the others feed the king's vanity. That shows correct assent on the matter, and suggests he does not treat the king's favour, which is not up to him, as a good to be bought with lies. This is candour owed to the one he counsels, the good faith that founds justice (R1, R6, R8). It is labelled acting well as a person making progress, not a sage's perfect act (R5). The motive is only inferred, so the row is flagged under R1.

self: You, receiving subscriptions from friends to cover your expenses in exhibiting public games, refuse a large sum sent by a man of bad character: "Am I to accept a present from a man when I would not accept his offer to drink a glass of wine with him?"

source_quote: when he was receiving subscriptions from many of his friends to cover his expenses in exhibiting public games, would not receive a large sum which was sent him by Fabius Persicus
source_reason: Am I to accept a present from a man when I would not accept his offer to drink a glass of wine with him?

source_verdict: If you want an instance of magnanimity, take the case of Julius Graecinus ... Ought we to call this receiving presents, or rather taking one's pick of the senate?
stoic_judgement: "Am I to accept a present from a man when I would not accept his offer to drink a glass of wine with him?"
stoic_reason: The money is an external, only material for moral purpose (Discourses 1.29). He refuses it from the judgement that taking a benefit binds him to the giver, and that a bond with a man of bad character is worse than lacking the funds. This is an act from correct judgement, so it is well done (R1, Discourses 4.8). He is acting well as a man making progress, which is our convention, not a claim of sage virtue (R5). As a man raising subscriptions, he weighs who gives as well as what is given (R6).

other: You see a philosopher, in a city where thirty tyrants have slain thirteen hundred citizens, consoling its mourning elders, encouraging those who despair of the republic, and reproaching rich men for their avarice.
self: You, a philosopher in a city where thirty tyrants have slain thirteen hundred citizens, console its mourning elders, encourage those who despair of the republic, and reproach rich men for their avarice.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Tranquillity of Mind 5 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his letter to his friend Serenus
source_quote: Yet Socrates was in the midst of the city, and consoled its mourning Fathers, encouraged those who despaired of the republic, by his reproaches brought rich men, who feared that their wealth would be their ruin, to a tardy repentance of their avarice, and moved about as a great example to those who wished to imitate him, because he walked a free man in the midst of thirty masters.
source_lesson: you may know, therefore, that even in an oppressed state a wise man can find an opportunity for bringing himself to the front, and that in a prosperous and flourishing one wanton insolence, jealousy, and a thousand other cowardly vices bear sway.
source_verdict: moved about as a great example to those who wished to imitate him, because he walked a free man in the midst of thirty masters.
modernised: [{"source": "its mourning Fathers", "vignette": "its mourning elders", "why": "'Fathers' is the Roman title for senators or leading citizens; a reader today would take it literally as parents grieving their children."}]
stoic_judgement: "in a city where thirty tyrants have slain thirteen hundred citizens, consoling its mourning elders, encouraging those who despair of the republic, and reproaching rich men for their avarice"
stoic_reason: He reproaches the rich for avarice, so he judges that craving externals is the fault. He keeps doing his citizen's work of consoling and exhorting while the tyrants are killing, so he does not treat safety and life, which are not up to him, as the good. Read that way (R1, inferred as in R2), these are appropriate acts done in his role (R6) from correct judgement, and so acting well as one making progress (R5). The most visible virtue is courage, endurance under peril, with justice (kindness, good fellowship) and wisdom also at work (R8).

other: You see an exile, told that civil war will soon restore all exiles, answer, "My wish is that my country should blush at my being banished, rather than mourn at my having returned."
self: You, an exile told that civil war will soon restore all exiles, answer, "My wish is that my country should blush at my being banished, rather than mourn at my having returned."
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 6.37 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise to Liberalis, citing Hecaton for the story of Callistratus
source_quote: did not wish to be restored to their homes at the cost of a public disaster, but preferred that two should suffer unjustly than that all should suffer alike
source_reason: My wish is, that my country should blush at my being banished, rather than that she should mourn at my having returned.
source_lesson: These two persons, who did not wish to be restored to their homes at the cost of a public disaster, but preferred that two should suffer unjustly than that all should suffer alike, are thought to have acted like good citizens; and in like manner it does not accord with the character of a grateful man, to wish that his benefactor may fall into troubles which he may dispel; because, even though he may mean well to him, yet he wishes him evil.
source_verdict: are thought to have acted like good citizens
stoic_judgement: "My wish is that my country should blush at my being banished, rather than mourn at my having returned."
stoic_reason: He judges that his return, an external that is preferred but not good, is not worth his country's disaster. He would rather bear exile than wish evil on the city. By R1 and R6 this is acting well in the role of citizen, since disregarding the interests of one's country is what reason deprecates (DL 7.108). By R5 it counts as acting well while making progress. He also shows no assented grief at the exile (R2): he treats the shame as his country's, not an evil to himself.
also_in: Seneca, On Benefits (c. 56-64 CE; Miriam Griffin and Brad Inwood, 2011)

other: You see a philosopher laughingly refuse the emperor's offer of two hundred thousand sesterces, saying that if the emperor meant to tempt him, he ought to have offered his entire kingdom.
self: You laughingly refuse the emperor's offer of two hundred thousand sesterces, saying that if the emperor meant to tempt you, he ought to have offered his entire kingdom.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 7.11 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, the author, recounting what he says he has heard about Demetrius
source_quote: he laughingly refused it, thinking it unworthy of himself to boast of having refused so small a sum
source_reason: If he meant to tempt me, he ought to have tried to do so by offering his entire kingdom.
source_lesson: I must here repeat a proof of his magnanimity.
source_verdict: I must here repeat a proof of his magnanimity.
stoic_judgement: laughingly refuse the emperor's offer ... saying that if the emperor meant to tempt him, he ought to have offered his entire kingdom
stoic_reason: The quip shows he takes the money as a bribe meant to tempt him. He refuses because he will not sell his moral purpose for an external, which is not up to him and is not good. By R1 this shows the judgement behind the act, so by R5 it is acting well as one making progress. His laughter is contempt for the bribe, not an assented passion such as anger (R2). R8 gives temperance as the main virtue, since he restrains the craving for wealth; refusing to be corrupted by an emperor also touches justice and courage.

other: You see one of Julius Caesar's veterans, whose cause against his neighbours is going against him, remind Caesar that he once brought him water in his helmet in Spain, because his commander's memory was confused by a multitude of incidents.
self: You are one of Julius Caesar's veterans; your cause against your neighbours is going against you, and you remind Caesar that you once brought him water in your helmet in Spain, because your commander's memory was confused by a multitude of incidents.
contested_note: Seneca's lesson approves the act. Epictetus's framing does not settle two things: whether the veteran pursues the land as a preferred indifferent or craves it as a good, and whether urging a personal favour on a judge in the middle of a lawsuit is fair dealing or an appeal against the merits of the case (it was 'going against him'). The approval comes from Seneca's text, not from a Stoic rule applied to this act (R9).
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 5.24 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, writing to Liberalis
source_quote: asked for a return for the benefit which he had conferred
source_reason: Because his commander’s memory was confused by a multitude of incidents, and because his position as the leader of vast armies did not permit him to notice individual soldiers
source_lesson: I shall therefore ask for the return of a benefit, whenever I am either reduced to great straits, or where by doing so I shall act to the advantage of him from whom I ask it.
source_verdict: To act as he did is not so much to ask for a return as to take it when it lies in a convenient position ready for us, although we have to stretch out our hands in order to receive it.
stoic_judgement: because his commander's memory was confused by a multitude of incidents
stoic_reason: The one judgement shown is that Caesar had forgotten, not that he was ungrateful. That is a correct and charitable use of impressions, and reminding a forgetful man of a benefit is an appropriate act (R1, R6; Seneca: asking for a return when in straits is fitting). But the vignette does not show whether the veteran treats the disputed fields, an external, as a good he must have. So the praise is provisional (R1, R5).

other: You see two slaves drive their mistress through the captured city, telling the victors she is a most cruel mistress they are leading away for punishment, so she might be saved from murder.
self: You and another slave drive your mistress through the captured city, telling the victors she is a most cruel mistress you are leading away for punishment, so she might be saved from murder.
contested_note: The rescue is done by deceiving the victors. Epictetus says 'one ought not to lie' (Handbook 52), but that line comes as an example in a passage about logic, not a ruling on deceiving armed enemies to save a life. The earlier Stoics, as reported, allowed a falsehood used without assent to deceit, for example toward enemies or for someone's safety. So Epictetus's own framing does not settle whether the stratagem is blameless (R9). Seneca, the source, praises the act outright.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 3.23 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, citing Claudius Quadrigarius
source_quote: they ran before every one else along the streets, which they well knew, to the house in which they had been slaves, and drove their mistress before them; when they were asked who she might be, they answered that she was their mistress, and a most cruel one, and that they were leading her away for punishment. They led her outside the walls, and concealed her with the greatest care until the fighting was over; ... they also returned to their own countrymen, and themselves restored their mistress to them.
source_reason: if thereby their mistress might be saved from murder
source_lesson: Believe me, it is the mark of no slavish soul to purchase a noble deed by the semblance of crime.
source_verdict: Believe me, it is the mark of no slavish soul to purchase a noble deed by the semblance of crime.
stoic_judgement: so she might be saved from murder
stoic_reason: R1: the vignette shows the judgement behind the act. They act for a preferred thing, another's life (Discourses 2.10, 'cleave to that which is naturally more fit to be chosen'). They treat their own reputation, which is not up to them (Handbook 1), as nothing beside that. So it is acting well as people making progress (R5), and comes nearest to justice as kindness, 'a knowledge which is disposed to do good' (R8).

other: You see a king, on reading a sharp letter from the man who rescued his shipwrecked soldier and whose estate he then gave that soldier, order the property restored and the soldier branded, so men may see how sacred is the table of hospitality.
self: You, a king, on reading a sharp letter from the man who rescued your shipwrecked soldier and whose estate you then gave that soldier, order the property restored and the soldier branded, so men may see how sacred is the table of hospitality.
contested_note: The source says Philip acted 'so much enraged' at the letter. On Epictetus's terms (Handbook 20, Discourses 1.18) and Seneca's De ira, a just sentence given from assented anger is badly done (R2), so the verdict would be vice. Seneca here also says 'let us see within what limits one ought to keep in punishing', which leaves the branding in question. He also notes that Philip acted only after the sharp letter, having first given the estate 'with his eyes shut'. The vignette shows only the guardian's motive, so Epictetus's framing gives virtue for the vignette but vice for the source's Philip.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 4.37 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, writing to Aebutius Liberalis
source_quote: straightway ordered Pausanias to restore the property to its former owner, and to brand that wickedest of soldiers, that most ungrateful of guests, that greediest of shipwrecked men, with letters bearing witness to his ingratitude
source_reason: Go, let men see how sacred a thing is the table of hospitality; show them your face, that upon it they may read the decree which prevents its being a capital crime to give refuge to the unfortunate under one’s roof.
source_lesson: There is no disgrace in altering one’s plans according to circumstances.
source_verdict: There is no inconsistency in giving up an intention which we have discovered to be wrong and have condemned as wrong; we ought candidly to admit, “I thought that it was something different; I have been deceived.”
stoic_judgement: order the property restored and the soldier branded, so men may see how sacred is the table of hospitality
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the king acting from the judgement that the law of hospitality must be upheld and the wrong he had done undone. This is a ruler, in his role, restoring what is due and punishing as a guardian of the public good, not as an enemy (R1, R6), so it counts as acting well, under justice (R5, R8). His willingness to reverse his own wrongful grant shows wisdom.

Guiding another toward fitting work is appropriate in a teacher's role (Handbook 30, Discourses 2.10). But the other man's choice is up to him, not to the one who 'lays hands' on him, and the vignette does not show whether this is counsel within a relationship or coercion of a stranger.

source_quote: Isocrates laid hands upon Ephorus and led him away from the forum
source_reason: thinking that he would be more usefully employed in compiling chronicles
source_lesson: for no good is done by forcing one's mind to engage in uncongenial work: it is vain to struggle against Nature.
source_verdict: for no good is done by forcing one's mind to engage in uncongenial work: it is vain to struggle against Nature.

By R1 and R5 this reads as acting well, and it is nearest to wisdom: seeing what work suits a nature. By R6, though, whether it is appropriate depends on a role (teacher to pupil) that the vignette does not state.

source_verdict: How far happier is he who is indebted to no man for anything except for what he can deprive himself of with the greatest ease\!
stoic_judgement: he does not think him worth fetching back: "It is a shame that he should be able to live without me, and I not without him."
stoic_reason: His words show the judgement that the slave, a piece of property and so not up to him (Handbook 1), is no good he must have. To crave it would make him a slave to what is outside his control (Discourses 1.4), so his letting it go proceeds from a correct judgement and is acting well (R1, R5). The virtue is chiefly wisdom, seeing what is and is not his own, with temperance in refusing the craving for property (R8).

source_quote: She did not cease to make frequent mention of the name of her Drusus, to set up his portrait in all places, both public and private, and to speak of him and listen while others spoke of him with the greatest pleasure: she lived with his memory

If, on the other hand, showing a milder and better regulated spirit, you try to follow the example of the latter most exalted lady, you will not be in misery, nor will you wear your life out with suffering.

other: You see a great orator attend to no business and not even read letters in the last two hours of the day, for fear some new trouble should arise, using them to get rid of his weariness.

contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle the motive. If 'fear some new trouble should arise' means he judges unwelcome news, which is not up to him, an evil he must shut out, it is an assented passion and so vice (R2, Discourses 2.13). If it is caution about guarding his rest, a preferred indifferent, it is a good feeling and so virtue (R4). Seneca simply praises the practice, and his praise is not by itself a Stoic verdict (R9).

speaker: Seneca, writing to Serenus
source_quote: would not attend to any business after the tenth hour: he would not even read letters after that time for fear some new trouble should arise, but in those two hours  used to get rid of the weariness which he had contracted during the whole day
source_reason: for fear some new trouble should arise
source_lesson: We must humour our minds and grant them rest from time to time, which acts upon them like food, and restores their strength.
source_verdict: Men’s minds ought to have relaxation: they rise up better and more vigorous after rest.

stoic_judgement: for fear some new trouble should arise, using them to get rid of his weariness
stoic_reason: He gives himself rest, which is by nature to be preferred, so that he can return to his work restored. If his 'fear' is rational caution (DL 7.116), keeping impressions he cannot yet handle well away from his hours of rest, this is an orderly appropriate act from a correct judgement, acting well as one making progress (R1, R4, R5, R6). It shows temperance as orderliness, and wisdom in judging what the mind needs (R8).

self: You, a philosopher whom the emperor has condemned, are summoned by the centurion from your game of draughts to join those going to be executed, and you count your men and tell your companion, "Mind you do not tell a lie after my death, and say that you won."
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Tranquillity of Mind 14 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, writing to Serenus
source_quote: he answered, "I thank you, most excellent prince."... he passed the ten intervening days before his execution without the slightest despondency... He was playing at draughts when the centurion in charge of a number of those who were going to be executed bade him, join them: on the summons he counted his men and said to his companion, "Mind you do not tell a lie after my death, and say that you won;"
source_reason: you are enquiring whether our souls are immortal, but I shall presently know... "I have decided," answered Kanus, "at that most swiftly-passing moment of all to watch whether the spirit will be conscious of the act of leaving the body."
source_lesson: Here was peace in the very midst of the storm: here was a soul worthy of eternal life, which used its own fate as a proof of truth, which when at the last step of life experimented upon his fleeting breath, and did not merely continue to learn until he died, but learned something even from death itself. No man has carried the life of a philosopher further.
source_verdict: Whatever he meant, it was a magnanimous answer... it is marvellous how that man spoke and acted, and how peaceful he was... Here was peace in the very midst of the storm: here was a soul worthy of eternal life
stoic_judgement: summoned ... to join those going to be executed, count his men and tell his companion, "Mind you do not tell a lie after my death, and say that you won."
stoic_reason: Called to his death, he goes on with the game and attends only to what is up to him: the truth of the score and his companion's honesty. Death, which is not up to him, he treats as nothing dreadful (Handbook 5), so the act proceeds from a correct judgement (R1, R2 by contrast). Read as endurance of the most fearful external, this is acting well as one making progress (R5), and is nearest to courage (R8).
also_in: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020); source: Seneca, On the Tranquility of Mind

other: You see a man whose party is defeated in the civil war, all fallen into one man's power, drive the sword into his breast to give himself that freedom it could not give his country.
self: You, whose party is defeated in the civil war, all fallen into one man's power, drive the sword into your breast to give yourself that freedom it could not give your country.
contested_note: Seneca (source) praises Cato's death as noble. The earlier Stoics (DL 7.130) allow a reasonable exit for one's country or under intolerable conditions. Epictetus allows the 'open door' but warns against leaving without God's signal (Disc. 1.9) and holds that no tyrant can take a man's freedom, which lies in the moral purpose. On that view, dying 'to be free' of Caesar may rest on judging an external an evil. His framing does not decide whether Cato's act was a reasoned appropriate exit or a passion.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Providence 2 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, writing to Lucilius
source_quote: with one hand he will open a wide path to freedom ... he drove the sword into his sacred breast
source_reason: his sword ... will still perform good and noble deeds; it will give to Cato that freedom which it could not give to his country
source_lesson: Men are raised to the level of the gods by a death which is admired even by those who fear them.
source_verdict: How could they fail to view their pupil with interest when leaving his life by such a noble and memorable departure?
stoic_judgement: to give himself that freedom it could not give his country
stoic_reason: The vignette shows a motive, freedom, so it can be judged (R1). Read through Epictetus's own picture of the 'open door' and of keeping the character one's role demands (R6), a reasoned exit rather than life on Caesar's terms is courage. But Part 1 places freedom in the moral purpose, which Caesar cannot touch. If Cato judged subjection to another's power an evil he must escape, his death proceeds from a false judgement about externals (R2). Since Epictetus's framing does not settle which judgement this is, the row is contested (R9). The source's high praise is not by itself the Stoic verdict.
also_in: Plutarch, How to Be a Leader (Jeffrey Beneker, 2019) || Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020); source: Plutarch (account in surrounding narrative) || Massimo Pigliucci, Cato Chronicles (2021)

other: You see a wife, ship-wrecked after her beloved husband died during a sea-voyage, keeping fast hold of his dead body, so eager to give him decent burial that she cares nothing about whether she shares it or no.
self: You are ship-wrecked after your beloved husband died during a sea-voyage, and you keep fast hold of his dead body, so eager to give him decent burial that you care nothing about whether you share it or no.
contested_note: Three things leave the verdict open (R9). (1) Epictetus does not settle the weighing: Discourses 2.10 says to 'cleave to that which is naturally more fit to be chosen', and staking her own life (a preferred indifferent) for a corpse may not choose the more preferred. Seneca himself calls the burial 'a less important end'. (2) The earlier Stoics, Chrysippus as Diogenes Laertius reports him, treated the corpse and its burial as indifferent. Our checked Part 1 texts do not record this; it comes from outside them. (3) 'Eager' and 'beloved' may show grief assented to, or a craving for burial as a good she must have. That would be a passion and a vice (R2, R4), not rational affection (Discourses 1.11). | From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as vice: Burial and her own life are both externals. Her role as wife makes burial an appropriate act (R6, Discourses 2.10), and indifference to death is not to be feared (Handbook 5). But the vignette shows her clinging to a corpse and ranking its burial above her own survival, which is the thing 'naturally more fit to be chosen' here. That reads as craving an external she cannot secure, assented to rather than a first movement (R1, R2, Discourses 1.4: he who craves what is not under his control is 'tossed to and fro with them').
source: Seneca, Complete Works: Consolation to Helvia 19 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, consoling his mother Helvia in exile
source_quote: she endured at the same time grief for him and fear for herself, and at last, though ship-wrecked, nevertheless rescued his body from the vanquished tempest.
source_reason: so eager to give him decent burial that she cared nothing about whether she shared it or no
source_lesson: You must now show a virtue equal to hers, recall your mind from grief, and take care that no one may think that you are sorry that you have borne a son.
source_verdict: my aunt did more when she risked her life in order to give her husband a tomb: it shows greater love to endure the same peril for a less important end.
stoic_judgement: so eager to give him decent burial that she cares nothing about whether she shares it or no
stoic_reason: Her own death is not up to her and is 'nothing dreadful' (Handbook 5), and burying her husband is an act her role as wife suggests (Discourses 2.10, Handbook 30). So holding fast to the body in the wreck, unmoved by fear, reads as acting well while making progress (R1, R5, R6). The main virtue at stake is endurance of peril, which is courage, with piety and faithfulness toward him, which fall under justice (R8).

other: You see a Roman general embrace his dying younger brother and receive his last kiss, then restrain his grief and make the heart-broken army, claiming the corpse, grieve only as it became Romans to grieve.
self: You, a Roman general, embrace your dying younger brother and receive his last kiss, then restrain your grief and make the heart-broken army, claiming the corpse, grieve only as it becomes Romans to grieve.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: Consolation to Polybius 15 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, imagining the Emperor Caesar himself addressing Polybius in consolation (the exempla are put in Caesar's own voice: 'my paternal uncle', 'my father')
source_quote: he embraced him and received his last kiss, but he nevertheless restrained not only his own grief but that of others, and when the whole army, not merely sorrowful but heart-broken, claimed the corpse of their Drusus for themselves, he made them grieve only as it became Romans to grieve, and taught them that they must observe military discipline not only in fighting but also in mourning.
source_lesson: It is your duty to imitate their constancy in enduring and triumphing over suffering, as far as it is permitted to a mere man to follow in the footsteps of the immortals.
source_verdict: He could not have checked the tears of others had he not first repressed his own.
stoic_judgement: embrace his dying younger brother and receive his last kiss, then restrain his grief and make the heart-broken army ... grieve only as it became Romans to grieve
stoic_reason: The embrace and last kiss are affection that is 'both affectionate and reasonable' (Discourses 1.11; R4), not the fault. Restraining his grief shows him refusing to judge the death an evil he is crushed by (Handbook 5, 16; R2, R4). Leading the army to mourn with discipline is what his role as general and brother asks (Discourses 2.10; R6). So he is acting well as one making progress (R5), chiefly through self-restraint over the passion of grief.

other: You see a daughter, when times change, publishing what survives of her father's true account of Roman events, a large part burned; his eloquence and independence under Sejanus had cost him his life and consigned him to oblivion.
self: You, when times change, publish what survives of your father's true account of Roman events, a large part burned; his eloquence and independence under Sejanus had cost him his life and consigned him to oblivion.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: Consolation to Marcia 1 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, writing to Marcia
source_quote: you restored to the use of man that genius of your father for which he had suffered, and made him in real truth immortal by publishing as an eternal memorial of him those books which that bravest of men had written with his own blood
source_lesson: I have reminded you of old hurts, and to prove that your present wound may be healed, I have shown you the scar of one which was equally severe.
source_verdict: You have done a great service to Roman literature: a large part of Cordus's books had been burned; a great service to posterity, who will receive a true account of events, which cost its author so dear; and a great service to himself, whose memory flourishes and ever will flourish... By Hercules, the state would have sustained a great loss if you had not brought him forth from the oblivion to which his two splendid qualities, eloquence and independence, had consigned him
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: Publishing her father's true history is the kind of act reason urges, honouring one's parents and giving posterity the truth (DL 7.108), and it fits her role as his daughter (R6). But the vignette states no motive, and *Discourses* 4.8 forbids praise until we know the judgement it proceeds from (R1). The label is therefore provisional: it rests on the act being appropriate in her role and on there being no sign of a bad judgement.

other: You see a high priest dedicating the temple of Jupiter hear his son's death announced; he pretends not to hear it and, without a single groan, pronounces the prayer begging that Jupiter would show himself gracious.
self: You are a high priest dedicating the temple of Jupiter and hear your son's death announced; you pretend not to hear it and, without a single groan, pronounce the prayer begging that Jupiter would show himself gracious.
contested_note: Seneca, writing as a Stoic consoler, praises the act outright ('worthy of the most exalted priesthood'). Epictetus would say that until we learn the judgement the act proceeds from, we should neither praise nor blame it (Discourses 4.8). Several judgements could lie behind it: duty to the office and the gods, which would be acting well; concern for appearance or reputation; or grief assented to but suppressed, which would still be a passion (R2). The vignette does not say which, so Epictetus's framing does not settle the verdict. | The labeller calls this label tentative:  But the vignette shows only the outward act, not the judgement behind it, so the praise is tentative (R1).
source: Seneca, Complete Works: Consolation to Marcia 13 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, consoling Marcia on the death of her son
source_quote: He pretended not to hear it, and pronounced the form of words proper for the high priest on such an occasion, without his prayer being interrupted by a single groan, begging that Jupiter would show himself gracious, at the very instant that he heard his son’s name mentioned as dead.
source_lesson: Worthy, indeed, of the most exalted priesthood was he who ceased not to revere the gods even when they were angry.
source_verdict: Worthy, indeed, of the most exalted priesthood was he who ceased not to revere the gods even when they were angry.

stoic_judgement: he pretends not to hear it and, without a single groan, pronounces the prayer begging that Jupiter would show himself gracious
stoic_reason: As high priest he carries out what his role asks (R6) and does not let an external, his son's death, overturn his own conduct, not even with an outward groan (Handbook 16; Discourses 2.10). This is read as acting well while making progress (R5), with endurance of a blow as the main virtue (R8). But the vignette shows only the outward act, not the judgement behind it, so the praise is tentative (R1).

other: You see an aging man, annoyed with his property manager, seize on the nearest excuse to vent his anger about plane trees he himself planted: "This wouldn't be happening if they were kept fertilized and watered."
self: You, an aging man annoyed with your property manager, seize on the nearest excuse to vent your anger about plane trees you yourself planted: "This wouldn't be happening if they were kept fertilized and watered."
source: Seneca, Letters on Ethics to Lucilius: Letter 12.1–4 (2015, tr. Margaret Graver & A. A. Long)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter to Lucilius, recounting his own visit to his villa
source_quote: Annoyed with him, I seized on the nearest excuse to vent my anger.
source_reason: This wouldn't be happening if they were kept fertilized and watered.
source_lesson: My suburban villa has done me a service; it has brought my age before me at every turn. Let us embrace old age and love it.
source_verdict: My suburban villa has done me a service; it has brought my age before me at every turn.
stoic_judgement: annoyed with his property manager, seize on the nearest excuse to vent his anger
stoic_reason: He does not merely feel a first flash of irritation (R3). He assents to anger and acts on it by seizing an excuse to blame another man. In Epictetus's terms that is a judgement that something outside his control (the decay of buildings and trees) is an evil someone must answer for. Under R2, with Handbook 20 and Discourses 1.18, this is acting badly. The fault lies chiefly in failing to restrain anger (temperance, R8), and secondarily in being unfair to the manager (justice).

other: You see a man whom a tyrant threatens with death and even with want of burial answer, “My half pint of blood is in your power: what a fool you must be if you suppose that I care whether I rot above ground or under it.”
self: When a tyrant threatens you with death and even with want of burial, you answer, “My half pint of blood is in your power: what a fool you must be if you suppose that I care whether I rot above ground or under it.”
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Tranquillity of Mind 14 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, writing to his friend Serenus
source_quote: A tyrant threatened Theodorus with death, and even with want of burial. “You are able to please yourself,” he answered, “my half pint of blood is in your power: for, as for burial, what a fool you must be if you suppose that I care whether I rot above ground or under it.”
source_lesson: The mind ought in all cases to be called away from the contemplation of external things to that of itself: let it confide in itself, rejoice in itself, admire its own works ; avoid as far as may be those of others, and devote itself to itself ; let it not feel losses, and put a good construction even upon misfortunes.
source_verdict: Moreover, we ought to cultivate an easy temper, and not become over fond of the lot which fate has assigned to us, but transfer ourselves to whatever other condition chance may lead us to, and fear no alteration, either in our purposes or our position in life
stoic_judgement: "My half pint of blood is in your power: what a fool you must be if you suppose that I care whether I rot above ground or under it."
stoic_reason: He grants that his body is under the tyrant's control. He judges that neither its death nor its burial is an evil to him, so the threat finds no fear to work on (Handbook 1 and 5; Discourses 1.29). Under R1 and R2, the judgement behind his answer is shown and it is correct. He refuses the passion of dread, so this is acting well as a person making progress (R5), and it is chiefly courage, the endurance of what is to be feared (R8).

other: You see a Roman who could not overcome the enemy King when his hand held a sword grasp the enemy's fire with his right hand, of his own accord paying the penalty of his mistake.
self: You could not overcome the enemy King when your hand held a sword, so you grasp the enemy's fire with your right hand, of your own accord paying the penalty of your mistake.
contested_note: Seneca, a Stoic, praises Mucius as a 'glorious example' tried by fortune. On Epictetus's framing the verdict turns on the judgement behind the burning. If he burns his hand because he judges his failure to kill the king an evil he must punish, that outcome was not up to him and the act comes from a false judgement. If he acts from contempt for pain and fidelity to his country (Discourses 2.10, role), it is well done. The vignette's 'penalty of his mistake' does not settle which.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Providence 3 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, replying to Lucilius's question why, if the world is ruled by providence, so many evils befall good men
source_quote: he grasped the enemy’s fire with his right hand, and of his own accord paid the penalty of his mistake? because he overcame the King with his hand when it was burned, though he could not when it held a sword
source_lesson: it is ill fortune alone that discovers these glorious examples.
source_verdict: Was Mucius unhappy, because he grasped the enemy’s fire with his right hand, and of his own accord paid the penalty of his mistake? because he overcame the King with his hand when it was burned, though he could not when it held a sword? Would he have been happier, if he had warmed his hand in his mistress’s bosom;
stoic_judgement: of his own accord paying the penalty of his mistake
stoic_reason: He freely gives up his body, which Handbook 1 says is not up to us. That suggests he does not judge pain or the loss of a hand to be an evil, which fits courage as endurance (R8). He also holds himself, not fortune, to account for his failed attempt (Discourses 1.11). But the vignette shows only that he chose this and calls it a penalty. Under R1 his fuller motive is thin, and R9 says Seneca's praise is not by itself a Stoic verdict.

other: You see a man, purely by chance, find himself at the midday show in the arena, expecting some amusement or wit, something relaxing to give people's eyes a rest from the sight of human blood.
self: You, purely by chance, find yourself at the midday show in the arena, expecting some amusement or wit, something relaxing to give people's eyes a rest from the sight of human blood.
contested_note: Seneca's lesson is that a mind still making progress should keep away from crowds and spectacles altogether, because the pleasure of the sight lets faults slip in. On that view, even sitting in the seat is a risk the progressor should not take. Epictetus's framing (Part 1) judges only the judgement acted from, and the vignette shows a benign one, so it does not settle whether chance attendance is itself a lapse.
source: Seneca, Letters on Ethics to Lucilius: Letter 7.3–5 (2015, tr. Margaret Graver & A. A. Long)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter to Lucilius
source_quote: Purely by chance, I found myself at the midday show
source_reason: expecting some amusement or wit, something relaxing to give people's eyes a rest from the sight of human blood
source_lesson: The mind that is young and not yet able to hold on to what is right must be kept apart from the people.
source_verdict: Nothing, though, is as destructive to good character as occupying a seat in some public spectacle, for then the pleasure of the sight lets the faults slip in more easily.

stoic_judgement: purely by chance, find himself at the midday show in the arena, expecting some amusement or wit, something relaxing to give people's eyes a rest from the sight of human blood
stoic_reason: He is there by chance, and the vignette shows only a wish for harmless relief from bloodshed. That wish treats no external as a good he must have and assents to no cruelty, so R7 applies: his presence is an act reason neither urges nor forbids, with no judgement about good or evil at stake. R1 bars both praise and blame beyond this, since we do not see how he uses the impression once the slaughter begins.
