other: You see the emperor's sister, who has lost her son, the emperor's chosen heir, raging against the emperor's wife, because the brilliant prospect once in store for her own child seems now transferred to the wife's son.
self: You, the emperor's sister, having lost your son, the emperor's chosen heir, rage against the emperor's wife, because the brilliant prospect once in store for your own child seems now transferred to her son.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: Consolation to Marcia 2 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his letter of consolation to Marcia, who has mourned her son for three years
source_quote: His mother never ceased to weep and sob during her whole life, never endured to listen to wholesome advice, never even allowed her thoughts to be diverted from her sorrow. She remained during her whole life just as she was during the funeral, with all the strength of her mind intently fixed upon one subject. I do not say that she lacked the courage to shake off her grief, but she refused to be comforted, thought that it would be a second bereavement to lose her tears, and would not have any portrait of her darling son, nor allow any allusion to be made to him. She hated all mothers, and raged against Livia with especial fury, because it seemed as though the brilliant prospect once in store for her own child was now transferred to Livia’s son. Passing all her days in darkened rooms and alone, not conversing even with her brother, she refused to accept the poems which were composed in memory of Marcellus, and all the other honours paid him by literature, and closed her ears against all consolation. She lived buried and hidden from view, neglecting her accustomed duties, and actually angry with the excessive splendour of her brother’s prosperity, in which she shared. Though surrounded by her children and grandchildren, she would not lay aside her mourning garb, though by retaining it she seemed to put a slight upon all her relations, in thinking herself bereaved in spite of their being alive.
source_reason: because it seemed as though the brilliant prospect once in store for her own child was now transferred to Livia’s son.
source_lesson: Plague on it\! what madness this is, to punish one’s self because one is unfortunate, and not to lessen, but to increase one’s ills!
source_verdict: I here put the best construction on what is really most contemptible and foreign to your character. ... If, on the other hand, showing a milder and better regulated spirit, you try to follow the example of the latter most exalted lady, you will not be in misery, nor will you wear your life out with suffering.
stoic_judgement: raging against the emperor's wife, because the brilliant prospect once in store for her own child seems now transferred to the wife's son
stoic_reason: She rages because she holds the throne her son was to have, an external not up to her, to be a good. She holds its passing to another's son to be an evil done to her. That is envy and anger assented to (Handbook 19, 20; Discourses 1.18), so she acts badly even with no deed shown (R1, R2). A sustained rage with a stated grievance is no first movement (R3), and the fault is the judgement, not her love for her son (R4).

other: You see a man cheerfully and willingly drain the poison the state assigned to him, taking it as though it were a charm to make him immortal, and arguing about death until death itself.
self: You cheerfully and willingly drain the poison the state assigned to you, taking it as though it were a charm to make you immortal, and arguing about death until death itself.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Providence 3 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, addressing Lucilius directly
source_quote: he took that draught which the state assigned to him as though it were a charm to make him immortal, and argued about death until death itself... Socrates cheerfully and willingly drains his poison
source_reason: as though it were a charm to make him immortal
source_lesson: it is ill fortune alone that discovers these glorious examples.
source_verdict: How much more is this man to be envied than he who is served on precious stones, whose drink a creature trained to every vice, a eunuch or much the same, cools with snow in a golden cup?
stoic_judgement: cheerfully and willingly drain the poison the state assigned to him, taking it as though it were a charm to make him immortal, and arguing about death until death itself
stoic_reason: He judges death, which is not up to him, to be nothing dreadful, the very judgement of Handbook 5 ('death is nothing dreadful, or else Socrates too would have thought so'). So he acts from a correct judgement about what is and is not up to him, and his act is well done (R1, R5). His cheerfulness is rational joy, not a passion (R4), and he keeps to his role as a philosopher, arguing to the end (R6, Discourses 1.4).

other: You see a wealthy man with a bad memory, wanting to appear learned, spend a great deal of money on slaves who know Homer, Hesiod and the lyric poets by heart, whom he asks for verses to quote.
self: You, a wealthy man with a bad memory, wanting to appear learned, spend a great deal of money on slaves who know Homer, Hesiod and the lyric poets by heart, whom you ask for verses to quote.
source: Seneca, Letters on Ethics to Lucilius: Letter 27.5–8 (2015, tr. Margaret Graver & A. A. Long)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter to Lucilius, giving instructions to himself while Lucilius stands by
source_quote: So he devised an expedient: he spent a great deal of money on slaves, one of whom was to know Homer by heart, another Hesiod, plus nine more, each assigned to one of the lyric poets. It is no wonder the cost was high, since any that were not to be found he paid to have instructed. Once he had assembled this staff, he began to pester his dinner guests. ... Yet Sabinus was of the opinion that any knowledge possessed by anyone in his household was something he knew himself.
source_reason: he wanted to appear learned
source_lesson: Excellence of mind cannot be borrowed or bought. I think too that if it were for sale, it would not find a buyer. Yet wickedness is purchased every day.
source_verdict: Excellence of mind cannot be borrowed or bought. I think too that if it were for sale, it would not find a buyer. Yet wickedness is purchased every day.
stoic_judgement: wanting to appear learned, spend a great deal of money on slaves who know Homer, Hesiod and the lyric poets by heart, whom he asks for verses to quote
stoic_reason: He treats reputation, which Handbook 1 lists among things not under our control, as a good worth buying. He seeks to seem learned rather than to be so, using externals as a substitute for his own moral purpose (R1, R2, Discourses 2.13: the singer who craves applause). Unchecked vanity is a failure of temperance (R8), and mistaking what is not one's own for one's own is a failure of wisdom.

other: You see a Roman equestrian risen from humble beginnings, investing at home and abroad with money flooding in, spend the whole day at a seriously ill friend's bedside, then die of sudden angina by dawn.
self: You, a Roman equestrian risen from humble beginnings, investing at home and abroad with money flooding in, spend the whole day at a seriously ill friend's bedside, then die of sudden angina by dawn.
contested_note: From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as virtue: Sitting all day with a seriously ill friend is an act reason urges (DL 7.108, 'intercourse with friends'), and his sudden death is not up to him, so it is neither good nor evil for his moral purpose (Handbook 1). But the vignette shows only outward acts, so under R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45) we cannot yet say the act was well done. The 'virtue' label is provisional, given only because the shown act is of an appropriate type; it is not a confirmed verdict.
source: Seneca, Letters on Ethics to Lucilius: Letter 101.1–4 (2015, tr. Margaret Graver & A. A. Long)
speaker: Seneca, writing to Lucilius
source_quote: While privately investing at home and abroad, and engaging in every type of public business in pursuit of profit, just at the moment when everything was going his way and with money flooding in, he was carried off.
source_lesson: How foolish it is to plan out one's life when one is not even master of tomorrow!
source_verdict: Everything is uncertain, believe me, even for those who are fortunate. No one should make himself any promises concerning the future.
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: The vignette shows only outward acts. He invests and makes money, he spends the day at a sick friend's bedside, and then he dies, which is not up to him and is no act of his. Sitting with a sick friend is an appropriate act of the kind reason urges (intercourse with friends, DL 7.108), and wealth is a preferred indifferent. But until we learn the judgement each act proceeds from, we may 'neither praise his action nor blame it' (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45; R1). He is also not shown treating the money, or a future he cannot command, as a good he must have (R2). So no Stoic verdict follows. 'neutral' is entered only because the field is required. Under R7 it does not apply, since unknown judgement is not neutral, and the row should be rewritten or flagged.

source_quote: ...when the state could spare him, he dug his own land? because he waged war against riches as keenly as against Pyrrhus? because he supped beside his hearth off the very roots and herbs which he himself, though an old man, and one who had enjoyed a triumph, had grubbed up while clearing his field of weeds?

contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not fully settle the case. Read one way, the remark is calm indifference to the officer's words and practical attention to the praetor, who decides: acting well. Read another way, the praetor's opinion is itself an external not up to the Rhodian. If he treats the praetor's approval as a good he must have (Discourses 2.13, the singer who wants applause), or if the line is a cutting retort spoken in anger (the 'sting and bite' Plutarch condemns), it is acting badly. Plutarch, a Platonist and not a Stoic, praises the remark as an apt alternative to angry revenge. By R9 that praise is not by itself a Stoic verdict.

Both reputation and property are 'not under our control' (Handbook 1). Choosing between preferred indifferents can be appropriate (Discourses 2.10), but the vignette does not show whether he craves them as goods or only selects them with reason. The laying down of arms, done from repentance, is a turn to a correct judgement and could be called well done in itself. Only the earlier war, whose motive is not shown, is clearly bad. 'Repent' shows the judgement that his war on his country was wrong, so by R1 and R5 the act proceeds from a correct judgement and counts as acting well for a person making progress. His earlier taking up of arms was an error, but the act judged here is the laying down. Justice is the virtue most at stake, as the apportioning of what is due to one's country (R8).

By the role-based reading (R6), with the war treated as the main act, this is acting badly and fails justice (R8).

contested_note: Seneca, the source, condemns the act as ingratitude toward a benefactor. Epictetus's framing does not settle it without the motive. If Antonius sincerely judged the dictator a tyrant justly killed, then condemning him and honouring the killers could be a correct judgement. Some Stoic-leaning Romans admired the tyrannicides, and Seneca himself, at On Benefits 2.20, faults Brutus's political judgement rather than the killing as such. If instead he spoke falsely to secure power and safety, it is acting badly. So R9 applies: Epictetus's framing does not settle the case, and Seneca's praise or blame is not by itself a Stoic verdict. | From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as virtue: Under R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45), we may neither praise nor blame until we learn the judgement the act proceeds from. The vignette shows only outward acts: declaring the killing just and sending the assassins to provinces. It does not show whether he treats justice to his country as the good (R6, his role as a leader and citizen, which ranks above a private benefactor's favour) or treats safety, office and the people's mood, which are externals not up to him, as goods he must secure (R2). The 'virtue' label is provisional. R7 forbids defaulting to 'neutral' when the judgement is unknown, so the row is flagged for rewrite rather than settled.

If they reversed a verdict they thought deserved, out of resentment of the pressure, they acted badly. Seneca's passage addresses only whether the defendant owes them a benefit (he does not, since they did not intend to help him). If the influence is a bribe or pressure on them to acquit, the same refusal is injustice. If they let a man they believed guilty go free only to avoid seeming swayed, they acted for reputation, which is not up to them (Handbook 1, 19).

stoic_judgement: in agitated fear lest he be too slow in repaying them, because he is afraid that men will speak unfavorably of him

Like the citharoede who wants applause (Discourses 2.13), this is an assented passion and so acting badly even with no outward deed (R1, R2). It is not a mere first movement (R3), and it is not rational caution (R4), because the fear is aimed at men's opinion and not at what he owes.

That is an assented passion and acting badly (R1, R2; *Handbook* 1, 19; *Discourses* 2.13). He 'must himself of necessity be changed and tossed to and fro with them' (*Discourses* 1.4). stoic_judgement: whose desires fortune has satisfied, finishing his life still brooding on some plan for going further, never having limited his empire because he was satisfied

This is the assented craving of Discourses 2.13 and Handbook 19 ('you will not wish to be a praetor ... but a free man'), so under R1-R2 he acts badly. The vignette shows this as greed, not as a king doing his duty for a preferred indifferent (R6). It is a failure of temperance (restraint of appetite, R8), resting on a failure of wisdom about what is up to us.

source_verdict: You will think him an even greater man for having rejected this gift than for having earned it.
stoic_judgement: refuse it, saying, "You do not need a citizen who needs more than one citizen's share."

The refusal comes from correct judgement, so it is acting well as one making progress (R5). It is chiefly restraint of the desire for more (temperance), with fair dealing and good fellowship toward fellow citizens (justice) also at stake (R8).

source_quote: someone who steals something sacred
source_lesson: Therefore, someone who steals something sacred seems to be impious, even if wherever he took what he stole is still a place within the boundaries of the world, and in the same way even the sage can be robbed.
source_verdict: An impious man certainly does not do harm to a god, who is protected from attack by his divine nature, but he is nevertheless punished on the grounds that he acted as though he were harming a god. stoic_judgement: break into a temple and steal something sacred, a thing that religious observance has assigned to a divinity

Unlike hasty bathing in Handbook 45, its type is not indifferent: taking what is assigned to the god for one's own use shows the judgement that an external thing is worth more than piety and fair dealing. That is acting badly from a bad judgement (Discourses 4.8, R1). Each actual act is either right or wrong (Inwood, R7), and piety falls under justice (Arius 5b2, R8).

other: You see a philosopher reject a god's offer of our wealth to keep, on condition he give none of it away, saying he will not tie himself to that inescapable burden but go back to his own riches.
self: You reject a god's offer of our wealth to keep, on condition you give none of it away, saying you will not tie yourself to that inescapable burden but go back to your own riches.
contested_note: Wealth is a preferred indifferent, which by nature one should 'cleave to' (Discourses 2.10, DL 7.105). If 'burden' means he judges wealth itself an evil, as the source's Demetrius does ('the very things that harm all peoples'), then he is shunning an external, and Epictetus's framing would count that as a faulty aversion, not acting well. If he only refuses wealth he cannot use as material for his purpose, for example by giving it, the refusal is appropriate. The vignette's wording does not settle which.
source: Seneca, On Benefits (c. 56-64 CE; Miriam Griffin and Brad Inwood, 2011)

source_quote: he would reject the offer ... Demetrius laughed and refused it, thinking that it was not even worth boasting about rejecting that amount
source_reason: I certainly will not tie myself to that inescapable burden, nor will I send my disencumbered self into the deep sewers of wealth. ... Set me free and let me go back to my own riches. I know the kingdom of wisdom in all its greatness and security. I possess all things just in the sense that they belong to everyone.
source_lesson: I am certain that providence gave him the way of life he has and the rhetorical skill he possesses so that our age would have an example to follow and a rebuke to heed.
source_verdict: he is a man of superb wisdom ... Let me bear witness to this outstanding man; I heard him say something magnificent
stoic_judgement: saying he will not tie himself to that inescapable burden but go back to his own riches
stoic_reason: Under R1, he refuses because wealth he may not give away would bind him to an external. He keeps instead his 'own riches', the moral purpose that alone is up to him (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.29, 1.4: whoever craves externals 'can be neither faithful nor free'). That is a correct judgement about what is good, and so the act is done well under R5. Restraining the appetite for wealth is chiefly temperance (R8).

On that view, exhausting oneself and neglecting other duties for an opportunity that fortune withholds shows a judgement that the outward repayment is a good he must secure. source_reason: to focus on and devote himself to this one thing, not to miss any opportunity
source_lesson: But he returned your favor even if you did not receive a benefit.
source_verdict: You are being unjust if you demand concrete repayment when you can see that my intentions have not been wanting.
stoic_judgement: wear himself out day and night, setting aside all his other responsibilities to focus on repaying a benefit, not to miss any opportunity
stoic_reason: The will to repay is up to him and is already complete. The chance to repay a rich, healthy, fortunate man is not, so wearing himself out for it reads as craving an external, like the citharoede who wants the applause (Discourses 2.13; R1, R2). Setting aside all his other responsibilities omits appropriate acts his other roles require, which is an error (Handbook 30, Discourses 2.10, Arius 11a; R6).

speaker: Seneca, arguing in his own voice against an objector who says that effort alone does not count as repayment

And if on that journey I was shipwrecked and lost all the money I had borrowed to pay your ransom, and if I was myself imprisoned in the very chains I was trying to free you from
source_reason: to pay your ransom
source_lesson: Virtue constantly struggling against fortune shines forth even if it does not carry out its intended action.

stoic_judgement: borrow money against his own property and sail in harsh winter along shores beset by bandits to pay his captured benefactor's ransom

That is a role-appropriate act chosen for a reason, so it is well done (R1, R6), and he acts as one making progress (R5). The outcome, someone else having already paid, was not up to him (Handbook 1), so it neither adds to nor takes from the act (Discourses 1.29). Justice is primary because repaying a benefit is fair dealing and good faith (R8); courage also fits, since he endures winter seas and bandits.

Under Discourses 4.8 and Handbook 42, an act that proceeds from a bad judgement is done badly, even if he sincerely holds it (R1). His role as a friend asks him to respect what is his friend's, not to use the friendship as a title to sell it (R6). The failure is chiefly one of giving each his due (R8).

source_quote: I will repay my creditor even if he is going to go straight off and squander it on fancy foods; if he assigns my debt to a mistress, I will even make that payment. And I will give him his money even if he takes the coins and lets them fall through the holes in his pockets.

stoic_judgement: because his job is to make the return, not to look out for it afterward

Repaying in good faith is his own doing and what his role as debtor asks; what the creditor does with the money is not up to him (Handbook 1; Discourses 1.29). Rules: R1 (the motive is shown), R6 (the debtor's role is one-sided, his side only) and R5 (acting well while making progress).

Repayment is a preferred indifferent and may be sought, and he seeks it without blame to his neighbour (fair dealing, good fellowship), so it is acting well as one making progress (R5); the main virtue is justice, with temperance in restraining the rebuke (R8).

source_quote: the thought of death used to bother me deeply. Indeed, there was a time in my life when I was thinking about it almost every day, and on some days more than once. ... Still, the thought of my consciousness one day ceasing to exist did upset me.
source_lesson: death itself is not under our control \(it will happen one way or another\), but how we think about death most definitely is under our control. That’s the part we can and need to work on.

stoic_judgement: thinking about it almost every day, and on some days more than once, upset by the thought of his consciousness one day ceasing to exist
stoic_reason: This is not a sudden, unconsidered shock (fragment 9, R3). It is a recurring, considered distress, which shows assent to the judgement that his death, not up to him, is dreadful. By Handbook 5 'the judgement that death is dreadful, this is the dreadful thing', so it is an assented passion and counts as acting badly even with no outward deed (R2). His knowing that death is natural while still dreading it is like Handbook 52: ready with the argument, yet not living by it (R1).

speaker: Massimo Pigliucci, the author, illustrating Epictetus's teaching on impressions with his own example
source_quote: Someone may call me fat, as indeed happened somewhat frequently when I was a young boy. Well, is it true? At one time in my life it was. In which case, why get offended? What does it even mean to feel insulted by a fact?
source_reason: Conversely, is it not true? Then the fellow who hurled the insult is both childish in his behavior and factually wrong. How is that going to injure *me*?
source_lesson: Whether we perceive someone else's remark as an insult or not is entirely up to us, quite regardless of the intention of our interlocutor.
source_verdict: In which case, why get offended? What does it even mean to feel insulted by a fact? ... How is that going to injure *me*? If anything, he is the one who loses in the confrontation.
stoic_judgement: decline to get offended, asking what it even means to feel insulted by a fact
stoic_reason: Under R1 and R2, his question shows the judgement he acts from: a true remark about his body, which is not up to him, is not an evil and so no insult. As Handbook 20 puts it, it is our own judgement that insults us, not the man who reviles. He withholds assent from the impression of injury and uses the impression correctly, so he acts well as one making progress (R5).

contested_note: Life and health are preferred indifferents, and Discourses 2.10 says we should act for what is 'naturally more fit to be chosen'. On that reading, working against disease and death could be an appropriate act if he treats death only as a rejected indifferent, not as an evil. The vignette does not show fear, clinging, or a judgement that death is evil, so Epictetus's framing does not settle it. Pigliucci's verdict of hubris rests on things not in the vignette: self-importance, a cult-like following, unwillingness to 'leave the party', and cost to others.

Under R1 and R2 this judgement, not the arguing itself, is acting badly: a failure of wisdom about what is and is not up to us.

source: Massimo Pigliucci, How to Be a Stoic (2017)
speaker: Massimo Pigliucci, in imagined conversation with Epictetus
source_quote: But I shall lie on a hard bed. ... I shall not have a proper house.
source_lesson: compared to what will be happening and should be absorbing our full attention, those are minor details
source_verdict: Tough teacher, isn't he? But by now all of this makes perfect sense from within the Stoic framework, right?
stoic_judgement: "But I shall lie on a hard bed. I shall not have a proper house.": raised as a protest against bearing illness and death, treating the lack of a soft bed and a house as evils that would make dying bad
stoic_reason: By R2 and Handbook 5, his aversion is aimed at externals not up to him (bed, house; Handbook 1, Discourses 3.2). His protest reads as the judgement that these are evils, as with the singer's anxiety for applause (Discourses 2.13), not as a mere preference for a preferred indifferent (Discourses 2.10). Because it is a failure to endure hardship, the main virtue at stake is courage (R8), with wisdom also failing, since he does not see what is up to him.

other: You see a forty-one-year-old woman with ALS, who can no longer brush her teeth, scratch an itch, or stand, take a cocktail of morphine, pentobarbital, and chloral hydrate prescribed by her doctor to end her life.
self: You are forty-one and have ALS, can no longer brush your teeth, scratch an itch, or stand, and you take a cocktail of morphine, pentobarbital, and chloral hydrate prescribed by your doctor to end your life.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle the case without her judgement. The open-door passages, and the earlier Stoics' 'reasonable exit' for incurable illness, support a reasoned departure. Epictetus also warns students not to leave before the god gives the signal (Discourses 1.9), and Musonius's endurance on Gyara is held up as the tougher course. So the verdict turns on whether she left by reasoned choice among indifferents or from aversion to externals (her body) judged evil. Pigliucci, the source, calls it 'the dignified way out', which by itself is not a Stoic verdict (R9).
source: Massimo Pigliucci, How to Be a Stoic (2017)
speaker: Massimo Pigliucci, relating Betsy Davis's story to Epictetus in an imagined conversation
source_quote: Betsy took a cocktail of morphine, pentobarbital, and chloral hydrate prescribed by her doctor and died peacefully.
source_reason: Betsy was suffering from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease. She had almost completely lost control of her muscles; at forty-one, she not only was unable to perform but could no longer brush her teeth or scratch an itch, let alone stand.
source_lesson: Just as, for the Stoics, death itself is what gives urgent meaning to life, the possibility of leaving life voluntarily gives us the courage to do what is right under otherwise unbearable circumstances.
source_verdict: She took the dignified way out, thanks to the recently enacted California law on assisted suicide.
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the outward act (taking the prescribed cocktail) and her condition, but not the judgement she acts from. Under R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45) the act can be neither praised nor blamed until we know it, and under R7 unknown judgement is not `neutral`. The `virtue` label is therefore provisional. It rests on Epictetus's 'open door' (if the smoke is excessive, I go out): a reasoned departure from a condition contrary to nature, chosen as 'naturally more fit to be chosen' (Discourses 2.10), would be acting well. If she acted from the judgement that her body's ruin is a true evil, it would instead be a passion (R2) and `vice`.

source_verdict: He distinguished himself already on the campaign trail, refusing to go around canvassing for votes with the aid of a "nomenclator," a person in charge of reminding him who the people he was talking to were, helping him pretend that he knew them better than he actually did.

stoic_judgement: refuse an aide to remind him who voters are ... frankly admitting when he doesn't know them
stoic_reason: Refusing to feign acquaintance and openly admitting ignorance best reads as the judgement that deceit is not to be done even for an office, which is not up to us (Handbook 1, 52). That is good faith, the foundation of justice (R8, Cicero De Officiis 1.23), and an act that proceeds from a correct judgement is well done for one making progress (R1, R5). Under R1 this reading is inferred: the vignette shows the honest act, but not why he chooses it.

other: You see a dictator, on his triumphal return to Rome, parade a painting he ordered of his dead arch-enemy ripping off his own guts when his dagger failed, to dehumanize him.
self: You, a dictator on your triumphal return to Rome, parade a painting you ordered of your dead arch-enemy ripping off his own guts when his dagger failed, to dehumanize him.
source: Massimo Pigliucci, Cato Chronicles (2021)
speaker: Massimo Pigliucci, the blog author, retelling the episode in a series inspired by Goodman and Soni's Rome's Last Citizen
source_quote: it was Caesar who ordered the first known portrait of the death of Cato, seen ripping off his own guts when his dagger failed ... The dictator paraded the painting during his triumphal return in Rome
source_reason: with the intention of dehumanizing him

source_verdict: Interestingly, it was Caesar who ordered the first known portrait of the death of Cato, seen ripping off his own guts when his dagger failed, with the intention of dehumanizing him. The dictator paraded the painting during his triumphal return in Rome, but it backfired, inspiring pity for his vanquished foe among the people.
stoic_judgement: parade a painting he ordered of his dead arch-enemy ... to dehumanize him
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement behind the act (R1). He treats his enemy's standing and his own triumph, things not up to him, as goods worth winning by degrading a dead man, and that is a bad judgement acted on (R2; Handbook 1, 19). Justice, giving each his due and dealing with others without blame, is what he fails, and the vanity and enmity behind it fail temperance (R8).

self: You, the first Roman emperor visiting a dead Stoic's house, interrupt a sycophant criticizing that Stoic, saying, "To seek to keep the established constitution unchanged is a sign of a good citizen and a good man."
contested_note: The author reads the act as political savvy. Augustus embraced Republican values and Cato's memory only 'in theory' while ending the Republic, so the source's verdict differs from a reading of the words alone. Under Discourses 4.8, until we know the judgement he acts from, his framing does not settle the case.
source: Massimo Pigliucci, Cato Chronicles (2021)
speaker: Massimo Pigliucci, narrating his Cato Chronicles series
source_quote: he interrupted a sycophant who was criticizing the Stoic figure, saying that "To seek to keep the established constitution unchanged is a sign of a good citizen and a good man."
source_reason: "To seek to keep the established constitution unchanged is a sign of a good citizen and a good man."
source_verdict: Ironically, Augustus actually embraced — in theory — both Republican values and Cato's memory, probably because he was a savvier politician than Caesar himself.
stoic_judgement: "To seek to keep the established constitution unchanged is a sign of a good citizen and a good man."
stoic_reason: Augustus's words state a correct judgement: Cato's goodness lay in his moral purpose and his role as citizen, not in his success. Refusing a flatterer's slander of a dead man is fair dealing (R1, R6, R8). But the vignette gives only his words, not whether he acts from that judgement or for political advantage. Handbook 52 warns that we are ready with the right arguments while doing otherwise, so the praise is provisional (R1, R9).

other: You see a statesman commanding a city, unable to persuade his own side's cavalry with words to stop looting the city and killing the locals, simply bribe them to go away on behalf of the population.
self: You, commanding a city and unable to persuade your own side's cavalry with words to stop looting the city and killing the locals, simply bribe them to go away on behalf of the population.
source: Massimo Pigliucci, Cato Chronicles (2021)
speaker: Massimo Pigliucci, narrating Cato's last days at Utica (drawing on Goodman and Soni's Rome's Last Citizen)
source_quote: Cato intervened again on behalf of the population, and since he was unable to persuade the soldiers with his words, he simply bribed them to go away. He then kept alert despite fatigue and stress, supervising the preparation of the ships in order to allow as many people to flee before the arrival of Caesar, even buying out of his pocket passage for those who were too poor to afford it.
source_reason: Cato intervened again on behalf of the population, and since he was unable to persuade the soldiers with his words, he simply bribed them to go away.
source_verdict: Cato, however, wasn't done yet being Cato.
stoic_judgement: "unable to persuade ... with words ... simply bribe them to go away on behalf of the population": he acts for the locals' safety, which his command makes his charge, and treats money as a mere material to spend for it.
stoic_reason: The motive is shown (R1): he acts for the population, so the act proceeds from a correct judgement. As commander of the city he owes the townspeople protection (R6, Discourses 2.10), and he uses an indifferent, money, for what is by nature preferable, their lives, after reason in words has failed. That is acting well as one making progress (R5).

other: You see the most prestigious member of a resistance against Caesar silently move his chair to give the highest-ranking ex-consul, manifestly less competent than himself, pride of place, refusing to break the laws they fight for.
self: You, the most prestigious member of a resistance against Caesar, silently move your chair to give the highest-ranking ex-consul, manifestly less competent than yourself, pride of place, refusing to break the laws you fight for.
contested_note: The source's verdict differs. Goodman & Soni, with Pigliucci partly agreeing, criticize Cato for yielding to a manifestly less competent man, which arguably caused the disaster. Plutarch praises the refusal to break the laws. Within the Stoic framing it is also not fully settled whether wisdom, which should 'cleave to that which is naturally more fit to be chosen' (*Discourses* 2.10), required taking command to secure the preferred outcome, or whether keeping the law was the appropriate act.
source: Massimo Pigliucci, Cato Chronicles (2021)
speaker: Massimo Pigliucci, citing Goodman & Soni and Plutarch
source_quote: Without a word, Cato simply picked up his chair, walked around the king and the ex-consul, and placed his chair on the other side — which gave Metellus Scipio pride of place in the center.
source_reason: the latter was the highest ranking officer, and Cato saw himself as fighting to uphold the law that he had seen far too many times being trampled by ambitious men, from Sulla in his youth to Caesar just a few years before ... He refused to break the laws in whose support they were waging war [against] one who broke them.
source_verdict: Here, however, is another case where Goodman and Soli criticize Cato, possibly with some good reason. ... He may have passed on the opportunity to take complete charge of the situation, but Cato nonetheless played an important role in the last days of the resistance.
stoic_judgement: refusing to break the laws they fight for
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement he acts from: fidelity to the law he fights for, which he puts above command and prestige. Office and outcome are not up to us (*Handbook* 1), and craving them would make him 'subordinate himself to others' (*Discourses* 1.4). So the act proceeds from a correct judgement and is acting well as one making progress (R1, R5). It also gives each his due by rank, as his role in the council asks (R6, R8).

other: You see a Roman statesman who has failed of election to the praetorship spending the day whereon he failed of election in play.
self: You have failed of election to the praetorship, and you spend the day whereon you failed of election in play.
contested_note: Seneca (Letters 71.11) praises the act as bearing defeat 'with an equally stout heart'. Epictetus's framing does not settle it from the act alone: play on the day of defeat could come from the correct judgement that office is not up to us, or from distraction, bravado or numbing grief over a loss judged an evil, which would be acting badly (R2). The label follows the likeliest reading; the source's verdict is clearer than Epictetus's framing allows.
source: Massimo Pigliucci, Cato Chronicles (2021)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter to Lucilius, quoted by Massimo Pigliucci
source_quote: The day whereon he failed of election, he spent in play; the night wherein he intended to die, he spent in reading.
source_lesson: Cato will bear with an equally stout heart anything that thwarts him of his victory, as he bore that which thwarted him of his praetorship.
source_verdict: Cato will bear with an equally stout heart anything that thwarts him of his victory, as he bore that which thwarted him of his praetorship.
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: The vignette shows only an outward act (spending the day of his electoral defeat in play), not the judgement behind it. By Handbook 45 and Discourses 4.8 ('until you learn the judgement from which a man performs each separate act, neither praise his action nor blame it') this alone can be neither praised nor blamed (R1). The provisional 'virtue' rests on the likeliest reading, that he judged the praetorship, an office not up to him (Handbook 1), to be no good of his and so was not disturbed by losing it (Discourses 2.13, the singer who wants applause). Under R9, Seneca's praise does not by itself make it a Stoic verdict.

other: You see a statesman, unterrified amid the din of civil war, be the first to attack the armies that are already making for the Alps, plunging face-forward into the civil conflict.
self: You, unterrified amid the din of civil war, are the first to attack the armies that are already making for the Alps, plunging face-forward into the civil conflict.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle the act. Fearlessness alone does not show whether attacking was what reason and his role required or was rashness. The source (Seneca, via Pigliucci) praises Cato as a hero, but a source's praise is not by itself a Stoic verdict (R9). Seneca himself elsewhere (Letters 14.12-13) questions whether the wise man should join a civil conflict at all.
source: Massimo Pigliucci, Cato Chronicles (2021)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter to Lucilius, as quoted by Massimo Pigliucci
source_quote: who was unterrified amid the din of civil war, who was first to attack the armies that were already making for the Alps, who plunged face-forward into the civil conflict
source_lesson: \[hero\] is exactly the sort of expression and attitude which I should give him.
source_verdict: \[hero\] is exactly the sort of expression and attitude which I should give him.
stoic_judgement: unterrified amid the din of civil war
stoic_reason: Fear is the judgement that something not up to us, here death and the dangers of war, is an evil (Handbook 5; Discourses 2.13). 'Unterrified' shows he does not make that judgement, which comes nearest to courage, the knowledge of what to endure (R2, R8). But the vignette never says why he attacks, whether for his country and his role as statesman or from rashness or love of glory, so the act itself is only weakly shown to proceed from correct judgement (Discourses 4.8, R1, R6). We label it acting well as one making progress (R5), with a flag.

other: You see a commander leading the remains of a beaten army on foot over sun-baked hills, with no supplies, wearing heavy armor, always the last to drink of the few springs they find.
self: You lead the remains of a beaten army on foot over sun-baked hills, with no supplies, wearing heavy armor, always the last to drink of the few springs you find.
contested_note: Seneca, a Stoic, praises the act outright as proof that thirst and toil can be endured. Epictetus's rule (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45) withholds praise until the judgement behind the act is known, and the vignette shows only the outward conduct. So his framing does not fully settle the verdict.
source: Massimo Pigliucci, Cato Chronicles (2021)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter to Lucilius, quoted by Massimo Pigliucci
source_quote: Cato, on foot, led an army through African deserts. ... he marched over sun-baked hills, dragging the remains of a beaten army and with no train of supplies, undergoing lack of water and wearing a heavy suit of armor; always the last to drink of the few springs which they chanced to find.
source_lesson: You see that man can endure toil ... You see that thirst can be endured
source_verdict: You see that thirst can be endured: he marched over sun-baked hills, dragging the remains of a beaten army and with no train of supplies, undergoing lack of water and wearing a heavy suit of armor
stoic_judgement: always the last to drink of the few springs they find (the vignette shows a steady choice, but does not state the motive)
stoic_reason: Enduring thirst and toil without supplies is bearing what is not up to him, and drinking last fits his role as commander, putting his men's need before his own appetite (R6, R8). But by Discourses 4.8 and R1 we cannot praise the act until we know the judgement it proceeds from. Drinking last could come from judging thirst no evil and his duty to his men a good, or from a wish for reputation. The vignette implies the first reading but does not state it.

other: You see a Roman statesman attack the two all-powerful leaders above him in rank simultaneously, at a time when none dared fall foul of the one without endeavoring to oblige the other.
self: You attack the two all-powerful leaders above you in rank simultaneously, at a time when none dares fall foul of the one without endeavoring to oblige the other.
contested_note: Seneca, a Stoic, praises the act as freedom from fear of those above him in rank. Epictetus's rule (Discourses 4.8) says neither to praise nor blame until the judgement is known. The vignette shows only a bold act against the powerful, which could come from justice and indifference to their favour, or from anger, ambition or love of glory. His framing does not settle it on this text.
source: Massimo Pigliucci, Cato Chronicles (2021)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter to Lucilius (quoted by Massimo Pigliucci)
source_quote: Cato, on foot, led an army through African deserts. ... for Cato attacked Caesar and Pompey simultaneously, at a time when none dared fall foul of the one without endeavoring to oblige the other. ... Cato inflicted exile upon himself and finally death, and war all the while.
source_lesson: You see that man can endure toil ... You see that thirst can be endured ... You see that honor, and dishonor too, can be despised ... You see also that man can be free from fear of those above him in rank ... You see that death can be scorned as well as exile
source_verdict: But he withstood her, on all occasions, and in his last moments, at the point of death, showed that a brave man can live in spite of Fortune, can die in spite of her.
stoic_judgement: "attack the two all-powerful leaders ... simultaneously, at a time when none dared fall foul of the one without endeavoring to oblige the other". This shows only indirectly that he did not court either man's favour. His motive is not shown.
stoic_reason: The contrast suggests he refused to treat the favour of the powerful, which is not up to him, as a good. That would make him free rather than 'subordinating himself to others' (Discourses 1.4, Handbook 19), and so acting well, chiefly in courage (R2, R5, R8). But R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45) forbids praising an outward act until the judgement behind it is known, so this verdict rests on an inference.

other: You see a consul who pushed a law raising the penalty for bribery to ten years of exile offer to defend the patently guilty consul-elect, because he needs two new consuls to hold firm against a conspirator.
self: You pushed a law raising the penalty for bribery to ten years of exile, and now you offer to defend the patently guilty consul-elect, because you need two new consuls to hold firm against a conspirator.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing is not fully decisive. Defending the accused is a recognized role for a Roman advocate (R6), and the motive is the country's preservation, which the earlier Stoics (DL 7.108) list among befitting concerns. One could therefore read the act as an appropriate choice of the preferred. Cato, the Stoic in the episode, held the opposite view: prosecution was required. Pigliucci's verdict is mixed, praising political savvy while saying it bordered on hypocrisy or opportunism.
source: Massimo Pigliucci, Cato Chronicles (2021)
speaker: Massimo Pigliucci, summarizing Goodman and Soni's Rome's Last Citizen
source_quote: Cicero, somewhat unexpectedly, offered to defend Murena, while Cato was set to deliver the closing argument against him
source_reason: "[Cicero's] calculation was brutally simple. He needed two new, unsullied consuls to hold firm against Catiline. The conviction and exile of one of them would mean political chaos at the worst possible time. And so Murena was to be acquitted."
source_lesson: on the one hand, Cicero displayed political savvy and an ability to compromise in order to achieve his objectives, though at times his willingness to adjust to the situation on the ground bordered on hypocrisy or opportunism. On the other hand, Cato was the light of virtue and integrity that inspired his followers, and that was much admired by Cicero, even though it was that very same sense of honor that led him to fail to build the sort of political coalition that might have turned the fortunes of the Republic and avoided descent into empire.
source_verdict: By contrast, they claim that Cato was "trapped" by his idealism, as he simply could not avoid prosecuting a corrupted politician, given his own public stance (and coherent private practice) on the matter.
stoic_judgement: because he needs two new consuls to hold firm against a conspirator
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement behind the act (R1): the Republic's stability is treated as weighty enough to justify getting a patently guilty man acquitted under the very law the consul pushed. Care for one's country is appropriate (R6), but its safety is an external. Choosing it over justice and good faith (Handbook 52; Cicero De Officiis 1.23) is the moral purpose using externals badly. So, following Epictetus first (R9), it is acting badly, chiefly against justice (R8).

other: You see a writer mix the reasoning and ideas of others with his own and deliberately conceal the authors' names, so hasty critics will tweak Plutarch on his nose and insult the Seneca in him.
self: You mix the reasoning and ideas of others with your own and deliberately conceal the authors' names, so hasty critics will tweak Plutarch on your nose and insult the Seneca in you.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle it. Handbook 52 condemns lying, but no rule of his addresses silent non-attribution done for no profit. The motive can also be read charitably, as protecting the ideas from careless dismissal rather than as vanity or wishing humiliation on others. Montaigne (the speaker) presents the practice approvingly, so the source's verdict differs from this label (R9). | The source's author judges it well (inferred); Epictetus's framing gives vice
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Montaigne, in Of Books, as quoted by Farnsworth in his introduction of Montaigne
source_quote: When I transplant the reasoning and ideas of others into my own soil and mix them with mine, I deliberately conceal the names of the authors.
source_reason: I do this to rein in the temerity of those hasty criticisms thrown at every kind of writing, especially contemporary writings by living authors, and writings that use common language – language that invites anyone to be a critic, and that can make the conception and design of the book seem just as common. I want them to tweak Plutarch on my nose, and to burn themselves by insulting the Seneca in me.
source_lesson: The truth of this assessment will be seen in the pages ahead.
source_verdict: The truth of this assessment will be seen in the pages ahead.
stoic_judgement: deliberately conceal the authors' names, so hasty critics will tweak Plutarch on his nose and insult the Seneca in him
stoic_reason: Under R1 the vignette shows a motive: to steer how critics judge his book, and to have them disgrace themselves. Critics' verdicts are reputation, not up to us (Handbook 1), and Handbook 42 says the critic who judges wrongly harms only himself. So contriving concealment to trap critics treats their opinion as something to be managed and punished. It reads as a failure of justice (honesty toward readers and the authors he uses) from a misjudgement of what is up to him (R2, R8).

other: You see a Stoic writer heap quotations from the rival philosopher Epicurus upon his reader, so that those who value the speaker, not the thing spoken, may understand the best ideas are common property.
self: You, a Stoic writer, heap quotations from the rival philosopher Epicurus upon your reader, so that those who value the speaker, not the thing spoken, may understand the best ideas are common property.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter (Epistles 12.11)
source_quote: I shall continue to heap quotations from Epicurus upon you
source_reason: so that all persons who swear by the words of another, and put a value upon the speaker and not upon the thing spoken, may understand that the best ideas are common property.
source_lesson: the best ideas are common property.
source_verdict: This book will take the same liberty.
stoic_judgement: so that those who value the speaker, not the thing spoken, may understand the best ideas are common property
stoic_reason: The vignette shows his judgement (R1): he assents to an idea for its truth, not for the speaker's reputation, which is an external. He acts to correct others' false judgement out of goodwill toward his reader (R4). That is an act that 'proceeds from correct judgements', so it is labelled virtue as acting well while making progress (R5). It comes nearest to wisdom, the right use of impressions and assent; justice also fits, since he teaches others for their good (R8).

other: You see a man tell his own pain it is only pain, the same pain a wretch ridden with gout despises, the dyspeptic endures for his fancy foods, and a girl bears bravely in childbirth.
self: You tell your own pain it is only pain, the same pain a wretch ridden with gout despises, the dyspeptic endures for his fancy foods, and a girl bears bravely in childbirth.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in conversation with his own pain
source_quote: Seneca's conversation with his own pain, which he belittles by thinking of people who endure the same or worse without complaint
source_reason: the same pain that is despised by that wretch who is ridden with gout, that the dyspeptic endures for his fancy foods, that a girl bears bravely in childbirth
source_lesson: If you see them putting up with things that you can't, it makes your reaction seem more clearly to be your own doing.
source_verdict: They usually suggest viewing a thing as small, as unimportant, as something to which we should rise superior; and one can have any or all of this without the overtones of vituperation and dislike.
stoic_judgement: tell his own pain it is only pain, the same pain a wretch ridden with gout despises, the dyspeptic endures for his fancy foods, and a girl bears bravely in childbirth
stoic_reason: Pain belongs to the body, which is not up to us. By telling it that it is 'only pain' that others bear, he refuses to assent to the impression that it is an evil or something dreadful (Handbook 5; Discourses 1.1). This is the correct use of impressions, an act that proceeds from a correct judgement, so it is acting well as one making progress (R1, R2, R5). Enduring hardship is courage (R8).

other: You see death terrifying to one man, coveted by a second, and indifferent to a third.
self: You find death terrifying, while a second man covets it and a third is indifferent to it.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Montaigne, in 'On Democritus and Heraclitusi' (1580), quoted by Farnsworth to support the Stoic thesis
source_quote: Death is terrifying to Cicero, coveted by Cato, indifferent to Socrates.
source_lesson: Let us therefore find no excuses in the external qualities of things; what we make of them is up to us. Our good or bad depends on no one but ourselves.
source_verdict: Let us therefore find no excuses in the external qualities of things; what we make of them is up to us. Our good or bad depends on no one but ourselves.
stoic_judgement: death terrifying to one man
stoic_reason: Death is not up to us and is nothing dreadful. 'The judgement that death is dreadful, this is the dreadful thing' (Handbook 5), so standing terror of death is an assented passion and counts as acting badly even with no outward deed (R2). It is presented as his settled view of death, not a sudden involuntary blench, so the R3 first-movement exception does not apply. The vice is the failure of courage, which is knowledge of what is and is not to be feared (R8).

other: You see a king, in his flight from the enemy, drink some water which is muddy and fouled by cadavers and declare he has never drunk anything more pleasant, having never drunk before when he was thirsty.
self: You, a king in flight from the enemy, drink some water which is muddy and fouled by cadavers and declare you have never drunk anything more pleasant, having never drunk before when you were thirsty.
contested_note: From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as virtue: The king shows the judgement that the foul water, an external, is no evil to him: what made it sweet was his own need, not the quality of the drink. That is the kind of correct use of impressions that Discourses 4.8 calls 'well done' (R1), and it is contentment with what is at hand, close to self-restraint over appetite (R8). Read as a person making progress, not a sage (R5), he is acting well. Drinking when thirsty is itself appropriate: it cleaves to what is naturally to be preferred (Discourses 2.10). | The labeller calls this label tentative:  Labelled neutral and flagged.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Cicero, in the Tusculan Disputations
source_quote: When Darius, in his flight from the enemy, had drunk some water which was muddy and fouled by cadavers, he declared that he had never drunk anything more pleasant
source_reason: he had never drunk before when he was thirsty
source_lesson: Who does not see that appetite is the best sauce? ... the pleasure of eating lies in having an appetite, not in being glutted.
source_verdict: then will you perceive that they who pursue pleasure most attain it least, and that the pleasure of eating lies in having an appetite, not in being glutted.
stoic_judgement: not shown ("declare he has never drunk anything more pleasant" reports a sensation; "having never drunk before when he was thirsty" is the narrator's explanation, not the king's judgement)
stoic_reason: Drinking when thirsty and finding it sweet is natural, and the vignette shows no judgement that the drink, or his own comfort, is a good or an evil. Under Discourses 4.8 and Handbook 45 we can neither praise nor blame it (R1). Read strictly, it fits R7 only weakly as an act and feeling with no judgement about good or evil at stake. Labelled neutral and flagged.

other: You see a young lady, hearing her host joke (there was nothing to it) that he fed his guests a pie made out of a cat, stricken with horror into a violent stomach disorder and fever.
self: You hear your host joke (there was nothing to it) that he fed his guests a pie made out of a cat, and you are so stricken with horror that you develop a violent stomach disorder and a fever.
contested_note: Fragment 9 and R3 allow that a sudden shock may disturb even the wise without assent. If her horror and sickness were an involuntary bodily revulsion of that kind, the verdict would be neutral. Reading it as vice rests on taking sustained horror, severe enough to cause fever, as assent to 'this is an evil', which is our reading and is not stated. Montaigne presents her as a pitiable victim of imagination, not as someone at fault.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Montaigne, telling of a gentleman he knows
source_quote: One of the young ladies in the party was so stricken with horror that she developed a violent stomach disorder and a fever. It was impossible to save her.
source_lesson: It is not much better – it may even be worse – if the mind makes such a discovery afterwards.
source_verdict: Reactions to what we eat feel unavoidable as we are having them, and seem to be brought about by the food rather than anything in ourselves; but those reactions often owe as much to us as they do to what is on the plate.
stoic_judgement: hearing her host joke (there was nothing to it) that he fed his guests a pie made out of a cat, stricken with horror
stoic_reason: Read by Handbook 5 and the third field of Discourses 3.2, it is not the pie that disturbs her but her judgement: she assents rashly to a false impression (it was only a joke) and judges a past external, what she ate, to be something dreadful. That horror is an assented passion (R2) rather than a passing shudder (R3), since it lasts long enough to produce illness and fever, so it is acting badly in the use of impressions (R1, R2).

other: You see a man whose baker is out of bread, and when the overseer, or the steward, or his tenants offer him some, he says, "Bad bread!"
self: When your baker is out of bread and the overseer, or the steward, or your tenants offer you some, you say, "Bad bread!"
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in Epistles 123.2–3
source_quote: "Bad bread!" you say
source_lesson: Cultivation is called for in cases like the one Seneca describes above, as when learning how to take satisfaction from simple and natural pleasures.
source_verdict: Wait; it will become good. Hunger will make even that bread taste delicate and seem to be from the finest flour. For that reason we should not eat until hunger bids us; I will wait until I can get good bread or cease to be fussy about it.
stoic_judgement: "Bad bread!"
stoic_reason: Offered plain bread when his own baker has none, he calls it bad. He gives an external the name of evil, and his desire is fixed on fine bread, which is not up to him. That is fussy appetite, the kind of judgement *Handbook* 5 and *Discourses* 3.2 call the fault, and not temperance (R1, R2, R8). It is not a first movement: it is a verdict he voices, so R3 and R7 do not apply.

other: You see people sweating and belching, being overfed like fatted oxen, as they pursue pleasure.
self: You are sweating and belching, being overfed like a fatted ox, as you pursue pleasure.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Cicero, in a passage from Tusculan Disputations 5.97, 99–100, quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: sweating and belching, being overfed like fatted oxen ... they who pursue pleasure most
source_lesson: then will you perceive that they who pursue pleasure most attain it least, and that the pleasure of eating lies in having an appetite, not in being glutted.
source_verdict: they who pursue pleasure most attain it least, and that the pleasure of eating lies in having an appetite, not in being glutted.
stoic_judgement: as they pursue pleasure
stoic_reason: They eat past need because they treat the pleasure of eating as a good to chase. That is a desire set on externals, not on their own moral purpose, so the overeating comes from a bad judgement and is badly done (Discourses 4.8, 1.29; the first field of Discourses 3.2). R1 is met because the motive is stated, not just the heavy eating (Handbook 45). R2 applies, and R8 names restraint of appetite as temperance.

other: You see a Roman general weeping over the death of an eel-like fish he owned and, ridiculed by another general, replying that these tears were more than his mocker shed over his three late wives.
self: You, a Roman general, weep over the death of an eel-like fish you owned and, ridiculed by another general, reply that these tears were more than he shed over his three late wives.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Ward Farnsworth, recounting Plutarch's anecdote (alluded to by Johnson)
source_quote: weeping over the death of an eel-like fish that he owned; Crassus replied that the tears were more than Domitius had shed over his three late wives
source_lesson: Of the same nature are the irregular appetites of the mind; though they are often excited by trifles, they are equally disquieting with real wants: the Roman, who wept at the death of his lamprey, felt the same degree of sorrow that extorts tears on other occasions.
source_verdict: Of the same nature are the irregular appetites of the mind; though they are often excited by trifles, they are equally disquieting with real wants: the Roman, who wept at the death of his lamprey, felt the same degree of sorrow that extorts tears on other occasions.
stoic_judgement: replying that these tears were more than his mocker shed over his three late wives
stoic_reason: Tears alone do not decide (R4, R1). But when challenged, he stands by his tears and ranks the fish's death as worth more grief than wives. That shows assent on reflection, not a first movement (R3): he judges the loss of an external he owned to be an evil, which is grief as a faulty judgement about what is not up to us (Handbook 5, 16; Discourses 1.29; R2).

other: You see a man turn pale and tremble and say, "How will he receive me, how will he listen to me?"
self: You turn pale and tremble and say, "How will he receive me, how will he listen to me?"
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Epictetus, quoted by Farnsworth (Discourses 2.13.17)
source_quote: turns pale and trembles and says, "How will he receive me, how will he listen to me?"
source_lesson: It was a lively feature of Epictetus's classroom style that those who worried or complained about externals would customarily be denounced as slaves.
source_verdict: Slave, he will act as *he* sees fit. Why do you care about other people's business?
stoic_judgement: say, "How will he receive me, how will he listen to me?"
stoic_reason: His words show he treats the other man's reception, which is not up to him, as a good he must have and its loss as an evil. This is the anxiety of the citharoede who wants applause (Discourses 2.13), an assented passion and so acting badly even with no outward deed (R2). His pallor and trembling might alone be a first movement (R3, fragment 9), but his words show he has assented to the impression (R1).

other: You see a Stoic teacher, himself a former slave, afraid as the emperor comes amid thunder and lightning with death and life and pleasure and pain.
self: You, a Stoic teacher and a former slave, are afraid as the emperor comes amid thunder and lightning with death and life and pleasure and pain.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Epictetus, in a Discourse
source_quote: when he comes with them, amid thunder and lightning, and I am afraid of them
source_lesson: Someone attached to externals is enslaved to whoever controls them; Stoic philosophy thus is a way to liberation.
source_verdict: what else do I do but acknowledge my master, like a runaway slave?
stoic_judgement: afraid as the emperor comes ... with death and life and pleasure and pain
stoic_reason: He fears death and pain, which are not up to him, so the passion is the judgement that these externals are evils. That makes the emperor, who controls them, his master (Handbook 5, 14; Discourses 2.13, 1.29). Under R2 an assented passion is acting badly even with no outward deed. R3 does not apply, because the fear is of what the emperor brings, not a startle at a sudden shock.

other: You see a person in fear and distress, regarding the events that are coming as evil, sit down and pray, "Lord God, let me not be distressed."
self: You are in fear and distress, regarding the events that are coming as evil, and you sit down and pray, "Lord God, let me not be distressed."
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Epictetus, lecturing and rebuking the person who prays to be spared distress
source_quote: Then we say, "Lord God, let me not be distressed." ... So are you going to sit down and pray that your nose will stop running?
source_lesson: What, then – has he given you nothing to help with your situation? Hasn't he given you endurance, hasn't he given you greatness of spirit, hasn't he given you courage?
source_verdict: Moron, don't you have hands? ... Better to wipe your nose and stop praying.
stoic_judgement: in fear and distress, regarding the events that are coming as evil
stoic_reason: The person assents to the judgement that coming externals, which are not up to them, are evil. That is fear and distress as a passion, so it is acting badly even with no outward deed (R2; Handbook 5, Discourses 2.13). Praying to be spared distress also hands to God what is already up to them, the use of impressions and the endurance, greatness of spirit and courage given for it (R1, Discourses 1.1).

other: You see a man groveling before another man and flattering him contrary to his own opinion, for the sake of a dinner.
self: You grovel before another man and flatter him contrary to your own opinion, for the sake of a dinner.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Epictetus (Discourses 4.1.55), quoted by Farnsworth after noting Epictetus's classroom habit of denouncing complainers as slaves
source_quote: groveling before another man, or flattering him contrary to his own opinion
source_reason: for a mere dinner ... for the sake of a prefecture or consulship
source_lesson: It was a lively feature of Epictetus's classroom style that those who worried or complained about externals would customarily be denounced as slaves.
source_verdict: you can confidently say he is not free. ... People who do these things for petty ends you can call petty slaves, while those who do them for grand purposes can be called mega slaves, as they deserve.
stoic_judgement: flattering him contrary to his own opinion, for the sake of a dinner
stoic_reason: He treats a dinner, which is not up to him, as a good worth giving up his self-respect and his honest opinion for. So he craves an external and subordinates himself to the man who can give or withhold it (Discourses 1.4, Handbook 1). The vignette shows this judgement (R1), and the deed proceeds from a bad judgement (Discourses 4.8, R2). Saying what he does not think is also deceit (Handbook 52).

other: You see a slaveholder living on familiar terms with his household slaves.
self: You, a slaveholder, live on familiar terms with your household slaves.
contested_note: Seneca, a Stoic, praises the act outright as befitting 'a sensible and well-educated man'. Epictetus's framing does not settle it, because the vignette does not show the judgement. The familiarity could come from seeing the slaves as fellow men under the same Fortune (acting well), or from convenience, laxity or a wish to be liked (not acting well). Under R9 the source's praise is not by itself the verdict.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter to Lucilius, answering an imagined objector's refrain
source_quote: you live on familiar terms with your slaves
source_lesson: No, they are rather our fellow-slaves, if one reflects that Fortune has the same rights over them and over us.
source_verdict: This befits a sensible and well-educated man like yourself.
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: Living on familiar terms with one's slaves is an appropriate type of act, near justice (kindness, good fellowship). It treats them as men subject to the same Fortune, to whom we stand in a relationship of 'us in relation to them' (R6, R8). But Discourses 4.8 says 'until you learn the judgement from which a man performs each separate act, neither praise his action nor blame it', so the label is provisional (R1). It cannot be neutral, because an unknown judgement is not positive evidence for neutral (R7).

other: You see a millionaire who has, by his own choosing, made himself a slave to a serving-maid.
self: You, a millionaire, have, by your own choosing, made yourself a slave to a serving-maid.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter (Epistles 47.17)
source_quote: One is a slave to lust, another to avarice, another to ambition, and all are slaves to fear. I will name you an ex-consul who is slave to a little old woman, a millionaire who is slave to a serving-maid; I will show you youths of the noblest birth in serfdom to pantomime players!
source_lesson: No servitude is more disgraceful than that which is self-imposed.
source_verdict: No servitude is more disgraceful than that which is self-imposed.
stoic_judgement: "by his own choosing, made himself a slave to a serving-maid": he treats something only she can give (her favour, or what he craves from her) as a good he must have, and so subordinates his own choice to her.
stoic_reason: Under R2 and R1, his self-chosen servitude is an assented craving for something not up to him. As Discourses 1.4 says, whoever craves what is not under his control 'can be neither faithful nor free' and must subordinate himself to those 'able to procure or prevent' it. That is acting badly, even with no further deed shown.

other: You see a grown-up going crazy over paintings and sculpture, regarding each piece as a thing of value and paying an expensive price for it.

source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, citing Aristo of Chios
source_quote: we elders go crazy over paintings and sculpture, making our folly more expensive
source_lesson: How contemptible are the things we admire – like children who regard every toy as a thing of value, who prefer a necklace bought for a few pennies to their own parents or their brothers.
source_verdict: How contemptible are the things we admire... making our folly more expensive
stoic_judgement: going crazy over paintings and sculpture, regarding each piece as a thing of value
stoic_reason: "Going crazy over" externals shows an assented craving: the judgement that things not up to us are goods one must have. Epictetus says that whoever craves what is not under his control 'can be neither faithful nor free' (Discourses 1.4; Handbook 1, 19). Under R1 and R2 this is acting badly, a failure of temperance (restraint of appetite, R8) that rests on a failure of wisdom about what is good.
