stoic_reason: By Discourses 1.4, a man who craves what is not up to him must 'end by subordinating himself to others' who can grant or withhold it. 'Made himself a slave' shows that self-imposed subordination, so the act comes from treating something she controls as a good he must have (R1, R2). It is also unbefitting of his role as an ex-consul (R6, Discourses 2.10).

other: You see a man hear the report "His ship is lost" and add on his own the notion that the man whose ship is lost fares badly.
self: You hear the report "His ship is lost" and add on your own the notion that the man whose ship is lost fares badly.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Farnsworth, quoting Epictetus, Discourses 3.8.5
source_quote: The notion that he fares badly, each man adds on his own.
source_lesson: When confronted with a report or an event or an object, in short, the Stoic tries to just see it as it is.
source_verdict: Stoicism regards this process as a trap.
stoic_judgement: add on his own the notion that the man whose ship is lost fares badly
stoic_reason: The report is only that the ship is lost. To add that the man fares badly is to assent to the impression that an external, not up to us, is an evil. That is an error in assent, the judgement that disturbs men (Handbook 5; Discourses 1.29, 3.2), and so acting badly even with no outward deed (R1, R2). 'Adds on his own' marks a voluntary judgement, not an unwilled first movement (R3).

other: You see a Spartan, after Philip has forced his way into the Peloponnesus, told his people will suffer greatly unless they get back into Philip's good graces, reply, "Coward; what can people suffer who do not fear death?"
self: You, a Spartan, after Philip has forced his way into the Peloponnesus, are told your people will suffer greatly unless they get back into Philip's good graces, and you reply, "Coward; what can people suffer who do not fear death?"
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
chapter: Chapter Four: DEATH — 2. Fearlessness of death
speaker: Montaigne, in "A Custom of the Isle of Cea" (1580), drawing on Plutarch's Apophthegmata Laconica (Sayings of the Spartans)
source_quote: "Coward," he replied; "what can people suffer who do not fear death?" ... to which he replied, "By holding death in contempt."
source_reason: "what can people suffer who do not fear death?"
source_verdict: Freedom from the fear of death is regarded by the Stoic as one of the central goals of philosophical work, from which many other liberties and goods follow. One who regards death without fear steps more lightly through life, and is free from many other fears as well; for death is the master fear that lies behind them.
stoic_judgement: "Coward; what can people suffer who do not fear death?"
stoic_reason: He refuses to treat death or the harms Philip can do, which are not up to him, as evils, and so will not subordinate himself to the man who can bring them about (Handbook 5; Discourses 1.4, 2.13). Under R1 the act proceeds from a correct judgement, so it is acting well as one making progress (R5); it most nearly shows courage, knowledge of what should be endured and feared (R8).

other: You see a man who has carried out many to be buried, and who now clings tenaciously to life.
self: You have carried out many to be buried, and now you cling tenaciously to life.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Marcus Aurelius, in a passage of his Meditations (4.50), quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: clung tenaciously to life
source_lesson: It is a simple but still useful help toward contempt of death to call to mind those who have clung tenaciously to life.
source_verdict: What did they gain beyond those who died early? Regardless, they were all buried somewhere eventually
stoic_judgement: now clings tenaciously to life
stoic_reason: Clinging 'tenaciously' to life, after seeing so many buried, reads as craving something not under his control and treating death as dreadful. Handbook 5 calls 'the judgement that death is dreadful' the dreadful thing, so this is an assented passion (R2), not the reasoned preference for life that Discourses 2.10 allows, and not a mere first movement (R3).

other: You see a man in a discussion about death object that he looks upon this very circumstance, not to exist after having existed, to be very miserable.
self: You object in a discussion about death that you look upon this very circumstance, not to exist after having existed, to be very miserable.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Cicero, in the Tusculan Disputations, answering an interlocutor who objects that non-existence after life is miserable
source_quote: I look upon this very circumstance, not to exist after having existed, to be very miserable.
source_lesson: A classic Stoic response to death is to contemplate its similarity to our position before birth, which we have no reason to think was difficult.
source_verdict: What, more so than not to have existed at all? It follows that those who are not yet born are miserable because they are not; and we ourselves, if we are to be miserable after death, were miserable before we were born: but I do not remember that I was miserable before I was born; and I should be glad to know, if your memory is better, what if anything you recollect of your own situation.
stoic_judgement: he looks upon this very circumstance, not to exist after having existed, to be very miserable
stoic_reason: He judges death, which is not up to him, to be an evil. Handbook 5 names exactly this as the fault: 'the judgement that death is dreadful, this is the dreadful thing.' So under R1 and R2 this is an error of assent (the third field), and so acting badly, even though no outward deed or felt dread is shown.

other: You see a man who has run away drive a sword into his vitals to be saved from arrest.
self: You have run away, and to be saved from arrest you drive a sword into your vitals.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, quoted by Farnsworth (Epistles 4.4), answering an imagined objector who says it is difficult to scorn life
source_quote: a third, to be saved from arrest after running away, drives a sword into his vitals
source_reason: to be saved from arrest after running away
source_lesson: Do you not suppose that virtue will be as effective as overwhelming fear?
source_verdict: Do you not suppose that virtue will be as effective as overwhelming fear?
stoic_judgement: to be saved from arrest
stoic_reason: He kills himself so as not to fall into arrest, which is outside his control. That treats an external as the greatest evil: an aversion directed at what is not up to him, an assented passion of fear acted on (Handbook 1, 5; Discourses 3.2; R1, R2). The exit Epictetus allows comes from correct judgement, but here the vignette shows only flight from an external, so it is a failure of courage, rooted in a failure of wisdom about what is good and evil (R8).

other: You see a man in a dream, shown the celestial things by a heavenly guide, marveling at these things yet still turning his eyes back to earth from time to time.
self: You, in a dream, shown the celestial things by a heavenly guide, marvel at these things yet still turn your eyes back to earth from time to time.
contested_note: From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as vice: The vignette shows an outward act, glancing back at earth, but not the judgement behind it. By Handbook 45 and Discourses 4.8 (R1) we should say only that he looks back, not that he looks badly. The "yet still" framing suggests he still treats earthly things (glory, empire, the external) as goods to cling to, which would be a failure of wisdom about what is up to us. Under R7 an unknown judgement cannot be labelled neutral, so the label rests on that reading and is marked contested.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Cicero, in the 'Dream of Scipio' (On the Republic 6.19–20): Africanus speaking to Scipio, introduced by Farnsworth
source_quote: Though marveling at these things, I was still turning my eyes back to earth from time to time.
source_lesson: If it appears as small to you as it really is, look always up to these celestial things, and down on those human ones. For what renown in men's mouths can you attain, what fame worth seeking?
source_verdict: The intended effect is to help us naturally reach some of the familiar Stoic conclusions, such as the repetitive character of human life and the perishability of it.
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: Marveling at the heavens and glancing back at earth are outward acts. The vignette does not show whether he treats earthly fame as a good, which is the judgement that would make the glance a fault (*Discourses* 4.8, *Handbook* 45; R1). Glancing is a type of act reason neither urges nor forbids, and no judgement about good or evil is shown, so it is neither well nor badly done (R7). This is a weak neutral: R1 says such a row should be rewritten or flagged.

other: You see a Roman commander, seeing his ship being seized by the enemy, run himself through with his sword and answer his men asking "where is the Commander?": "All is well with the Commander!"
self: You, a Roman commander, see your ship being seized by the enemy, run yourself through with your sword, and answer your men asking "where is the Commander?": "All is well with the Commander!"
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle this case. He holds that 'the door is open' when staying is unreasonable, but he warns his students not to leave life from fear, without the god's signal (Discourses 1.9, 1.29; not in the primer's Part 1). If Scipio killed himself because he judged capture an evil, that is fear and acting badly. If he did so because his role as commander made surrender shameful and death the reasonable exit, it is appropriate. The earlier Stoics allowed a 'reasonable exit' (DL 7.130), and Cato's similar death was praised by Seneca and treated as a question by later readers. Seneca's praise for 'glory' and 'ancestors' is not by itself a Stoic verdict (R9).
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter (Epistles 24.9), quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: He ran himself through with his sword. To the men who were asking “where is the Commander?” he answered, “All is well with the Commander!”
source_lesson: It was a great deed to conquer Carthage, but a greater deed to conquer death.
source_verdict: That statement made him the equal of his ancestors, and it did not allow the glory of the African Scipios, ordained by destiny, to be interrupted. It was a great deed to conquer Carthage, but a greater deed to conquer death.
stoic_judgement: "All is well with the Commander!"
stoic_reason: His calm words as he dies show the judgement that death, an external not up to him, is no evil and that his moral purpose is still sound. That is the opposite of the passion of dread (Handbook 5; Long §9.4 under R2), so under R1 and R5 he acts well as one making progress, with bravery as knowledge of what is to be endured (R8). Whether this exit was appropriate depends on a judgement the vignette does not show (R9).

other: You see a king of Sparta, asked how people could live in freedom while Philip forces his way into the Peloponnesus, reply, "By holding death in contempt."
self: You are a king of Sparta, and when asked how people could live in freedom while Philip forces his way into the Peloponnesus, you reply, "By holding death in contempt."
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Montaigne, citing Plutarch's Apophthegmata Laconica (Sayings of the Spartans)
source_quote: Agis was similarly asked how people could live in freedom; to which he replied, "By holding death in contempt."
source_reason: "By holding death in contempt."
source_lesson: Freedom from the fear of death is regarded by the Stoic as one of the central goals of philosophical work, from which many other liberties and goods follow.
source_verdict: He who has learned to die has unlearned slavery. He is above any power, and certainly beyond it.
stoic_judgement: asked how people could live in freedom while Philip forces his way into the Peloponnesus, reply, "By holding death in contempt."
stoic_reason: The king's answer voices the correct judgement of Handbook 5: death is nothing dreadful, and freedom comes from not craving or shunning what is not up to us (Discourses 1.4). Spoken in his role as king, to stiffen his people against Philip, it is an act that proceeds from correct judgement. So under R1, R5 and R6 it is acting well, and under R8 it comes nearest to courage, the knowledge of what should be endured and feared.

other: You see a Greek general, asked which of three generals should be held in highest esteem, two rivals or himself, reply, "You must first see us die before deciding."
self: You, a Greek general asked which of three generals should be held in highest esteem, two rivals or yourself, reply, "You must first see us die before deciding."
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Montaigne, in 'That Men Are Not to Judge of Our Happiness Till After Death'
source_quote: Epaminondas, asked which of the three should be held in highest esteem, Chabrias, Iphicrates, or himself, replied, “You must first see us die before deciding.”
source_reason: “You must first see us die before deciding.”
source_lesson: And the way one confronts death when it arrives is considered a test of that achievement, and of character – perhaps the true test.
source_verdict: And the way one confronts death when it arrives is considered a test of that achievement, and of character – perhaps the true test.
stoic_judgement: reply, "You must first see us die before deciding."
stoic_reason: His reply shows a judgement he acts from (R1): character is not proven until it meets death, so he will not rashly rank himself above his rivals. This is the third field of training, avoiding rashness in assent (Discourses 3.2), and it mirrors Handbook 45's 'until you have decided what judgement prompts him, how do you know'. It also declines to grasp at reputation, which is not up to us (Handbook 1). That counts as acting well as one making progress (R5), nearest to wisdom (R8).

other: You see a hog aboard a ship during a very great storm, not in the least concerned, while a philosopher points to it to encourage those near him who are most frightened.
self: You are a hog aboard a ship during a very great storm and are not in the least concerned, while a philosopher points to you to encourage those near him who are most frightened.
contested_note: The source's verdict differs from Epictetus's framing. Montaigne, retelling the sceptic Pyrrho, holds up the hog's unconcern as a better condition than reason-tormented fear, a model to envy. For Epictetus calm without reason is not the good. The good is a right moral purpose, a correct judgement that the storm and death are not evils, which no hog can have. The frightened passengers' fault is their judgement, not their possession of reason (Handbook 5). | The source's author judges it well (inferred); Epictetus's framing gives neutral
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Montaigne, in 'That the Taste of Good and Evil Things Depends in Large Part on the Opinion We Have of Them'
source_quote: was not in the least concerned
source_lesson: What good is knowledge if it causes us to lose the peace of mind and the calm we would enjoy without it, and leaves us in a condition worse than that of Pyrrho's hog?
source_verdict: To those near him who were most frightened, he pointed to a hog that was there and that was not in the least concerned, and sought to encourage them by its example.
stoic_judgement: not shown (the vignette's subject is a hog: "not in the least concerned" is a state, not a judgement, because a hog has no moral purpose to assent with)
stoic_reason: Good and evil lie only in moral purpose and the use of impressions (Discourses 1.1, 1.29). A wrong act is one 'done ... by a rational creature' (Arius 11a), so a hog's calm in the storm is neither acting well nor badly. R7 applies because no judgement about good or evil is at stake, and R1 because no judgement is shown. Its fearlessness only resembles courage and is not the virtue.

self: You value too lightly the things that you have, just because you have them, and overvalue things that are foreign, things that are absent, and things that don't belong to you.

self: You strike the athlete you are training with your staff after everyone present applauds his wrestling, saying, "If you had done it artfully they would not have applauded you."
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle two points. First, treating applause as proof of bad work is itself a hasty assent about an external: on the Stoic view applause is indifferent, not a sign of fault, so the third field (assent) may count this against him. Second, the blow is acceptable in his role only if it comes from calm correction and not anger (Handbook 20; Discourses 1.18), and the vignette does not say which. The source (Farnsworth, Seneca) praises the story without reservation, but under R9 that praise is not by itself a Stoic verdict.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Farnsworth, quoting Aelian
source_quote: an athlete he was training competed in wrestling and everyone who was present applauded
source_lesson: Mass popularity suggests a want of quality or integrity in whoever obtains it.
source_verdict: “You did it badly, and not as you should have,” he said. “You should have done better. If you had done it artfully they would not have applauded you.”
stoic_judgement: "If you had done it artfully they would not have applauded you."
stoic_reason: The trainer refuses to treat the crowd's applause, which is not up to him or his student, as the measure of good work. He judges the wrestling by the standard of the art, as Epictetus's singer should have done (Discourses 2.13; Handbook 19). In his role as trainer he corrects his student by that standard (R1, R6). The words show the judgement behind the correction, so per R5 we read it as acting well while making progress.

other: You see people make jokes about a man's bald head, his weak eyes, his thin legs, his height, and he asks how it is an insult to be told what is obvious.
self: When people make jokes about your bald head, your weak eyes, your thin legs, your height, you ask how it is an insult to be told what is obvious.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, speaking in the voice of the wise man who answers his mockers (On the Constancy of the Wise Man 16.3), quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: They make jokes about my bald head, my weak eyes, my thin legs, my height. How is it an insult to be told what is obvious?
source_lesson: That habit makes criticism from others easier to take.
source_verdict: That habit makes criticism from others easier to take.
stoic_judgement: he asks how it is an insult to be told what is obvious
stoic_reason: His question shows the judgement that mockery of his bald head, eyes, legs and height, which are body and not up to him, does him no harm. So he does not assent to the impression of being insulted (Handbook 20; Handbook 1; R1, R2 by contrast). Acting from a correct judgement about externals is acting well as one making progress (Discourses 4.8; R5), and the act is chiefly right use of impressions (R8).

other: You see an orator who knows he has written a good speech, has it committed to memory, and will deliver it well, still nervous because he wants to be praised by the audience.
self: You know you have written a good speech, have it committed to memory, and will deliver it well, yet you are still nervous because you want to be praised by the audience.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Epictetus, in Discourses 2.16.5
source_quote: When the orator knows that he has written a good speech, that he has it committed to memory, and that he will deliver it well, why is he still nervous?
source_reason: He wants to be praised by the audience.
source_lesson: About oratory he has been instructed; about praise and blame he has not been instructed.
source_verdict: We practice things that will win praise; we should practice the art of not needing it.
stoic_judgement: still nervous because he wants to be praised by the audience
stoic_reason: Like the citharoede of Discourses 2.13, he has done everything up to him well, yet stays anxious because he wants applause, which is not under his control. That is an assented passion from the judgement that an external is a good he must have, so it is acting badly even with no outward deed (R1, R2). It is not a first movement: the vignette gives a lasting motive, not an unwilled start (R3).

other: You see a man take an insult lightly, saying: "If I deserve this, there is no insult; it is justice. If I don't deserve it, let the one who does the injustice blush."
self: You take an insult lightly, saying: "If I deserve this, there is no insult; it is justice. If I don't deserve it, let the one who does the injustice blush."
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in On the Constancy of the Wise Man 16.3
source_quote: to take insults lightly, but merely someone of sense – one who might say: "Do I deserve these things that happen to me? If I deserve them, there is no insult; it is justice. If I don't deserve them, let the one who does the injustice blush."
source_reason: If I deserve them, there is no insult; it is justice. If I don't deserve them, let the one who does the injustice blush.
source_lesson: You need not be a sage to take insults lightly, but merely someone of sense
source_verdict: You need not be a sage to take insults lightly, but merely someone of sense
stoic_judgement: "If I deserve this, there is no insult; it is justice. If I don't deserve it, let the one who does the injustice blush."
stoic_reason: The vignette shows his judgement (R1). He does not assent to the impression that he has been harmed: an insult is only one's own judgement (Handbook 20), and if the other man is wrong, the one deceived is the one who suffers (Handbook 42). So he refuses the passion of anger (R2 inverted) and acts well as a person making progress (R5). His main virtue is restraint of anger and wounded vanity (R8), resting on a correct view of what is up to him.

other: You see an old gentleman, remembering how often cuckoldry gave him jokes about others, marry a wife found where women are available to anyone for money, and openly tell guests of it.
self: You, remembering how often cuckoldry gave you jokes about others, marry late in life a wife found where women are available to anyone for money, and openly tell your guests of it.
contested_note: Montaigne and Farnsworth praise the act as having 'an air of philosophy', and Seneca (Constancy 17) praises laughing at oneself to disarm ridicule. Epictetus's framing settles it only if the motive is aversion to mockery. If the man truly judged ridicule to be no harm, owning the jest could instead be acting well. Under R9, the source's praise is not by itself a Stoic verdict. | The source's author judges it well (stated); Epictetus's framing gives vice
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Montaigne, in Of Presumption (1580), quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: he protected himself by marrying a wife he found in a place where women are available to anyone for money ... there was nothing he talked about more often or more openly than this plan of his when entertaining guests in his home
source_reason: Remembering how often the subject of cuckoldry had given him material for stories and jokes about others
source_lesson: It curbed the private chattering of those who would mock him, and blunted the force of the insult.
source_verdict: The following example of a gentleman known to many has an air of philosophy about it, does it not?
stoic_judgement: remembering how often cuckoldry gave him jokes about others, marry a wife found where women are available to anyone for money, and openly tell guests of it
stoic_reason: Under R1 and R2, the vignette implies that he plans his marriage around escaping the mockery he once aimed at others. That treats his reputation, which is not up to us (Handbook 1), as a good he must secure. Like the singer who wants applause (Discourses 2.13), he is still subordinated to those who can mock him. He does not hold, as in Handbook 20, that only his own judgement can insult him. Making a jest of his household also falls short of the self-respect and propriety his role as a husband asks (R6).

other: You see a king of Macedonia, who has had water dumped on him while walking along the street, tell his attendants urging punishment, "He did not dump the water on me, but on the man he thought I was."
self: You are a king of Macedonia, and when someone dumps water on you as you walk along the street and your attendants say you should punish the man, you reply, "He did not dump the water on me, but on the man he thought I was."
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Montaigne, citing Plutarch and Diogenes Lærtius
source_quote: The king's attendants said that he should punish the man. "Ah, but he did not dump the water on me," the king replied, "but on the man he thought I was."
source_reason: he did not dump the water on me ... but on the man he thought I was.
source_lesson: if you receive an insult that is wrongful, you may consider it to have been directed at someone else – the person you were thought to be. It was a case of mistaken identity.
source_verdict: if you receive an insult that is wrongful, you may consider it to have been directed at someone else – the person you were thought to be. It was a case of mistaken identity.
stoic_judgement: tell his attendants urging punishment, "He did not dump the water on me, but on the man he thought I was."
stoic_reason: His words show he does not assent to the impression that he has been insulted (Handbook 20). He treats the offender as deceived about who he is (Handbook 42), so he declines the anger and punishment his attendants urge. This is acting from a correct judgement (R1, R2 in reverse, R5), and restraint of anger falls under temperance (R8).

other: You see a philosopher who is told that people speak ill of him reply, “Not at all. There is nothing in me of what they say.”
self: You are told that people speak ill of you, and you reply, “Not at all. There is nothing in me of what they say.”
contested_note: Epictetus's own advice for this exact case (Handbook 33: told that someone speaks ill of you, do not defend yourself but say 'he did not know my other faults') prefers humble non-defence to a claim of innocence. On that reading the reply's self-acquittal is not what Epictetus would counsel, though its freedom from disturbance is. Addison's paraphrase also makes the reply right only after one has checked whether the reproaches are true. Montaigne and Farnsworth present it as plainly well done.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Montaigne, relating anecdotes borrowed and condensed from Plutarch and Diogenes Lærtius, quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: When Socrates was told that people spoke ill of him, he said, “Not at all. There is nothing in me of what they say.”
source_lesson: if you receive an insult that is wrongful, you may consider it to have been directed at someone else – the person you were thought to be. It was a case of mistaken identity.
source_verdict: A last perspective: if you receive an insult that is wrongful, you may consider it to have been directed at someone else – the person you were thought to be. It was a case of mistaken identity.
stoic_judgement: "Not at all. There is nothing in me of what they say.": he treats the ill-speaking as aimed at a person he is not, so it does not touch what is his own.
stoic_reason: It is not the one who reviles who insults, but one's judgement that one is insulted (Handbook 20). His reply shows he does not count reputation, which is not up to us, as his good or evil. So he assents to no anger or distress, and he sees correctly what belongs to him (R1, R2). Under R5 this is acting well as one making progress.

other: You see a person who spends time extravagantly, as if it were free, now ill and clasping the knees of physicians as the danger of death draws nearer.
self: You spend time extravagantly, as if it were free, and now, ill, you clasp the knees of physicians as the danger of death draws nearer.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Ward Farnsworth, quoting Seneca (On the Shortness of Life 8.2)
source_quote: everyone spends it extravagantly, as if it were free. But see how these same people clasp the knees of physicians if they fall ill and the danger of death draws nearer; see how ready they are, if threatened with capital punishment, to spend all that they have to live longer\!
source_lesson: If we fail to grasp that time is more important than money, for example, we might compare the distress typically felt by those who are running out of each.
source_verdict: No one values time; everyone spends it extravagantly, as if it were free.
stoic_judgement: spends time extravagantly, as if it were free, now ... clasping the knees of physicians as the danger of death draws nearer
stoic_reason: The person first treats time and their own conduct as worthless. Then they cling in desperate supplication to others, who control what is not up to them, because they judge death the dreadful thing. This is an assented passion of fear (Handbook 5; Discourses 2.13), not a first movement (R2, not R3). Seeking a physician would be a fitting choice of a preferred indifferent (Discourses 2.10), but clasping his knees shows the craving and dread that make a man 'subordinate himself to others' (Discourses 1.4).

other: You see a man ask, of a robber and an adulterer, "This robber, this adulterer, shouldn't they have been destroyed?"
self: You ask, of a robber and an adulterer, "This robber, this adulterer, shouldn't they have been destroyed?"
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Epictetus, replying to an interlocutor who asks whether robbers and adulterers should be destroyed
source_quote: this robber, this adulterer
source_lesson: If you put it this way, you will see how inhumane your question is.
source_verdict: Not at all, but rather ask this: “This man who has been misled and deceived about the most important things, who has been blinded – not in his vision, the ability to distinguish white from black, but in his judgment, the ability to distinguish good from evil – shouldn’t we destroy him?”
stoic_judgement: "This robber, this adulterer, shouldn't they have been destroyed?"
stoic_reason: The question carries the judgement that wrongdoers are enemies who have harmed us and deserve destruction. Discourses 1.18 calls this judgement a mistake: the robber has already lost the greatest thing, a right moral purpose, so 'what ground is left for you to be angry at him?' Under R1 and R2, acting from this angry and inhumane judgement is acting badly; it fails kindness, the part of justice concerned with doing others good.

other: You see a spectator at the games Fortune is holding run from the theater as soon as the trinkets (honors, riches, influence) are brought in, knowing these small things come at a high price.
self: You run from the theater where Fortune is holding games as soon as you see the trinkets (honors, riches, influence) being brought in, because you know these small things come at a high price.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in an epistle (Epistles 74.7), quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: the wise run from the theater as soon as they see the trinkets being brought in
source_reason: They know that these small things come at a high price.
source_lesson: Again, Seneca had a knack for visual comparisons to bring a point to life – here, the cost of things that usually seem free.
source_verdict: So it is that the wise run from the theater as soon as they see the trinkets being brought in. They know that these small things come at a high price.
stoic_judgement: knowing these small things come at a high price
stoic_reason: He judges honors, riches and influence, which are not up to us (Handbook 1), to be small things not worth his freedom, so he refuses to crave them. This is the man making progress of Discourses 1.4, who knows that whoever craves what is not under his control 'can be neither faithful nor free.' The act proceeds from a correct judgement (R1, R5), and its main virtue is restraint of appetite for externals (R8).

other: You see a learned, pious scientist watch a criminal dragged to execution and ask himself, "Who knows whether this man is not less culpable than me?"
self: You watch a criminal dragged to execution and ask yourself, "Who knows whether this man is not less culpable than me?"
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Samuel Johnson, citing Boerhaave
source_quote: he never saw a criminal dragged to execution without asking himself, "Who knows whether this man is not less culpable than me?"
source_reason: For, who can congratulate himself upon a life passed without some act more mischievous to the peace or prosperity of others, than the theft of a piece of money?
source_lesson: Johnson's version of self-prosecution:
source_verdict: Seneca turned the point into a method: prosecution of the self by the self.
stoic_judgement: ask himself, "Who knows whether this man is not less culpable than me?"
stoic_reason: His question shows the judgement he acts from. He will not condemn the criminal without knowing the judgement behind his acts (R1; Handbook 45, Discourses 4.8), and he turns his attention from the external spectacle to his own moral purpose, the mark of one making progress (Discourses 1.4). So he is acting well as a person making progress (R5). The virtue most at stake is wisdom: seeing what is truly his own concern and judging soundly (R8).

other: You see a man in Rome saying, "I'm not ambitious, but there's no other way to live in Rome; I'm not extravagant, but the city requires a significant outlay; it's not my fault I'm irritable, that's just my youth."
self: You say, "I'm not ambitious, but there's no other way to live in Rome; I'm not extravagant, but the city requires a significant outlay; it's not my fault I'm irritable, that's just my youth."
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca (Epistles 50.3–4), quoted by the author after his setup about self-serving excuses
source_quote: None of us recognizes that we ourselves are greedy or covetous. But while the blind at least ask for a guide, we wander around without one, saying "I'm not ambitious, but there's no other way to live in Rome. I'm not extravagant, but the city itself requires a significant outlay. It's not my fault that I'm irritable, that I haven't yet decided on a settled way of life – that's just my youth."
source_reason: there's no other way to live in Rome... the city itself requires a significant outlay... that's just my youth
source_lesson: Why do we fool ourselves? Our evil is not on the outside, it is within us, it is seated in our vitals – and it is that much harder to attain health when we do not know we are sick.
source_verdict: Why do we fool ourselves? Our evil is not on the outside, it is within us, it is seated in our vitals – and it is that much harder to attain health when we do not know we are sick.
stoic_judgement: "I'm not ambitious, but there's no other way to live in Rome; I'm not extravagant, but the city requires a significant outlay; it's not my fault I'm irritable, that's just my youth."
stoic_reason: His words show the judgement he acts from: that his ambition, spending and irritability are caused by things not up to him (the city, his age). But desire, aversion and choice are 'our own doing' (Handbook 1), and a wrong act has 'no other cause than the decision of our will' (Discourses 1.11). The false judgement about what is up to him is acting badly (R1, R2), and calling his irritability 'not my fault' assents to the passion instead of treating it as a first movement (R3 does not apply).

other: You see a man saying of another, "That man has already injured me, but I have not yet injured him."
self: You say of another man, "That man has already injured me, but I have not yet injured him."
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in On Anger (3.26.5)
source_quote: "That man has already injured me, but I have not yet injured him."
source_lesson: Do not count only this hour or this day; consider the whole character of your mind. Even if you have done no evil, you are capable of it.
source_verdict: But perhaps you have already harmed, perhaps you will someday harm, someone else.
stoic_judgement: "That man has already injured me, but I have not yet injured him."
stoic_reason: He assents to the impression that another has injured him, though by Epictetus no one can harm what is truly his, and 'it is your judgement that these men are insulting you' (Handbook 20; Discourses 1.18). This is the judgement from which anger springs, so it counts as acting badly even with no outward deed (R1, R2). His complacent sense of his own innocence also fails to see the capacity for fault in himself, which is the error Seneca names (R8).

other: You see a wise man, surprised by a loud noise from the sky, turn pale and tense, while his judgment remains sound and intact and he does not give consent to his fear.
self: You, surprised by a loud noise from the sky, turn pale and tense, while your judgment remains sound and intact and you do not give consent to your fear.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Montaigne, in Of Constancy, describing the Stoic position (quoted by Farnsworth)
source_quote: it is in his nature to react to a loud noise from the sky or from a collapsing building (for example) by turning pale and tense
source_lesson: First, some involuntary reactions can't be helped.
source_verdict: provided his judgment remains sound and intact, that the seat of his reason does not suffer any damage or change, and that he does not give consent to his fear and pain
stoic_judgement: surprised by a loud noise from the sky, turn pale and tense, while his judgment remains sound and intact and he does not give consent to his fear
stoic_reason: The paling and tensing is one of the 'swift and unconsidered motions which forestall the action of the intellect' (fragment 9), so it is a first movement and no fault (R3). The vignette says he does not assent, so no passion forms (R2 does not apply). The positive evidence for neither-good-nor-bad is the involuntary reaction itself (R7), and no further act from a correct judgement is shown to praise (R1).

other: You see two philosophers going out into public: one weeps every time, seeing everything we do as wretchedness; the other laughs, seeing everything we do as absurdity.
self: You go out into public and laugh, seeing everything we do as absurdity, while another philosopher weeps every time he goes out, seeing everything we do as wretchedness.
contested_note: Two people are shown (the weeper and the laugher) and the question asks about "the person"; the labeller judged the first (Claude, two-person scan)
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in On Tranquility of Mind 15.2, quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: For the latter, every time he went out into public, used to weep; the former used to laugh.
source_reason: One saw everything we do as wretchedness, the other as absurdity.
source_lesson: Things should be made light of, and taken more easily: it is more civilized to laugh at life than to bewail it.
source_verdict: we should imitate Democritus rather than Heraclitus. ... Things should be made light of, and taken more easily: it is more civilized to laugh at life than to bewail it.
stoic_judgement: one weeps every time, seeing everything we do as wretchedness
stoic_reason: The vignette starts with two people, so I judge the first named, the weeper. His weeping is not a first movement (R3): it happens 'every time' and comes from a settled judgement that everything people do is wretched. That is grief assented to about things not up to him, since other people's acts are not his to control (Handbook 16, 'groan ... in the centre of your being'; R2). Tears alone would not decide it, but this judgement does (R4), so it is acting badly, a failure in the use of impressions.

other: You see a philosopher, taunted with the fact that his mother was a barbarian, being a Thracian, answer that even the mother of the gods came from Mount Ida.
self: You, taunted with the fact that your mother was a barbarian, being a Thracian, answer that even the mother of the gods came from Mount Ida.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in On the Constancy of the Wise Man 18.6, quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: Antisthenes was taunted with the fact that his mother was a barbarian, being a Thracian; he answered that even the mother of the gods came from Mount Ida \[in Crete\].
source_lesson: What matters is not how offense is given but how it is received.
source_verdict: Let us look at the examples of those whose forbearance we praise
stoic_judgement: taunted with the fact that his mother was a barbarian, being a Thracian, answer that even the mother of the gods came from Mount Ida
stoic_reason: His mild, joking reply treats his mother's foreign birth as no disgrace and the taunt as no injury. By Handbook 20, the insult lies only in one's own judgement, so he declines to assent to the impression that he has been insulted, and acts from a correct judgement (R1, R2 by contrast, R5). Most at stake is the restraint of anger under abuse, with seeing what is and is not up to him alongside it (R8).

other: You see a man telling himself that this acquaintance did not give him a civil greeting, that one did not embrace him as he kissed him, another did not invite him to dinner, another tried to avoid seeing him.
self: You tell yourself that this acquaintance did not give you a civil greeting, that one did not embrace you as you kissed him, another did not invite you to dinner, another tried to avoid seeing you.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in On Anger
source_quote: "This man did not give me a civil greeting; that one did not embrace me as I kissed him; that one broke off the conversation abruptly; that one did not invite me to dinner; that one tried to avoid seeing me."
source_lesson: But we need to be straightforward and to see things in their best light.
source_verdict: Suspicion and surmise – those deceptive provocations – ought to be banished from the mind.
stoic_judgement: telling himself that this acquaintance did not give him a civil greeting, that one did not embrace him as he kissed him, another did not invite him to dinner, another tried to avoid seeing him
stoic_reason: He is not flinching at a sudden slight (R3). He is deliberately rehearsing a list of others' acts, which are not up to him, as grounds for offence. That is assenting to the impression 'I have been insulted' (Handbook 20) and rashly judging others' conduct (Discourses 3.2, the third field), so per R1-R2 it is acting badly.

other: You see a judge quietly wiping out households that are a plague on the state, along with wives and children, with no gnashing of the teeth, for deterrence and the good of the community.
self: You quietly wipe out households that are a plague on the state, along with wives and children, with no gnashing of the teeth, for deterrence and the good of the community.
contested_note: Seneca (On Anger 1.19), a Stoic, praises the act: dispassionate, deterrent, for the state's good. Epictetus has no ruling on punishing whole families. His model judge sentences 'as a curator and guardian' of the offender's own good (fragment 22), and the Stoic account of justice as fair dealing and apportioning what is due counts against killing family members who are not shown to be guilty. His framing settles the spirit of the act (no anger) but not its substance (whether killing the innocent can be due). Our label differs from the everyday one, which would call it vice. | From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as vice: The judge is free of the passion of anger (R2, R4), and he acts from the judgement that the community's good is served. But wiping out wives and children whom the vignette does not show to be guilty treats people as tools of deterrence. That is not the 'curator and guardian' role a judge holds toward the person he sentences, and it is not justice as 'the apportioning of what is due' (R6, R8). An act 'done contrary to correct reason' is an error, however calmly it is done (R1, Arius 11a).
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in a passage from On Anger quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: If need be, reason silently, quietly wipes out whole families root and branch, and households that are a plague on the state it destroys along with wives and children; it tears down their very houses, levelling them to the ground, and exterminates the names of the enemies of liberty. All this it will do, but with no gnashing of the teeth, no violent shaking of the head
source_reason: concerned with deterrence and rehabilitation – with the good of the community and the good of the offender, very broadly understood – rather than with retribution
source_lesson: The Stoic disposition affects the spirit in which justice is administered and in which the good is pursued, but it does not imply mild views about the substance of those things or timidity in securing them.
source_verdict: nothing that would be unseemly for a judge, whose countenance should at no time be more calm and unmoved than when delivering a weighty sentence
stoic_judgement: with no gnashing of the teeth, for deterrence and the good of the community
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judge acting from reason and not from anger. He does not judge the offenders' wrongs to be an insult to himself (Handbook 20; Discourses 1.18), and he acts in his role for the community's good (R1, R2, R6), which is the spirit Seneca praises. But justice is 'the apportioning of what is due', and the vignette does not show that the wives and children have done anything for which this is due. So the act is labelled virtue (justice) only on the strength of the judge's shown judgement, and is marked contested (R9).

other: You see a judge, calm and unmoved, openly kill offenders as examples of wickedness slow to yield, not so much that they may be destroyed as that their destruction may deter others.
self: You, as a judge, calm and unmoved, openly kill offenders as examples of wickedness slow to yield, not so much that they may be destroyed as that their destruction may deter others.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, quoting Plato (Laws 11.934), in On Anger 1.19.7
source_quote: he will openly kill those whom he wishes to have serve as examples of the wickedness that is slow to yield ... how free he ought to be from all emotion when he proceeds to deal with a matter that requires the utmost caution – the use of power over life and death
source_reason: not so much that they themselves may be destroyed as that their destruction may deter others
source_lesson: The Stoic judge, in something like the spirit of the dispassionate physician, is concerned with deterrence and rehabilitation – with the good of the community and the good of the offender, very broadly understood – rather than with retribution.
source_verdict: you see how free he ought to be from all emotion when he proceeds to deal with a matter that requires the utmost caution – the use of power over life and death
stoic_judgement: calm and unmoved ... not so much that they may be destroyed as that their destruction may deter others
stoic_reason: The vignette shows the judgement behind the act (R1). The judge sentences without anger, for the future good of the community, not from the passion of revenge. Epictetus treats anger at wrongdoers as a faulty judgement (Discourses 1.18; R2). Acting from reason in the role of judge is what that role asks (R6), so by our convention this is acting well (R5). Justice is primary, as the apportioning of what is due. Temperance (no anger) and wisdom (weighing the future, not the past) also fit (R8).

other: You see a group of philosophers, probably other Stoics, deny that the wise man will ever grieve.

contested_note: Seneca (Consolation to Polybius 18.5-6) calls this wisdom 'harsh rather than brave' and proud. He holds that reason should only trim excessive grief, not remove it. Epictetus and the orthodox Stoics (DL 7.116; Handbook 16) hold that the wise man has no passions, though he may sympathize in words and shed involuntary tears. The dispute may be partly verbal: Seneca's permitted grief resembles first movements and involuntary tears (Letters 99.19). If it is not verbal, the source's verdict differs from Epictetus's (R9). | The source's author judges it badly (stated); Epictetus's framing gives virtue
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in the Consolation to Polybius, quoted by Farnsworth

source_verdict: I well know that there are those whose wisdom is harsh rather than brave, who deny that the wise man will ever grieve. But these people, it seems to me, can never have run into this sort of misfortune; if they had, Fortune would have knocked their proud philosophy out of them and forced them to admit the truth even against their will.
stoic_judgement: deny that the wise man will ever grieve
stoic_reason: The judgement they assent to is Epictetus's own: grief is the judgement that a loss is an evil, and the excellent man does not 'groan in the centre of his being' (Handbook 16, 5). Correct assent is acting well in the third field (Discourses 3.2), so it is labelled virtue under R1 and R5. The vignette shows no harshness toward a mourner and no denial of first movements or tears (R3, R4).

other: You see the defenders of a besieged city, men who know that as long as the path to death lies open the blockade is not complete, kill themselves rather than surrender.
self: You and your fellow defenders of a besieged city, knowing that as long as the path to death lies open the blockade is not complete, kill yourselves rather than surrender.
contested_note: Epictetus allows leaving life when it can no longer be lived fittingly (the 'open door'), and he holds that death is not an evil. But he also holds that captivity of the body, which is not up to us, is no evil to the moral purpose. If the defenders die because they judge enslavement or defeat itself an evil, they act from a false judgement about externals. If they die so as not to be made to act shamefully, and to keep faith with their city, they act well. The vignette's 'liberty' could mean either, so his framing does not fully settle it. Seneca (Ep. 66.13), quoted approvingly by Farnsworth, calls their souls great.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca (Epistles 66.13), quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: men who breathe their last in the arms of liberty
source_reason: men who know that, as long as the path to death lies open, the blockade is not complete
source_lesson: The Stoic sees honor in fighting to the death for a good cause, and takes a perspective broad enough to identify virtue on both sides of a conflict.
source_verdict: Great is Scipio, who lays siege to Numantia, and constrains and compels the hands of an enemy, whom he could not conquer, to resort to their own destruction. Great also are the souls of the defenders – men who know that, as long as the path to death lies open, the blockade is not complete, men who breathe their last in the arms of liberty.
stoic_judgement: men who know that as long as the path to death lies open the blockade is not complete
stoic_reason: The defenders act from the judgement that death is not dreadful (Handbook 5) and that their freedom stays up to them while the way out is open. They refuse to let the besieger's power over their bodies decide their choice, which is endurance in what is to be feared or endured (R1, R2 by contrast, R8: courage). Seneca's praise is not by itself the verdict (R9). The label rests on Epictetus's open-door teaching, which is not quoted in Part 1, together with Handbook 5.

That is what Handbook 20 asks: it is our judgement, not the striker, that insults us. Their wariness is rational caution, a good feeling (DL 7.116), not the passion of fear or anger. So this is acting well from a correct judgement (R1, R2, R4, R5), chiefly as restraint of anger (R8).

stoic_judgement: he bears a mind smooth and cheerful on all occasions, far remote from grief and above all from fear

A steady, cheerful mind amid them shows he does not assent to the judgement that externals are evils to be grieved or feared (Handbook 5, Discourses 2.13; R2 read in reverse). His cheerfulness is rational joy, a good feeling, not a passion (R4, DL 7.116), so he is acting well as a person making progress (R5). Freedom from fear is the main virtue at stake (R8).

stoic_reason: He held his friends as things not up to him, on loan and mortal, and he does not judge their loss an evil. What he keeps is his remembrance and gratitude for the time he had, so his sweetness in memory is rational joy, a good feeling, not a passion. That is acting well from a correct judgement about externals (R1, R4, R5; Handbook 1, 5; Discourses 1.11).

source_reason: he knew that better buildings would rise in place of those that had burned

stoic_judgement: no friend to the city's happiness, saying that fires at Rome trouble him for one reason only: he knows better buildings will rise in place of those that burned
stoic_reason: He is distressed not by the city's loss but by its coming good. That is grief at another's good fortune, the envy that Handbook 19 traces to judging externals (a city's prosperity) to be good or evil. It is an assented passion, so acting badly even with no outward deed (R1, R2). It is not the humble calm about outcomes that the chapter teaches: he foresees the rebuilding and resents it.

other: You see a man throw a stone at his dog but miss and hit his stepmother. "Not so bad!" he says.

contested_note: The source's verdict differs from Epictetus's. Plutarch, a Platonist and not a Stoic, and Farnsworth after him hold the man up as a comic model of turning a misfortune to good: 'This then we should practice.' Under R9 a source's praise is not a Stoic verdict. stoic_reason: His words treat an injury to his stepmother as welcome. That is a judgement against what his role toward a family member asks (R6, Handbook 30) and a failure of kindness (R1). The throw at the dog also suggests an assented passion, anger, though its motive is not stated (R2, R1). Calling an unwanted outcome 'not so bad' would be the Stoic reframing of what is not up to us. But here the outcome was his own act, and he is glad because the victim is someone he dislikes, so the reframing does not excuse it.

Reputation is not up to us (Handbook 1), and refusing to let the wish for it govern his speech is a correct judgement about his own moral purpose. By R1 and R5 this is acting well, as a person making progress; by R8 his refusal of cowardice is nearest to courage, with honesty (justice) also at stake.

other: You see a man who looks every day at the sun, the moon, the stars, the whole world and the sea ask, "So when will I see Athens again, and the Acropolis?"

source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Epictetus, addressing someone he calls a “wretch” (Discourses 2.16.32)
source_quote: “So when will I see Athens again, and the Acropolis?”
source_lesson: They regard life as lived in the mind more than at any physical site, and view the appetite for new locations as arising from the same source as the appetite for other new things: our sensibilities are too dull to appreciate what is around us already.
source_verdict: Wretch, isn’t it enough for you, what you look at every day?
stoic_judgement: "So when will I see Athens again, and the Acropolis?", asked by a man who looks every day at the sun, the moon, the stars, the whole world and the sea
stoic_reason: Read as Epictetus reads it, the man treats seeing Athens, an external not up to him, as a good he lacks. His discontent with what is before him every day is a desire for things outside his control, an assented craving (R2, Discourses 2.13). It is not a mere wish for a preferred indifferent, so it counts as acting badly. The vice is chiefly against temperance, the restraint of appetite (here for novelty and place), and also against wisdom about what is up to us (R8).

other: You see a man threatened with chains, prison and beheading refuse to reveal his secrets, saying, 'You can chain my leg, but Zeus himself can't overcome my will.'
self: You are threatened with chains, prison and beheading and refuse to reveal your secrets, saying, 'You can chain my leg, but Zeus himself can't overcome my will.'
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Epictetus
source_quote: I must die; so must I also die regretting something? I must be put in chains; must I also be wailing about something? I must be banished; does anyone prevent me from leaving with a smile, cheerful and easy-going? "Reveal your secrets." I don't speak; this much is up to me. "Then I will put you in chains." Man, what are you saying? Me? You can chain my leg, but Zeus himself can't overcome my will. "I'll throw you in prison." My poor body, you mean. "I'll cut your head off." When did I ever tell you that my neck was the only one that could not be severed? These are the things philosophers should think about, should write down daily, should use as exercise.
source_lesson: These are the things philosophers should think about, should write down daily, should use as exercise.
source_verdict: These are the things philosophers should think about, should write down daily, should use as exercise.
stoic_judgement: 'You can chain my leg, but Zeus himself can't overcome my will.'
stoic_reason: He judges that chains, prison and death touch only his body, which is not up to him, while his will (moral purpose) is his own and cannot be compelled. So he does not assent to the passion of fear (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.1, 1.18; R1, R2). Steady endurance under threat, acted on from correct judgement, is acting well as one making progress (R5), nearest to courage (R8).

other: You see a man criticizing a fellow very candidly, saying what is true without minding whether the fellow can stand the truth.
self: You criticize a fellow very candidly, saying what is true without minding whether the fellow can stand the truth.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)

source_quote: You criticized that one fellow more candidly than you should have
source_lesson: From here on, watch out – not so much that what you’re saying is true, but that the person you’re talking to can stand the truth.
source_verdict: as a result you didn’t correct him, you just offended him
stoic_judgement: saying what is true without minding whether the fellow can stand the truth
stoic_reason: The second field asks that we act 'upon good reasons, and not carelessly' (Discourses 3.2). He treats saying the truth as enough and is careless whether it can help the man, so he omits the appropriate act of correcting him in a way he can bear (Arius 11a). By R1 that careless judgement is acting badly. It is a failure of wisdom (circumspection) and of justice as kindness, 'a knowledge which is disposed to do good' (R8).

other: You see a wise man give a hand to a shipwrecked man, gladly and with an elevated spirit, bringing relief to his tears but not adding his own.
self: You give a hand to a shipwrecked man, gladly and with an elevated spirit, bringing relief to his tears but not adding your own.
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in On Mercy, quoted by Farnsworth in The Practicing Stoic
source_quote: All else that those who feel pity are inclined do, he will do gladly and with an elevated spirit; he will bring relief to another's tears, but will not add his own. To the shipwrecked man he will give a hand; he will give shelter to the exile, and charity to those in need.
source_reason: Sorrow is not suited to seeing things accurately, to understanding how to get things done, to avoiding dangers, or to knowing what is just. So the wise man will not indulge in pity, because there cannot be pity without mental suffering.
source_lesson: Seneca's position was that good Stoics will *do* all that would be done by anyone who feels pity for others, but that they will not feel the pity themselves; pity is considered a form of distress that serves no purpose and impairs good judgment.
source_verdict: So the wise man will not indulge in pity, because there cannot be pity without mental suffering. All else that those who feel pity are inclined do, he will do gladly and with an elevated spirit; he will bring relief to another's tears, but will not add his own.
stoic_judgement: gladly and with an elevated spirit, bringing relief to his tears but not adding his own
stoic_reason: He helps the man as Handbook 16 asks, giving the outward help and sympathy without groaning 'in the centre of his being'. So he does not judge the man's loss an evil (R4). His glad, elevated spirit is a good feeling acted on with reason, 'both affectionate and reasonable' (Discourses 1.11), not a passion (R2, R4). That is an act from correct judgement (R1), labelled virtue by convention (R5), and its nearest virtue is kindness, a part of justice (R8).

other: You see a sad man pack his trunk, embrace his friends, and embark on the sea for Naples, dreaming that there he can be intoxicated with beauty and lose his sadness.

source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Emerson, in Self-Reliance, quoted by Farnsworth
source_quote: I pack my trunk, embrace my friends, embark on the sea, and at last wake up in Naples

source_lesson: We owe to our first journeys the discovery that place is nothing.
source_verdict: I affect to be intoxicated with sights and suggestions, but I am not intoxicated.
stoic_judgement: dreaming that there he can be intoxicated with beauty and lose his sadness
stoic_reason: He acts from the judgement that an external thing (a place, its sights) can remove a disturbance that comes from his own judgements (Handbook 5). He seeks the good in what is not up to him rather than in his moral purpose (Discourses 1.29), so by Discourses 4.8 his act proceeds from a bad judgement and is badly done (R1, R2). Packing, travelling and embracing friends are not the fault in themselves; travel is an indifferent.

other: You see a young man walking by himself who, when asked what he is doing there alone, says, “I am conversing with myself.”

contested_note: The source's verdict differs from Epictetus's framing (R9). Crates, relayed by Seneca, says the young man converses 'with a bad man': an ignorant person alone plans badly and feeds his desires. That rests on the school view that every non-sage is bad, which Epictetus does not use to judge people making progress (R5). Talking with oneself could be the self-examination of the third field, the work of progress (*Discourses* 1.4), or the rehearsal of passions. The vignette does not say which. | From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as virtue: Epictetus approves of being able to converse with oneself in solitude (Discourses 3.13, where Zeus, alone, converses with himself), and turning one's attention to one's own moral purpose is the mark of progress (Discourses 1.4, R5). But under R1 (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 45), until we know the judgement he acts from we can neither praise nor blame, so this verdict is tentative and the row should be rewritten or flagged. | The source's author judges it badly (stated); Epictetus's framing gives neutral
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter (Epistles 10.1–2), relaying what 'they say' about Crates
source_quote: a young man walking by himself ... “I am conversing with myself,” he said
source_lesson: No ignorant person should be left alone. That is when they make bad plans and create future troubles, either for others or for themselves; it’s when they organize their ignominious desires.
source_verdict: Watch out, I beg of you, and listen carefully: you are conversing with a bad man.
stoic_judgement: not shown
stoic_reason: The vignette shows only an outward act: walking alone and 'conversing with myself'. It does not show what he talks over or what he treats as good or evil. By R1 (*Discourses* 4.8, *Handbook* 45), until we learn the judgement behind the act we may neither praise nor blame it. The label is therefore provisional: R1 asks for a rewrite, and R7 says an unknown judgement is not truly `neutral`.

other: You see a philosopher, discoursing about good and evil according to all the rules, thrown off the track when there is a loud noise or someone there laughs at him.

source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)

source_verdict: Philosopher, where are those things you were just talking about?
stoic_judgement: thrown off the track when there is a loud noise or someone there laughs at him
stoic_reason: Being derailed by someone's laughter shows assent to the impression that ridicule, which is not up to him, is an evil or an insult (Handbook 20; Discourses 2.13, the singer who wants applause). His words about good and evil are not put into practice (Discourses 1.4), so this is an assented passion, acting badly (R2). Losing the whole discourse goes beyond the momentary blench that fragment 9 excuses (R3), so it is not neutral (R7).

other: You see a student, receiving instruction in philosophical principles with a certain style and vividness of presentation, become captivated by the style and remain stuck there instead of progressing.

source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students, quoted by Ward Farnsworth
source_quote: some students become captivated by these things and remain stuck there – one a captive of style, another of syllogisms, another of ambiguities, another in some other roadside inn of the same kind
source_lesson: The Stoics thus warn against the risk of being beguiled by verbal formulations.
source_verdict: there they remain and waste away, as if among the Sirens
stoic_judgement: become captivated by the style and remain stuck there instead of progressing
stoic_reason: Under R1 and R2, the student is not judged for meeting a vivid style, but for staying with it. Remaining captivated shows assent to the impression that the style is worth having for itself. Instruction is only material for purifying the moral purpose, and he treats this roadside inn as the destination. That is a failure of progress in the sense of Discourses 1.4, a misuse of impressions, and so acting badly. It is not a mere first movement (R3), because the captivation persists and replaces progress.

source_quote: think that whatever *they* can't do, can't be done; who say that we are always talking of things greater than human nature can bear
source_reason: we are always talking of things greater than human nature can bear
source_lesson: Our lack of confidence is not the result of difficulty. The difficulty comes from our lack of confidence.
source_verdict: But how much more favorable is my own estimation of them\! They too can do these things, but they don't want to.
stoic_judgement: thinks that whatever they can't do can't be done, saying that we are always talking of things greater than human nature can bear
stoic_reason: Under R1, the vignette shows the judgement itself: a rash assent that right use of impressions and choice, which Epictetus says are 'under our control' (Handbook 1), lie beyond human nature. That is an error in the third field, assent, and it releases the person from the work of progress (Discourses 1.4). Handbook 42 and 52 say a sincere wrong judgement is still acting badly, so this is vice.

other: You see someone, approached by a grieving friend after a thousand such friends, sympathize with kindness and warmth but not go through mourning of their own, having seen it all too many times for that.

source_quote: In the best doctor of that sort we would find kindness, warmth, and compassion. There would be feeling. But emotion would be unlikely. You would sympathize but you would not go through mourning of your own.

source_lesson: But the result of this thought experiment, if accepted, is a state of mind about the same as what the Stoics seek.
source_verdict: I would take the second, but at any rate see no basis for admiring the first one more. The second one is the Stoic.
stoic_judgement: sympathize with kindness and warmth but not go through mourning of their own, having seen it all too many times for that
stoic_reason: Under Handbook 16 the comforter acts well: they sympathize outwardly but do not groan in the centre of their being, so they are not carried away by the impression that the friend is in the midst of external ills. Their kindness and warmth are affection joined with reason (Discourses 1.11; R4), which counts as acting well for a person making progress (R5).

other: You see a philosopher who has lost his wife and children when his country was sacked emerge calmly and say, "I have all my goods with me."
self: You lose your wife and children when your country is sacked, yet emerge calmly and say, "I have all my goods with me."
source: Ward Farnsworth, The Practicing Stoic (2018)
speaker: Ward Farnsworth, recounting the anecdote about Stilpo as Seneca's example of the Stoic wise man
source_quote: he loses his wife and children when his country is sacked, yet emerges calmly and says "I have all my goods with me."
source_reason: "I have all my goods with me."
